0.title: The Acts of the Apostles
0.overview:
Acts is not primarily a history of the early church — it is the history of the risen Christ continuing his work through the Spirit he promised and poured out. Luke begins with a deliberate hinge: the “former book” (his Gospel) recorded all that Jesus “began to do and to teach.” The operative word is began. What follows in Acts is what Jesus continued — not in the flesh now, but in the power of the Spirit, through the mouths and feet and wounds of his witnesses.

Luke wrote for Theophilus (“lover of God”), likely a Roman official being catechised in the faith. But the scope of the narrative exceeds any single reader. Luke traces the gospel’s movement along the spine of the Roman Empire — Jerusalem to Rome, Jewish synagogue to Gentile household, from a frightened upper room to Caesar’s capital. This is not accident; it is Providence. The same God who told Abraham “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” is the God who compels a tentmaker from Tarsus to stand in the Areopagus and announce that the Unknown God has a name.

The Holy Spirit is the true protagonist of Acts. He falls at Pentecost like a sovereign flame. He speaks through Philip on a desert road. He stops Paul from entering Asia. He binds Paul to go to Jerusalem though chains await. He is not a vague presence but a Person with a will — the third Person of the Trinity, sent by the risen Son at the command of the Father, to accomplish the Father’s eternal purpose: a people for his name drawn from every tongue and tribe and nation.

Reformed readers will find in Acts not an argument for the faith but something far more bracing: the sovereignty of God in mission. The gates of hell do not hold. Persecution only scatters the seed further. Imprisonment opens courts to preach. Shipwreck lands an apostle on the right island. Nothing is accidental; everything is appointed. The book ends with Paul in Rome, under house arrest, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” The final word is unhindered. The empire could chain the man but not the Word.

Read Acts with your eyes open to the God who is always working — in the upper room, in the council chambers, in the storm, in the jail at midnight. He is the same God today.

1.title: The Promise and the Wait
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, <sup>2</sup>until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. <sup>3</sup>He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. <sup>4</sup>And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me; <sup>5</sup>for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” <sup>6</sup>So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” <sup>7</sup>He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. <sup>8</sup>But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” <sup>9</sup>And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. <sup>10</sup>And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes, <sup>11</sup>and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” <sup>12</sup>Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. <sup>13</sup>And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James. <sup>14</sup>All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. <sup>15</sup>In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about one hundred and twenty) and said, <sup>16</sup>“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. <sup>17</sup>For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.” <sup>18</sup>(Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. <sup>19</sup>And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.) <sup>20</sup>“For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it’; and ‘Let another take his office.’ <sup>21</sup>So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, <sup>22</sup>beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us—one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.” <sup>23</sup>And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. <sup>24</sup>And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen <sup>25</sup>to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.” <sup>26</sup>And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
1.overview:
After the resurrection, Jesus spent forty days with his disciples — not hiding, not ascending immediately, but teaching. Teaching about the kingdom of God. There is something deliberate about those forty days. The same God who spent forty years preparing Israel in the wilderness, forty days preparing Moses on the mountain, forty days testing his Son in the desert, now spends forty days confirming to his apostles that the one who died is the one who lives — and that the one who lives will send what the Father promised. The disciples’ question — “will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” — is not stupid. It is premature. God’s timetable is always larger than ours.

The ascension is not absence — it is exaltation. The cloud that receives Jesus is the cloud of divine glory, the Shekinah, the same cloud that led Israel through the wilderness and filled the tabernacle and settled on Sinai. He goes up not to disappear but to reign. And the two men in white robes say what angels always say when humans stare too long at the sky: why do you stand looking into heaven? There is work to do. There is a promise to wait for. There is a world to witness to. The wait in the upper room is not passivity; it is obedience — and it is prayer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Risen Lord Sends His Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Acts opens not with a new beginning but with a continuation. Luke's second volume picks up exactly where his first left off: with the risen Jesus, present among his disciples, teaching them about the kingdom of God. The forty days between resurrection and ascension are not a footnote — they are the foundation of everything that follows. The disciples who will turn the world upside down do so not on the basis of a memory but on the basis of a living encounter with the risen Lord who has conquered death and now commissions his church from the throne of all authority.

The command to wait is itself an act of grace. Jesus knows his disciples are not yet capable of the mission he is giving them. They need the Spirit — not merely as a helper, but as the very power of God taking up residence within them. And the promise they receive is astonishing in its scope: 'you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.' These eleven frightened men, standing on a Galilean hillside watching their Lord disappear into a cloud, are being told that their testimony will reach the ends of the world. It did.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascension and the Reign of Christ

The ascension is not the absence of Jesus but the exaltation of Jesus. He who died and rose now reigns at the right hand of the Father (Psalm 110:1), exercising all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). The church does not act in the absence of its king; it acts under the authority of its enthroned king. The cloud that received him is the Shekinah glory — he enters the presence of the Father as conqueror, not refugee. Reformed theology insists that the ascension is essential to the gospel: without it, Christ does not send the Spirit (John 16:7), does not intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25), and does not prepare a place for us (John 14:2).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The disciples received the promise of the Spirit and were told to wait — not in despair but in expectancy. The ascension was not abandonment but commissioning. Now: The church in every generation lives in the same posture: between the ascension and the return, empowered by the same Spirit, bearing the same witness, awaiting the same Lord who will come in the same way he departed.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's deliberate hinge between his two volumes. The Gospel records what Jesus began to do and teach — Acts records what he continues to do and teach through his Spirit in his church. The word 'began' (ērxato) is not incidental; it frames the entire book of Acts as the ongoing ministry of the risen and ascended Christ. The church's mission is not a human project inspired by a good man's example; it is the continued action of the living Lord through human instruments.

verseByVerse.quote: He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, "you heard from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Many proofs' — the resurrection is not a matter of faith detached from evidence but of faith grounded in evidence: multiple appearances, over forty days, to groups of witnesses whose testimony overlapped and confirmed each other. The content of those forty days is striking: Jesus spoke 'about the kingdom of God' — the same subject that opened his public ministry (Mark 1:15). The kingdom he proclaimed has arrived in his resurrection; now he prepares his disciples to proclaim it to the world. The command to wait is not weakness but wisdom: they need the Promise before the mission.

verseByVerse.quote: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast John the Baptist himself had drawn (Luke 3:16) is now fulfilled in promise: the Spirit-baptism of Pentecost is imminent. John's water baptism was preparatory and symbolic; the Spirit's baptism will be the reality it pointed toward — actual immersion in the divine life, actual empowerment for mission. 'Not many days from now' — ten days, in fact. The disciples are not waiting indefinitely; they are waiting for a specific, promised, certain gift that is almost at the door.

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had come together, they asked him, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" He said to them, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples' question reveals that even after forty days of resurrection teaching, their categories for the kingdom were still thoroughly Jewish and national. Jesus does not rebuke the expectation of Israel's restoration — he redirects the question of timing. 'It is not for you to know times or seasons' — this is not evasion but liberation: the mission does not depend on eschatological calculation. They are to be witnesses, not prognosticators. The Father's sovereign timing is not their business; faithful presence is.

verseByVerse.quote: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: This is not a command but a promise — and it is the structural outline of the entire book of Acts. Jerusalem (chapters 1–7), Judea and Samaria (chapters 8–12), and the end of the earth (chapters 13–28) — the book's geography is the fulfillment of this single sentence. The witness is Spirit-powered, not human-engineered. And it is witness (martyres) — personal testimony to what has been seen and heard, not merely the propagation of an ideology. The Spirit's arrival is what makes the mission possible. (cf. Matt. 28:19–20; Isa. 49:6)

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes,
verseByVerse.commentary: The cloud is not weather — it is the Shekinah, the visible glory of the living God (Exodus 16:10; 1 Kings 8:10; Daniel 7:13). Jesus is received into the Father's presence in triumph. The disciples stand gazing — a posture Luke notes with a hint of gentle rebuke; the angels are about to redirect their attention. The ascension is a real, physical, observable event: Jesus does not fade or disappear; he is lifted and received. The bodily ascension of the incarnate Son is the guarantee of the bodily resurrection of all who are in him.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary: The angelic word is both encouragement and commission: stop gazing upward and get to work. The return is certain — 'this Jesus... will come in the same way' — personal, bodily, visible. The ascension guarantees the return; the cloud that received him is the same cloud that will accompany his coming (Daniel 7:13; Revelation 1:7). But the time between his going and his coming is not a time for passive expectation — it is the mission time, the time for witness to the ends of the earth. (cf. 1 Thess. 4:16; Rev. 1:7)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Waiting Church and the Reconstituted Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Ten days separate the ascension from Pentecost, and Luke fills them with a portrait of the waiting church that is both intimate and theologically rich. The eleven return to Jerusalem and gather in an upper room — the same city where Jesus was crucified, the same posture of dependence that Jesus had commanded. They are not cowering in fear; they are 'devoting themselves to prayer.' This is the first portrait of the church: a community of prayer, waiting in obedience, trusting the promise of the one who gave it.

Peter's leadership in the reconstitution of the twelve is remarkable. This is the man who denied Christ three times within earshot of a fire in the high priest's courtyard. Now he stands before 120 disciples, opens the Scriptures, and speaks with apostolic clarity about the fulfillment of Psalm 69 and Psalm 109 in the tragedy of Judas. The restoration of Peter is not merely personal; it is vocational — he is being reconstituted as the leader of the apostolic community precisely so that he can lead the reconstitution of the Twelve.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Apostolic College and Its Significance

The reconstitution of the Twelve to full number before Pentecost is theologically significant. The Twelve correspond to the twelve tribes of Israel and represent the eschatological people of God (Matthew 19:28). An incomplete Twelve would be a broken sign; Peter understands that the witness community must be whole before the mission begins. The qualifications for apostleship (eyewitness from John's baptism to the ascension, v. 22) mark the apostolic circle as a closed and historically anchored group — the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), not a renewable resource.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The 120 in the upper room waited in prayer — not passive resignation but active expectation, preparing themselves for what God was about to do. Now: The church's preparedness for any new movement of God is always the same: gathered in prayer, rooted in Scripture, submitted to appointed leadership, waiting on the Spirit whose timing is the Father's alone to determine.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James.
verseByVerse.commentary: The return to Jerusalem is an act of obedience — Jesus had commanded it (v. 4), and it was the city of his death and resurrection, the city of greatest danger for his followers. The list of the eleven preserves the apostolic memory with care: these names, in this configuration, are the foundation of the church that will turn the world upside down. The detail 'a Sabbath day's journey' (~2000 cubits) roots the event in the real geography of first-century Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said,
verseByVerse.commentary: 'With one accord' (homothumadon) — a word Luke will use repeatedly to describe the unity of the early church (2:46; 4:24; 5:12). The prayer is not occasional but devoted — the continuous, sustained intercession of a community that knows it depends entirely on a power it does not yet possess. Mary and the brothers of Jesus are present — the family that had once thought Jesus was out of his mind (Mark 3:21) now prays with the disciples who had abandoned him. The resurrection has reconstituted relationships. (cf. Col. 4:2; Phil. 4:6)

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's interpretation of Judas's betrayal is governed entirely by Scripture. 'The Scripture had to be fulfilled' — not because God forced Judas to betray, but because the Holy Spirit who inspired David foresaw and foretold the pattern of the righteous one abandoned by a close companion (Psalms 69 and 109). Judas was genuinely one of the Twelve — 'numbered among us,' 'allotted his share' — which makes his defection more sobering: nearness to Jesus is no guarantee of belonging to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: (Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's parenthetical note harmonizes with Matthew 27:3–8 (where the chief priests buy the field with the returned silver): the field came to bear Judas's name because it was purchased with the reward of his betrayal. The grim detail of his death signals the gravity of what he did — the one who sold the Author of life for silver came to a violent and shameful end. The 'Field of Blood' became a permanent, visible memorial in Jerusalem to what the betrayal cost.

verseByVerse.quote: "For it is written in the Book of Psalms, 'May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it'; and 'Let another take his office.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Two psalms converge on Judas's fate: Psalm 69:25 (the abandoned camp) and Psalm 109:8 (the transfer of office). Peter's citation of the second psalm is the scriptural warrant for what follows: the reconstitution of the Twelve. 'Let another take his office' is not merely an observation but a divine mandate. The apostolic office vacated by betrayal must be filled — and the Spirit who predicted the betrayal also predicted the replacement.

verseByVerse.quote: So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us — one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary: The qualification for apostleship is historically anchored: personal accompaniment of Jesus from the beginning of his ministry (the baptism of John) to the end (the ascension), and therefore personal witness to the resurrection. This is not a spiritual gift that anyone can receive; it is a historically bounded office. The apostolic circle is closed: it cannot be extended to those who did not see the risen Lord with their own eyes. This is why Paul's apostleship required a special resurrection appearance (1 Corinthians 15:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.
verseByVerse.commentary: Two men are identified as meeting the apostolic qualifications: Barsabbas (also called Justus — a Roman name suggesting his bicultural world) and Matthias. Both had been with Jesus throughout his ministry; both were qualified; neither is heard from again in Acts. The choice between them is not made by community vote alone but by prayerful discernment and the casting of lots — the decision belongs to God, not to institutional preference.

verseByVerse.quote: And they prayed and said, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You, Lord, who know the hearts of all' — the prayer is addressed to the risen Jesus (the same 'Lord' who had chosen the original twelve). The community can assess external qualifications; only God can read the hearts of both candidates. 'To go to his own place' — the phrase implies divine judgment on Judas: he has gone to the place appropriate for what he chose and who he was. The prayer's simplicity is striking: show us, Lord. We have done what we can; the choice is yours.

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lot was a legitimate Old Testament means of discerning the divine will (Proverbs 16:33; Leviticus 16:8), used here in the brief in-between period before the Spirit's arrival at Pentecost. After Pentecost, the lot disappears from the New Testament — the indwelling Spirit's guidance replaces it. Matthias is numbered with the eleven: the Twelve are reconstituted, the apostolic foundation is complete, and the community of witness is ready to receive the promised Spirit.

So how does God guide Old Joe today, if not by lots? Not by dice, omens, or 'putting out a fleece,' but by the settled means he has since given in fuller measure: his completed Word ('a lamp to my feet,' Ps. 119:105), the indwelling Spirit, prayer, sanctified wisdom, and the counsel of godly friends. The lot belonged to the brief gap before Pentecost and before the New Testament was written; we stand on the far side of both, and are the richer for it.

1.theology: The Ascension and the Reign of Christ. The ascension is the most neglected event in the Christian calendar — and one of the most theologically freighted. It is not simply that Jesus left; it is that he was enthroned. Psalm 110:1 — “The Lord says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool” — is the most-quoted Old Testament text in the New Testament. The early church was obsessed with it because it explained everything: Christ reigns now, at the Father’s right hand, over all things, for his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He is not waiting to begin his kingdom; his kingdom is already here, hidden but real, advancing through the witness of the Spirit-filled church. Every prayer prayed in his name, every sermon preached, every soul converted is an act of the reigning Christ extending his dominion.
1.examples:
Then: The disciples in Jerusalem, staring at the sky, confused about timing and kingdom, learning that faithfulness in the interval between the ascension and the return looks like prayer and witness. They had no map, no strategy document, no budget — only a promise and an upper room.

Now: We live in the same interval — between the first coming and the second, between the already and the not-yet. The temptation is still to stand looking into heaven, obsessing over the date of the return, while the mission sits unfinished at our feet. The command is unchanged: wait in prayer, go in the Spirit, witness to the ends of the earth. He is coming. In the meantime, there is work.

2.title: The Spirit Poured Out
2.text: <sup>1</sup>When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. <sup>2</sup>And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. <sup>3</sup>And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. <sup>4</sup>And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. <sup>5</sup>Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. <sup>6</sup>And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language. <sup>7</sup>And they were amazed and astonished, saying, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? <sup>8</sup>And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language? <sup>9</sup>Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, <sup>10</sup>Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, <sup>11</sup>both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians—we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.” <sup>12</sup>And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?” <sup>13</sup>But others mocking said, “They are filled with new wine.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. <sup>15</sup>For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. <sup>16</sup>But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel: <sup>17</sup>‘And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; <sup>18</sup>even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy. <sup>19</sup>And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; <sup>20</sup>the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day. <sup>21</sup>And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.’ <sup>22</sup>“Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know— <sup>23</sup>this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. <sup>24</sup>God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. <sup>25</sup>For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; <sup>26</sup>therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope. <sup>27</sup>For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. <sup>28</sup>You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.’ <sup>29</sup>“Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. <sup>30</sup>Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne, <sup>31</sup>he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. <sup>32</sup>This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses. <sup>33</sup>Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. <sup>34</sup>For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, <sup>35</sup>until I make your enemies your footstool.’ <sup>36</sup>Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.” <sup>37</sup>Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” <sup>38</sup>And Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. <sup>39</sup>For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.” <sup>40</sup>And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” <sup>41</sup>So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls. <sup>42</sup>And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. <sup>43</sup>And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. <sup>44</sup>And all who believed were together and had all things in common. <sup>45</sup>And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need. <sup>46</sup>And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, <sup>47</sup>praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
2.overview:
Everything changes on the day of Pentecost. The sound of a rushing wind fills the house — not a gentle breeze but a roar, a theophany, the breath of God filling the room as he once breathed life into Adam’s nostrils. Tongues of fire rest on each one of them — not one tongue over Peter, not one flame above the leaders, but one for each. The Spirit is poured out, as Joel said, on all flesh. This is not an upgrade of the old covenant. This is the new creation beginning.

Peter stands up. This is the same Peter who three times denied knowing Jesus by a charcoal fire. Now he stands before thousands and opens his mouth and the Scripture pours out — Joel, David, the resurrection, the exaltation, the gift of the Spirit. The sermon does not argue for the resurrection; it announces it. And the announcement lands with the force of a hammer: “they were cut to the heart.” Three thousand baptized in one day. The church is born not by strategy but by proclamation.

And then the four marks of the early church appear, simple and complete: the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers. Everything the church needs to be the church was given on that day and has never been taken back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Coming of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Pentecost is the hinge of all history after the cross. What the resurrection accomplished objectively — the defeat of sin and death — Pentecost applies subjectively: the Spirit of the risen Christ is poured out on his people, taking up residence within them, constituting them as the temple of the living God. The sound like a mighty rushing wind, the tongues of fire, the speaking in other languages — these are not theatrical effects but the signs of a new creation breaking into the old world. Wind and fire are the Old Testament signs of the divine presence (Exodus 3:2; 1 Kings 19:12; Ezekiel 37:9–10); their appearance at Pentecost announces that the God of the burning bush and the still small voice is now dwelling within his people.

The languages of Pentecost are the reversal of Babel. At Babel, human unity in pride was shattered by divine judgment into the confusion of languages. At Pentecost, the Spirit reunites humanity in the one language of the gospel — not by abolishing the diversity of human tongues but by speaking the wonders of God through all of them simultaneously. Every nation under heaven hears the mighty works of God in its own language. The church's mission is born in this moment: a community that crosses every linguistic barrier to declare the acts of the God who created every tongue.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit as the Presence of God

The Reformed tradition has insisted that the Spirit at Pentecost is not a new or separate divine presence but the fulfillment of everything the Old Testament promised about the eschatological age. Joel 2, Ezekiel 36–37, Jeremiah 31 — all point to a day when God's Spirit would be poured out on all his people, not just on judges and kings and prophets. That day has arrived. The Spirit's arrival is not an upgrade to the disciples' personal spirituality; it is the fulfillment of Israel's covenant hope, the inauguration of the new age, the down payment on the new creation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The crowd at Pentecost heard the wonders of God in their own languages — Parthians, Medes, Elamites, residents of Mesopotamia — the full breadth of the Diaspora. The gospel's first public proclamation was already international. Now: The church continues Pentecost's work every time the gospel crosses a language barrier, every time a translation is made, every time the wonders of God are declared in a tongue the missionaries had to learn. The Spirit who reversed Babel is still reversing it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.
verseByVerse.commentary: Pentecost (the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover) was already a pilgrimage feast that drew Jews from across the Diaspora to Jerusalem — God's timing is sovereign even in the liturgical calendar. 'Suddenly from heaven' — the Spirit's arrival is divine initiative, not human engineering. The sound like a rushing wind recalls Genesis 1:2 (the Spirit hovering over the waters) and Ezekiel 37:9–10 (the breath/wind that gave life to the dry bones). The new creation is being inaugurated.

verseByVerse.quote: And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
verseByVerse.commentary: Fire, the sign of God's purifying and commissioning presence (Exodus 3:2; Isaiah 6:6–7), rests 'on each one' — not just on the apostles but on every member of the 120. Joel's promise is fulfilled: not just on special leaders but on all flesh. The speaking in other tongues is the Spirit's immediate work — 'as the Spirit gave them utterance.' The church's first act is proclamation, and it begins in languages the speakers have not learned. Mission is the Spirit's first priority.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And at this sound the multitude came together and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Devout men from every nation under heaven' — Pentecost has already gathered the audience that the Spirit intends to reach. The miracle is deliberately public: the sound draws a crowd. And the crowd's bewilderment is specific — not bewilderment at noise or spectacle but at intelligibility: each one hears in his own native language. This is not ecstatic unintelligible speech but recognized, comprehensible proclamation of the mighty works of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were amazed and astonished, saying, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The miracle's stunning quality: Galileans — provincial, uneducated, speaking a recognizable regional dialect of Aramaic — are declaring the wonders of God in the native languages of Parthia, Pontus, and Rome. The Spirit is not limited by human geography, education, or ethnic background. He speaks through whoever he fills, in whatever language the hearer needs. The bewilderment is the appropriate response to the presence of a God who exceeds every human limitation.

verseByVerse.quote: Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes,
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's list of nations spans the known world from east (Parthia, beyond the Euphrates) to west (Rome), from north (Pontus, on the Black Sea) to south (Libya). The geographic breadth is deliberate: Pentecost is already a preview of the mission Jesus has just commissioned — 'to the end of the earth.' The inclusion of 'proselytes' — Gentile converts to Judaism — points toward the coming Gentile mission. The Spirit's reach from the first day exceeds every ethnic and national boundary.

verseByVerse.quote: Cretans and Arabians — we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The mighty works of God' (ta megaleia tou theou) — the content of the Pentecost proclamation is not personal testimony or moral exhortation but the declaration of divine acts: what God has done in the death and resurrection of Jesus. The gospel is always first and foremost the announcement of events. Every tongue in the list is hearing the same news: the God of Israel has acted in history, in the person of Jesus, and this news belongs to every language under heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, "What does this mean?" But others mocking said, "They are filled with new wine."
verseByVerse.commentary: Two responses to the same event: genuine bewilderment and dismissive mockery. The first response ('What does this mean?') is the honest question that opens the door for Peter's sermon. The second ('They are filled with new wine') is the characteristic response of those determined not to take the evidence seriously. Both responses appear at every proclamation of the gospel: the open question and the closed dismissal. Peter's sermon is addressed to both — it is the answer to the honest question, and it refuses to be silenced by the mocking one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–36 — Peter's Sermon: The Risen Christ Proclaimed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter's Pentecost sermon is the first Christian sermon ever preached, and it is a masterpiece of Spirit-given proclamation. The man who could not sustain his claim to know Jesus before a servant girl now stands before thousands in the city of the crucifixion and declares, 'God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.' The Spirit has not merely given Peter courage — he has given him understanding: the ability to read the entire story of Israel as the long preparation for this moment, to see David's psalms as prophecies of the resurrection, to connect the outpouring of the Spirit with the exaltation of the Christ.

The sermon has three movements: the explanation of Pentecost (vv. 14–21), the proclamation of Jesus's death, resurrection, and exaltation (vv. 22–32), and the declaration of his lordship and the call to repentance (vv. 33–36). Each movement is grounded in Scripture — Joel 2, Psalm 16, Psalm 110 — because Peter understands that the events he is describing are not novelties but fulfillments. The God who spoke through prophets has now spoken definitively through his Son, and the proof is standing outside an empty tomb and seated at the right hand of the Father.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter's Use of the Psalms

Peter's exegesis of Psalm 16 ('you will not abandon my soul to Hades') is christological: David wrote these words, but David died and was buried, so they cannot be David's own experience. They must be the prophetic voice of the greater Son of David, the one who actually did not see corruption because he was raised. This is the interpretive method that the risen Christ himself had modeled (Luke 24:27, 44): the psalms speak of him. Reformed hermeneutics sees in Peter's sermon the model of Christ-centered interpretation of all Scripture.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter's sermon was addressed to people who had been in Jerusalem at the crucifixion — 'this Jesus whom you crucified.' The gospel was first preached to those most directly implicated in it. Now: The gospel is always preached to those implicated in it: 'He was pierced for our transgressions' (Isaiah 53:5). The human race as a whole bears the guilt that the first sermon laid at Jerusalem's feet — and the invitation is the same: repent, be baptized, receive the Holy Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted his voice and addressed them: "Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter stands — the posture of authoritative teaching — and the eleven stand with him. This is apostolic testimony, not solo performance. His dismissal of the drunkenness charge is almost wry: it is 9 in the morning. No one is drunk. But the deflection of the mocking charge is not where Peter lingers; it is merely the door he opens to say what he actually means to say. The sermon is not an apology for Pentecost — it is the proclamation that Pentecost is the fulfillment of everything God promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel:"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'This is what was uttered through Joel' — the single most important interpretive move in Peter's sermon. What has just happened is not strange, unprecedented, or alarming; it is the fulfillment of a specific prophetic word spoken centuries earlier. Peter grounds the entire Pentecost event in Scripture before he explains it or applies it. The Spirit who inspired Joel is the Spirit who has just arrived. The church that witnesses Pentecost is living inside a story that was written before the world began.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joel 2:28–29 announces the democratization of the Spirit: the outpouring on 'all flesh' — sons and daughters, young and old, servants and free — means the end of the old order where the Spirit rested only on judges, kings, and prophets. Every distinction of gender, age, and social status is overridden by the sovereign gift of the Spirit. The phrase 'in the last days' is Peter's interpretive addition to Joel: Pentecost inaugurates the eschatological age, the final period of redemptive history before the return of Christ. (cf. Joel 2:28–29; Num. 11:29)

Note one phrase Old Joe may misread: 'in the last days.' Peter takes Joel's 'afterward' and declares 'the last days' to have arrived — at Pentecost. So in the Bible's reckoning the 'last days' are not only a short future window before the end; they are the whole gospel age, from Christ's first coming to his return ('in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son,' Heb. 1:2; 'it is the last hour,' 1 John 2:18). We have been living in the last days for two thousand years. (Scripture does also speak of these days intensifying as the end nears, 2 Tim. 3:1 — a note our dispensational friends rightly stress — but the era as a whole is already underway.) The effect is urgency, not date-setting: we live in the final act of God's story, awaiting only the King's return.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day."
verseByVerse.commentary: Joel's cosmic signs (vv. 19–20) frame the age between Pentecost and the final Day of the Lord — the entire church age is, in one sense, the time of portents preceding the great day. The signs may refer to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (which Jesus also described in cosmic terms, Luke 21:25) as the near fulfillment, with the final day as the ultimate horizon. The imagery of darkness and blood-moon belongs to the prophetic tradition of divine judgment on the old order as the new arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The climax of Peter's Joel citation is the promise that anchors his entire call to response: 'everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.' The invitation is universal ('everyone'), the condition is singular ('calls upon the name of the Lord'), and the result is certain ('shall be saved'). Peter has established that 'the Lord' in this context is Jesus — whose name is the only name given under heaven by which people must be saved (4:12). To call on Jesus is to call on the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men."
verseByVerse.commentary: The kerygma begins: Jesus of Nazareth, whose miraculous ministry they themselves witnessed ('as you yourselves know'), was delivered up to death. The double agency of the cross is stated with breathtaking precision: 'according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God' — divine sovereignty; 'you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men' — full human responsibility. Neither cancels the other. The cross is not an accident, a tragedy, or a surprise to God; it is the predetermined act of divine love that accomplishes salvation through real human wickedness.

verseByVerse.quote: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It was not possible for him to be held by it' — death could not contain the Author of life. The impossibility is not merely physical but ontological: the one who is Life itself cannot be permanently subject to death. 'Loosing the pangs of death' — the image is of birth pangs reversed, or of bonds dissolved. Death held Jesus as long as the three days required for the burial to be verified; then it could hold him no longer. God's raising of Jesus is not a rescue of a victim but the vindication of his beloved Son over the last enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David says concerning him, 'I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope."
verseByVerse.commentary: Psalm 16:8–9 is applied to Jesus on the grounds that David — who wrote it — died and was buried and could not ultimately say 'my flesh will dwell in hope' in the sense of bodily resurrection. So the Spirit who inspired David embedded these words as a prophecy of the greater Son of David whose flesh actually did dwell in hope — because God actually raised it. 'I saw the Lord always before me' — the posture of faith that sustained Jesus through the cross: the Father was always present, even in the darkness of Golgotha.

verseByVerse.quote: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You will not abandon my soul to Hades' — this is the key verse of Peter's exegesis. David's soul did go to Hades (the realm of the dead), and his body did see corruption in the tomb in Jerusalem. So this promise cannot be David's own ultimate experience; it must be prophetic. The 'Holy One' who would not see corruption is the Lord Jesus — whose resurrection body left no decomposition in the tomb. 'The paths of life' and 'gladness with your presence' describe the resurrection and exaltation: life and the Father's presence, restored and unending.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne,"
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's argument is tight and irrefutable: David died (verifiable fact), he was buried (his tomb is a known Jerusalem landmark), therefore Psalm 16 cannot be David's own autobiography — it must be prophecy. But David was more than a poet; he was 'a prophet' who knew the Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7): God swore with an oath to set one of David's descendants on his throne forever. David therefore looked forward, as a prophet, to the ultimate Davidic king whose reign would be permanent because death could not end it.

verseByVerse.quote: "he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's conclusion is direct: David foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ — specifically, that Hades would not hold him and his flesh would not decompose. Every word of Psalm 16 that could not be David's own experience is fulfilled in Jesus. And then Peter grounds everything in apostolic testimony: 'This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses.' The eleven standing behind Peter are the evidence. The resurrection is not a theological interpretation of events — it is an event to which these men are eyewitnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The logical chain is complete: the risen Jesus has been exalted to God's right hand, and from that position of supreme authority he has received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured it out — the event the crowd is witnessing is itself proof of Jesus's resurrection and exaltation. Peter's second Old Testament citation is introduced with the same logic used for Psalm 16: David did not ascend to heaven, so the psalm that follows cannot be about David. It must be about the one David calls his Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: "'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool."' Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary: Psalm 110:1 — the most quoted Old Testament text in the New Testament — presents a puzzle: David calls his own descendant 'my Lord.' A descendant is always lesser than an ancestor; for David to call a son 'Lord' requires that this son is more than merely human. The puzzle is resolved by the resurrection and exaltation: Jesus is the Son of David who is also the Son of God, now seated at the Father's right hand exercising all authority. The sermon's climax drives the point home: 'God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.'

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three thousand people respond to a single sermon, and the church is born in a day. This is the fulfillment of what Jesus promised: the Spirit working through the apostolic testimony to bring people to repentance and faith. The three thousand are not merely converted; they are incorporated — into the apostles' teaching, into fellowship, into the breaking of bread, into prayer. From its very first day, the church is not a collection of spiritually interested individuals but a community of practice, a body that learns together, eats together, prays together, and holds all things in common.

Luke's description of the early Jerusalem church is not an idealized fantasy — it is an account of what the Spirit produces when he fills a community with love for God and love for neighbor. The wonders and signs continue; the generosity is extravagant; the joy is contagious. 'And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.' The growth is God's work. The church's task is to be the kind of community that the Spirit is pleased to inhabit — devoted to his word, to each other, to the Lord's table, and to prayer.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Four Marks of the Apostolic Church

Acts 2:42 gives the church four defining practices: the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers. Reformed ecclesiology has seen in these four marks the essential shape of authentic church life in every generation. The apostles' teaching (now the New Testament) norms everything else; fellowship (koinōnia) is the shared life that the Spirit creates; the breaking of bread is the Lord's Supper that proclaims his death; and the prayers are the church's dependence expressed in corporate intercession. A church that is strong in all four will be healthy; a church that neglects any one will be impoverished.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church's generosity was economic: they sold possessions and distributed to those in need. No one among them was in lack. Now: The principle of Spirit-generated generosity is permanent, even if the specific form varies. The church that is filled with the Spirit will be a community where material resources flow toward those in need — not by compulsion but by the overflow of love that the Spirit produces.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, "Brothers, what shall we do?" And Peter said to them, "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘Cut to the heart’ — the Spirit-empowered proclamation of the crucified and risen Christ produces genuine conviction: the crowd recognizes their city’s guilt and their own implication. The question ‘What shall we do?’ is the best possible response to the gospel — the response of those who take it seriously enough to ask what it demands. Peter’s answer is two-fold: repent (a turning of the whole self) and be baptized in the name of Jesus (public incorporation into the community of the forgiven). Both produce forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

‘Baptized in the name of Jesus’ — preachers should explain the apparent tension with Matthew 28:19, where the risen Christ commands baptism ‘in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’ The two formulas are not contradictory: ‘in the name of Jesus’ is shorthand for the entire trinitarian authority invested in the risen Christ — to be baptized into Jesus is to be baptized into the God who raised him, the Spirit he poured out, the Father who sent him. The Petrine formula identifies the new covenant Lord; the Matthean formula explicates the divine identity of that Lord. Early church practice harmonized them (Didache 7), not because either was deficient, but because each illuminates different facets of the same saving act.

Oneness Pentecostals (the ‘Jesus Only’ movement, early 20th century) have used ‘in the name of Jesus’ passages to argue that trinitarian baptism is invalid and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three Persons but three manifestations of one Person — Jesus. The mainstream church, Eastern and Western Reformed traditions alike, reads the Lukan formula as abbreviation rather than contradiction: no theological reduction of the Trinity is warranted, since the same Acts 2:33 shows Jesus receiving the Spirit from the Father and pouring him out — a scene that requires three genuine divine agents. (cf. Mark 1:15; Rom. 6:3–4)

‘Be baptized... for the forgiveness of sins’ raises a question worth settling for Old Joe: does the water itself wash sins away? The Reformed and broadly Protestant answer is no — baptism is the God-given sign and seal of the forgiveness that is received through repentance and faith, not the cause of it. Forgiveness is by grace through faith in the blood of Christ (‘everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins,’ Acts 10:43; Eph. 1:7), which is why the dying thief was saved with no baptism at all (Luke 23:43). So we do not rest our hope in the water but in Christ, to whom the water points. (Our Roman Catholic and ‘Churches of Christ’ friends read it differently, holding that baptism actually conveys the new birth — ‘baptismal regeneration’; the difference is real, and turns on whether the rite signifies grace or effects it.)

verseByVerse.quote: "For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scope of the promise is breathtaking in its breadth: you (those present), your children (future generations), 'all who are far off' (Diaspora Jews and, by implication, Gentiles — cf. Ephesians 2:13). The boundary of the promise is not ethnic or geographic but covenantal: 'everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.' Election and invitation are held together: God calls, and the called must repent. The gospel is universal in its offer; the Spirit is sovereign in its application.

'The promise is for you and for your children' stands near the heart of a long, friendly disagreement among Bible-loving Christians over who should be baptized. The Reformed and Presbyterian (infant-baptist) reading sees an unbroken covenant pattern: God has always included the children of believers in the covenant and its sign (circumcision in the Old Testament, Gen. 17; now baptism), so believers' infants receive the sign as covenant children, awaiting their own personal faith. The Baptist (believer's-baptism) reading takes 'your children' simply as offspring who, like everyone, must themselves repent and believe to receive the promise — noting the very next clause, 'everyone whom the Lord our God calls' — and so baptizes only those who profess faith. Both honour Scripture and the gospel of grace; the difference turns on how much the old covenant sign carries over into the new. (It is held charitably even within Reformed circles, which include both convictions.) These notes are written from a Reformed vantage, but the point Old Joe must not miss is the one both sides shout together: the promise is sheer grace, and it is offered to him and his.

verseByVerse.quote: And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Save yourselves from this crooked generation' — the call to break with the spirit of the age that crucified the Lord. The exhortation continues beyond the recorded summary; Peter's sermon was probably much longer than Luke's digest. Three thousand respond — a number that recalls Sinai, where three thousand died for idolatry (Exodus 32:28). At the new Sinai, the Spirit's fire falls and three thousand are made alive. The new covenant reverses the old covenant's judgment: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary: The four marks of the apostolic church: the apostles' teaching (Scripture's authority mediated through eyewitness testimony), fellowship (koinōnia — the shared life of the Spirit), the breaking of bread (the Lord's Supper), and the prayers (corporate, expectant, dependent intercession). 'Devoted themselves' (proskarterous) — not casual attendance but persistent, committed practice. The church's health in every generation is measured by the depth of these four devotions, not by the excitement of its programs or the size of its crowds. (cf. Col. 3:16; Heb. 10:24–25)

verseByVerse.quote: And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common.
verseByVerse.commentary: Awe (phobos) — the instinctive recognition of the presence of the holy — was the community's characteristic atmosphere. The signs and wonders continue, authenticating the apostolic message and confirming the kingdom's arrival. 'All things in common' is not communist ideology but the natural outflow of Spirit-generated unity: when people genuinely share one Lord, one Spirit, and one hope, the sharing of material goods follows organically. The first church was not organized into economic sharing; it was loved into it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary: The economic sharing is concrete, voluntary, and needs-driven: not equal distribution regardless of need, but generous response to actual need. 'As any had need' — this is pastoral generosity, not mechanical redistribution. The Spirit who fills the community also fills them with discernment about whose need is genuine and love that compels response. Peter will later clarify (5:4) that the property was entirely at each person's disposal — the giving is the miracle, not the compulsion.

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.commentary: The rhythm of the early church: public (temple) and private (homes), corporate worship and domestic fellowship, praise and witness. 'Glad and generous hearts' — the joy is inseparable from the generosity; the Spirit who fills produces both simultaneously. 'The Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved' — the growth is attributed entirely to God. The church does not grow itself; the Lord adds to it. The community's task is faithful witness and Christ-shaped life; the harvest belongs to the Lord of the harvest.

2.theology: The Sovereignty of God at the Cross. Acts 2:23 is the Reformed doctrine of divine sovereignty distilled to a sentence. The cross happened “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.” The word translated “definite plan” means God’s eternal counsel, his settled, unalterable purpose. This is not foreknowledge in the Arminian sense of God merely looking ahead and seeing what humans would choose. This is foreordination: God planned the cross before the world began (1 Peter 1:20, Revelation 13:8). Total depravity and sovereign grace appear in one verse: the guilt is wholly human, the purpose is wholly divine. The cross is the intersection of man’s worst deed and God’s greatest gift.
2.examples:
Then: The feast of Pentecost was transformed on this day from an agricultural harvest festival into the birthday of the church. Devout Jews from fifteen regions of the empire heard the mighty works of God proclaimed in their mother tongues and were cut to the heart. The harvest that day was three thousand souls.

Now: Every Lord’s Day is a Pentecost echo. The same Spirit, the same Word, the same call to repentance — and the same Lord who adds to his church those who are being saved. The question for every preacher and every congregation is whether we are as devoted to the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers as that first gathering was. The form has not changed. The power has not diminished.

3.title: The Lame Man and the Living Lord
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. <sup>2</sup>And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple. <sup>3</sup>Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms. <sup>4</sup>And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.” <sup>5</sup>And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them. <sup>6</sup>But Peter said, “I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!” <sup>7</sup>And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. <sup>8</sup>And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. <sup>9</sup>And all the people saw him walking and praising God, <sup>10</sup>and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. <sup>11</sup>While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s Portico. <sup>12</sup>And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk? <sup>13</sup>The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. <sup>14</sup>But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, <sup>15</sup>and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses. <sup>16</sup>And his name—by faith in his name—has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all. <sup>17</sup>“And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. <sup>18</sup>But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. <sup>19</sup>Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, <sup>20</sup>that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, <sup>21</sup>whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago. <sup>22</sup>Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you. <sup>23</sup>And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people.’ <sup>24</sup>And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days. <sup>25</sup>You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ <sup>26</sup>God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.”
3.overview:
Silver and gold has Peter none. This is not a confession of poverty but a declaration of what he does have: “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk.” The man at the Beautiful Gate has been lame from birth — forty years of sitting, of watching others enter the temple he could not enter, of reaching out his hand to receive what others chose to give. In one moment, at the word of Peter and the power of the risen Christ, his ankles are strengthened, and he goes in walking and leaping and praising God. He who could not enter the temple now cannot stop praising the God of the temple.

But Luke wants us to see more than a healing. The sermon that follows is the point. Peter will not let the crowd look at him; he points them past himself to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob who has glorified his servant Jesus. The healing is a sign — what God has done in this man’s body is a picture of what God is doing in the world: the lame are walking, the guilty are forgiven, the dead are raised. All of it through the name that is above every name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Healing at the Beautiful Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first healing in Acts is a proclamation before it is a miracle. A man lame from birth — the most visible of the beggars at the most prominent of the temple gates — receives not what he asked for but something infinitely greater than what he asked for. 'Silver and gold I do not have, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk.' The apostolic church has no money; it has the name of the risen Jesus. And that name is sufficient to do what the temple system, for all its magnificence, could never do: make a broken man whole.

The healing is not an isolated wonder — it is the first public demonstration that the resurrection of Jesus has real, physical consequences in the world. The same power that raised Jesus from the dead is now at work through his apostles, restoring what sin and suffering have broken. The man who enters the temple courts walking and leaping and praising God is a picture of what the gospel always does: it restores the dignity and wholeness of those who come to the risen Jesus with empty hands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Miracles in Acts and the Kingdom of God

The healing miracles of Acts are 'signs' — they point beyond themselves to the reality of the kingdom of God breaking into the fallen world. They are not magic, not the manipulation of impersonal forces, but the personal power of the risen King exercised through his authorized representatives. Reformed theology sees the apostolic signs as the authentication of the apostolic message: they confirm that the gospel being proclaimed is genuinely from God. The age of redemption has dawned; creation itself is beginning to be restored.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The lame man begged daily at the Beautiful Gate, dependent on the charity of worshippers. The gospel gave him back his legs — but more than his legs, his dignity, his place in the worshipping community, his standing before God. Now: The gospel continues to restore what sin has broken — not always physically, but always in the dimensions that matter most: relationship with God, identity as beloved children, and the sure hope of a resurrection body that will never again be broken.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms from those entering the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary: The hour of prayer (3pm — the time of the evening sacrifice) places this encounter in the context of Israel's daily rhythm of worship. Peter and John are not on a healing mission; they are going to pray. The lame man is going to beg — his daily expectation is coins, not a cure. Luke's detail that he was lame 'from birth' is crucial: this is not a recoverable injury but a congenital condition that has marked his entire life and excluded him from full participation in the temple community he daily approaches.

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.
verseByVerse.commentary: His request is entirely reasonable and entirely mistaken: he asks for what he knows how to ask for. The economy of the kingdom operates differently from the economy of alms — it does not give what is expected but what is needed. Peter and John could have walked past, as thousands had walked past before them. But they stop — not because they have money but because they have something better than money. The encounter about to happen will redefine what 'blessing' means.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, "Look at us." And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Look at us' — Peter directs the man's attention before he speaks the word of healing. The man fixes his attention expecting a coin; what he receives is a restoration of his body and his place in society. Peter's direct gaze is the gaze of one who has something to give, not merely something to say. The apostolic ministry always begins here: with attention, with seeing the person in front of you, before giving what only the name of Jesus can give.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said, "I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!" And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth' — the name is the authority, and the authority is the resurrection. Peter acts as the authorized representative of the risen Lord whose name carries all the power of his risen person. The physical act of taking his hand mirrors the healing: Peter extends the hand of the risen community to the excluded man and raises him up — a gesture that is simultaneously an act of healing and an act of welcome. 'Immediately' — the kingdom does not rehabilitate gradually; it restores completely.

verseByVerse.quote: And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The man who had never walked in his life enters the place he had only ever approached as a beggar — now on his own feet, leaping, praising God. This is Isaiah 35:6 fulfilled: 'the lame shall leap like a deer.' The lame man's entry into the temple courts is itself a theological statement: Jesus has done what the temple system could never do, given him access and wholeness and a reason to praise. The gospel restores the dignity and place of those the world has written off.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people saw him walking and praising God, and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The witnesses 'recognized him' — this is important. The healing cannot be dismissed as a case of mistaken identity; the man was a daily fixture at the gate, known to the temple community. The wonder and amazement (thambous kai ekstaseōs) that fills the crowd is the appropriate response to the in-breaking of the kingdom. Luke uses this reaction to set up Peter's sermon: the crowd gathers, astonished, and Peter immediately turns their astonishment toward the risen Jesus who is the actual source of the healing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter cannot perform a miracle without preaching. The healing at the Beautiful Gate draws a crowd, and the crowd becomes a congregation. Peter's second sermon is structurally similar to his Pentecost sermon but addressed to a different situation: not the outpouring of the Spirit but the healing of a lame man. In both cases, Peter's interpretive move is the same — this is not our power or piety; this is the power of the risen Jesus, whom you rejected but God vindicated. The sermon is a masterpiece of brevity and christological density: Jesus is the Holy and Righteous One, the Author of life, the prophet Moses foretold, the fulfillment of the covenant with Abraham.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus as the Fulfillment of the Abrahamic Covenant

Peter's conclusion in vv. 25–26 grounds the gospel in the Abrahamic covenant: 'In your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed' (Genesis 22:18). The blessing has now come in the person of Jesus, the ultimate seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:16). The gospel is not the abandonment of God's promises to Israel but their fulfillment — not Plan B but Plan A arriving at its appointed time. Reformed biblical theology insists that the covenant of grace is one from Genesis to Revelation, finding its definitive expression in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to Israelites who bore the most direct responsibility for the crucifixion — 'you denied the Holy and Righteous One.' Yet the invitation is for their blessing and turning first. Now: The gospel is always offered first to those most implicated in the rejection of Jesus — which is to say, every human being. The one rejected and crucified is the one who now offers repentance and forgiveness to those who rejected and crucified him.

verseByVerse.quote: While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon's Portico. And when Peter saw it, he addressed the people: "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk?"
