verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's immediate deflection of the crowd's gaze is characteristic of apostolic ministry: 'not us — Jesus.' The wonder is real and warranted, but its object must be correct. The crowd is marveling at Peter and John; Peter will not accept the admiration. 'Our own power or piety' — neither human ability nor spiritual virtue produced this healing. The apostolic ministry is always transparent to the power working through it, refusing to absorb the glory that belongs to the risen Lord alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him."
verseByVerse.commentary: The title 'God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' is the covenant name of the God who made promises to the patriarchs — Peter is emphatically not announcing a new God. This is the same God, continuing the same story, now glorifying his servant Jesus. And the contrast is devastating: Pilate, the pagan governor, was inclined toward release; the covenant people 'delivered over and denied' the one their covenant God was glorifying. The irony is not rhetorical but historical and tragic.

verseByVerse.quote: "You denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary: Three titles pack enormous theological weight: 'the Holy and Righteous One' (the one who fulfilled all that the law demanded), 'the Author of life' (archēgon tēs zōēs — the pioneer and originator of life itself). The supreme irony of history: the people of the God of life killed the Author of life and released a murderer in his place. But God's response to this ultimate human wickedness was resurrection — and the apostles are the witnesses. The proclamation of the cross is inseparable from the proclamation of the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'His name — by faith in his name' — the repetition is emphatic: the name of the risen Jesus, received by faith, is the operative power behind the healing. The man is 'whom you see and know' — not a stranger but a recognized member of the temple community, identifiable to the crowd as the lame beggar of the Beautiful Gate. 'Perfect health in the presence of you all' — the healing is public, verifiable, and complete. Faith in Jesus restores what sin and suffering have broken: this is the concrete demonstration of the gospel's power.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I know that you acted in ignorance' — not an excuse but a mitigation and, more importantly, an open door. The crucifixion was a great sin; it was also the fulfillment of what 'all the prophets' had foretold — every prophet who spoke of the Messiah spoke of his suffering (Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, Zechariah 12). Both are simultaneously true: real guilt and fulfilled prophecy. The God who planned the cross for our salvation now offers the forgiveness of those who carried out his plan without understanding it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out,"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Repent therefore' — the call follows from the reality: if this Jesus whom you crucified is the risen Lord whom God has glorified, the only appropriate response is a complete turning of the self toward the God who has acted in him. 'That your sins may be blotted out' — the image is of a debt record erased, a charge sheet destroyed. The very sin of the crucifixion — the worst human act in history — can be blotted out by the grace of the one who was crucified. This is not minimal forgiveness but total removal. (cf. Luke 24:44–47; 1 Pet. 1:10–12)

verseByVerse.quote: "that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord' — repentance leads not merely to the removal of guilt but to the experience of God's renewing presence. Jesus currently reigns in heaven ('heaven must receive until...') but will return to complete 'the restoring of all things' — the full consummation of the new creation that his resurrection has already begun. The age between Pentecost and the return is the age of refreshing, of the Spirit's renewing work, of the ongoing offer of repentance to a world that crucified its Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses said, 'The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Deuteronomy 18:15 is the second great prophetic warrant for Peter's proclamation: Jesus is the prophet-like-Moses whom Israel was commanded to hear. The comparison is rich: both Moses and Jesus were deliverers rejected by their own people (Israel rejected Moses twice before he rescued them); both mediated the word of God; both prefigured the ultimate prophet who would speak not just the words of God but be the Word of God. 'You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you' — the call to hear Jesus is not optional; it is the command of Moses himself. (cf. Deut. 18:15; John 5:45–46)

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days."
verseByVerse.commentary: The warning is proportionate to the privilege: to be the people of God who have received the prophets' testimony and now stand before the fulfillment of all that testimony is to be in the most privileged and most accountable position in history. 'Every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people' — the stakes are eternal. And the witness is cumulative: 'all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel onward' — the entire prophetic tradition of Israel has been pointing toward 'these days,' these very days in which Peter speaks.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, 'And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.' God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter ends not with warning but with invitation grounded in covenant. The Abrahamic promise ('in your offspring all families of the earth shall be blessed' — Genesis 22:18) is being fulfilled in Jesus, the ultimate seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:16). And Israel is the first beneficiary, not the excluded party: 'sent him to you first.' Even in the city of the crucifixion, even to those directly implicated in the cross, the blessing comes first. The blessing is defined precisely as 'turning every one of you from your wickedness' — repentance is the form that the Abrahamic blessing takes in the age of the gospel.

3.theology: The Name of Jesus. “His name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong” (v. 16). This verse is not about a formula but about a person. The name in the ancient world carried the authority and presence of the one who bore it. When Peter speaks the name of Jesus, he is not invoking magic; he is acting in the delegated authority of the reigning Christ. The healing is an act of the risen Lord performed through his servant. Faith is the hand that reaches for what the name offers. And what the name offers is the full power of the one who conquered death — resurrection life, flowing through a living faith, into a broken body and a guilty conscience alike.
3.examples:
Then: A man lame from birth, set daily at the gate of the temple he could not enter, excluded by his condition from the presence he longed for. His whole life had been one long reaching-out of an empty hand. And then, in the name of Jesus, he entered the temple walking.

Now: The church still carries what the world cannot give. No program, no therapy, no government initiative can do what the name of Jesus does — not because those things are worthless, but because they cannot raise the dead. The church’s temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by its true wealth and to offer silver and gold instead. The world has plenty of silver and gold. It has only one name by which it can be saved.

4.title: Boldness Before the Council
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, <sup>2</sup>greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. <sup>3</sup>And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. <sup>4</sup>But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. <sup>5</sup>On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, <sup>6</sup>with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. <sup>7</sup>And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, “By what power or by what name did you do this?” <sup>8</sup>Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders, <sup>9</sup>if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, <sup>10</sup>let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man is standing before you well. <sup>11</sup>This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. <sup>12</sup>And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” <sup>13</sup>Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. <sup>14</sup>But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. <sup>15</sup>But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, <sup>16</sup>saying, “What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. <sup>17</sup>But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.” <sup>18</sup>So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. <sup>19</sup>But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you judge, <sup>20</sup>for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” <sup>21</sup>And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were glorifying God for what had happened. <sup>22</sup>For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old. <sup>23</sup>When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. <sup>24</sup>And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them, <sup>25</sup>who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? <sup>26</sup>The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’— <sup>27</sup>for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, <sup>28</sup>to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. <sup>29</sup>And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, <sup>30</sup>while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” <sup>31</sup>And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness. <sup>32</sup>Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. <sup>33</sup>And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. <sup>34</sup>There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold <sup>35</sup>and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need. <sup>36</sup>Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, <sup>37</sup>sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
4.overview:
The Sadducees are annoyed. They have tolerated a great deal, but the resurrection — they cannot have the resurrection preached in the temple courts. For the Sadducees, resurrection is not just wrong theology; it is a direct challenge to their authority. So they arrest Peter and John. But it is too late: five thousand have believed. The arrest comes after the harvest. This is the pattern in Acts: the Word goes out, the kingdom grows, the opposition rises — and the opposition never wins.

The next morning Peter stands before the same council that tried Jesus. He is not the same Peter. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he does not hedge, does not soften, does not negotiate. He gives them the name: Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead. And then the sentence that has stopped every comfortable ecumenism in its tracks: “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” The council marvels. They cannot deny the miracle — the healed man is standing right there. They can only warn. And Peter and John go back to the church and they pray.

The prayer is worth lingering over. They do not pray for safety. They do not pray for the opposition to relent. They pray for boldness. And the place is shaken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The gospel's first opposition comes not from Gentile pagans but from the Jerusalem religious establishment — the priests, the captain of the temple guard, and the Sadducees. Their problem is not with Peter's miracle but with Peter's preaching: the proclamation of resurrection in Jesus cuts directly against Sadducean theology and threatens the temple hierarchy's authority. They arrest the apostles, hold them overnight, and convene the full council of rulers, elders, and scribes — the same body that had condemned Jesus — to interrogate them the next morning.

What follows is one of the most remarkable scenes in Acts. Before the greatest concentration of religious power in Jerusalem, two unlettered Galilean fishermen speak with a clarity and courage that astonishes the council. Peter's defense is not a defense at all — it is a proclamation. 'This Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.' Exclusive, absolute, unembarrassed. The Spirit promised for persecution (Luke 12:11–12) has arrived.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Exclusivity of Christ

Peter's declaration in v. 12 — 'there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved' — is one of the clearest statements of Christ's exclusive salvific lordship in all of Scripture. Reformed theology has always insisted on this exclusivity as a corollary of the incarnation itself: if God became flesh in one particular person, in one particular place, at one particular time, then salvation is tied to that particular person. Plurality of saviors would require plurality of incarnations, which contradicts the logic of the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter and John were uneducated laymen standing before the supreme court of Israel. Their boldness astonished the council, who recognized that 'they had been with Jesus.' Now: The same Spirit who gave Peter and John their courage and clarity is given to every believer. The boldness to speak the name of Jesus in hostile contexts is not a personality trait — it is the Spirit's gift to those who ask (v. 31).

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary: The opposition comes while Peter is still speaking — the authorities cannot wait for the sermon to end. The annoyance is specifically theological: Sadducean theology denied resurrection (Acts 23:8), and the apostles are proclaiming resurrection as the central fact of the gospel. Every sermon Peter preaches is simultaneously a refutation of the Sadducean worldview. The religious establishment's stake in the status quo is threatened not by miracles but by the message that interprets them: Jesus rose, and his resurrection overturns their entire system.

verseByVerse.quote: And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary: The arrest cannot stop the word already spoken: 'many of those who had heard the word believed.' The gospel operates faster than the authorities can respond. Five thousand men now believe — the church that began with 120 in an upper room has grown exponentially in days. The pattern is established here and will repeat throughout Acts: opposition and growth run together. The more the authorities attempt to suppress the message, the more rapidly it spreads. Human authority cannot arrest a word that has already taken root in human hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family.
verseByVerse.commentary: The full weight of Jewish institutional authority is assembled: Annas (the power behind the high priesthood, the patriarch of the priestly clan), Caiaphas (who had prophesied that one man should die for the people, John 11:50), and all who belonged to the high-priestly family. This is the same Sanhedrin that had condemned Jesus to death. The concentration of religious, political, and social power facing two Galilean fishermen is absolute. And it will prove entirely insufficient against the Spirit who fills them.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, "By what power or by what name did you do this?"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By what power or by what name?' — the council asks precisely the right question, which is also the central question of the entire book of Acts. Everything turns on the name and the authority behind it. They expect the name to expose a source they can discredit and a power they can dismiss. What they receive instead is the most complete and uncompromising christological declaration they could have imagined — spoken with a boldness that leaves them no room to maneuver.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, "Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by whom he was healed,"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Filled with the Holy Spirit' — this is the fulfillment of Jesus's promise in Luke 12:11–12: 'when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.' Peter is not reciting a prepared speech; he is speaking as the Spirit gives utterance. And he begins with a rhetorical inversion: the council has framed this as an interrogation, but Peter immediately reframes it — they are being examined for 'a good deed.'

verseByVerse.quote: "let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that it is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone."
verseByVerse.commentary: The answer to 'by what name?' is given without hesitation or diplomacy: Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised. Both facts — the human guilt of the crucifixion and the divine act of the resurrection — are stated directly to the people most responsible for both. The citation of Psalm 118:22 applies the builder-and-stone metaphor directly to the council: they are the builders who rejected the stone, and God has made that rejected stone the cornerstone of the entire edifice of salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most exclusive and most comprehensive statement in Acts — and one of the most contested in the history of the church. Exclusive: salvation is in no one else; no other name. Comprehensive: 'under heaven,' 'given among men,' 'by which we must be saved' — the scope is universal and the necessity is absolute. This is not arrogance but logic: if God became flesh in one particular person, and if that person died and rose for the salvation of the world, then salvation is tied to that person. The incarnation itself entails the exclusivity of Christ (cf. John 14:6; 1 Tim. 2:5).

For Old Joe, this is also one of the great apologetic verses, for the world calls it narrow and arrogant: how can Jesus be the only way? Three things help. First, it is not a boast about Christians but a confession about Christ: if God himself became man and died and rose to save sinners, then salvation simply is found in him and nowhere else — not because we are better, but because there is only one Saviour who did this. Second, the one narrow door opens to all: narrow in the way (one Saviour), infinitely wide in the welcome ('whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved,' Rom. 10:13). Third, sincerity cannot save — a man can be sincerely wrong, as one who sincerely drinks poison thinking it medicine; salvation rests on the truth of who Christ is, not the earnestness of the seeker. As for those who never hear, Scripture's answer is honest and sobering: all are accountable for the light they have (Rom. 1:20), none seek God on their own (Rom. 3:11), the Judge of all the earth will do right (Gen. 18:25) — and therefore we must go and tell ('how are they to hear without someone preaching?' Rom. 10:14), leaving the secret things to God (Deut. 29:29). (Others soften the exclusivity — pluralism says all religions are valid paths; inclusivism says some may be saved through Christ without conscious faith in him. The historic and Reformed position is that salvation is through Christ alone, received by conscious faith in him, normally through the gospel preached.) Far from cruel, this is the most loving truth there is: if Jesus really is the only Saviour, then telling people is the kindest thing we could ever do.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they could say nothing against it.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They had been with Jesus' — the council's observation is the most accurate commentary on what they are witnessing. The boldness (parrēsia) of Peter and John is not natural confidence — it is the quality that comes from having spent three years with the Son of God and now being filled with his Spirit. The healed man standing beside them is the unanswerable argument: you cannot refute a walking miracle. The council's problem is not lack of evidence; it is the will to suppress the evidence they have.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying, "What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it."
verseByVerse.commentary: The council's private deliberation is a remarkable document of suppressed conscience: 'We cannot deny it.' The evidence is undeniable; the miracle is public knowledge; the healed man is standing in the room (v. 14). The problem is not lack of evidence — it is the will to believe. Their question 'What shall we do with these men?' is the same question the crowd at Pentecost asked from genuine openness (2:37); here it is asked from the desire for containment. The difference between saving faith and hardened unbelief is not the evidence available but the posture of the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name." So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The strategy is containment rather than refutation: suppress the name, stop the spread. The council understands that the power of the apostolic ministry lies entirely in the name of Jesus — remove the name, and the movement (they hope) will collapse. Their charge is sweeping: 'not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.' They are asking the apostles to do the one thing that the apostles regard as a divine obligation. The collision between human command and divine commission is now absolute.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and John answered them, "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter and John's response is the first and most ringing statement of Christian civil disobedience in history. They do not argue, threaten, or negotiate; they simply state the impossibility of compliance: 'whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge.' The judgment is submitted to the council's own conscience, which must know the answer. And then the personal statement: 'we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.' Eyewitnesses of the resurrection cannot be made to act as if they have not seen what they have seen (cf. Acts 5:29).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were glorifying God for what had happened. For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old.
verseByVerse.commentary: The council is constrained by the people's response: all Jerusalem is glorifying God for the healing of a man who has been lame for more than forty years. Political fear defeats theological hostility — the authorities cannot punish men the public regards as heroes without losing their own influence. Luke's note about the man's age underscores the magnitude of the miracle: forty years of lameness, instantaneously and completely healed. There is no natural explanation. The council knows it, the people know it, and the apostles are free — for now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–37 — Prayer, Power, and the Community of Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Peter and John return to their community and report what the council has said, the church does the only thing it knows to do: it prays. The prayer of Acts 4:24–30 is one of the most theologically rich prayers in the New Testament — a model of how the church addresses God in the face of hostility. It begins with God as sovereign Creator, grounds itself in the fulfillment of Psalm 2 in the crucifixion, and asks not for protection from suffering but for boldness to continue the mission and signs to confirm it. The church that prays this way is the church that the Spirit fills and the world cannot stop.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God and Human Responsibility

The prayer of 4:27–28 is one of the most explicit statements of divine sovereignty in Acts: 'Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel,' did 'whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.' The crucifixion is the supreme demonstration that God's plan is not thwarted by human wickedness but accomplished through it. Reformed theology sees here the foundation of confidence in mission: if God can use the greatest evil in history (the murder of his Son) for the greatest good (the salvation of the world), no opposition can ultimately frustrate his purposes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church shared everything — not because the apostles commanded it, but because the Spirit had filled them with love. Barnabas selling his field is the named example of an unnamed pattern throughout the community. Now: The Spirit-filled community is always a generous community. The test of genuine spiritual vitality is not the excitement of meetings but the openness of hands.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, "Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The apostles' first act on release is not strategy but prayer — returning to the community and lifting up the community's voice to God. 'Sovereign Lord' (despota) — not the polite 'Lord' (kyrios) but the absolute master with total authority over all he has made. The prayer begins with creation: before they address their immediate crisis, they anchor themselves in the most fundamental truth — the God who made everything is the God they are addressing. The council's threats, framed against the backdrop of the Creator's sovereignty, look very small.

verseByVerse.quote: "who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, 'Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed' —"
verseByVerse.commentary: The citation of Psalm 2 is inspired: the psalm describes the nations raging against God and his anointed, which is exactly what the council is doing. The church is reading the present situation through Scripture and finding that God has been here before — and won. The rulers gathered against the Lord's Anointed in Jerusalem two thousand years after Psalm 2 was written are simply repeating the pattern the psalm describes. The God who laughs at the nations' vain plotting (Psalm 2:4) is the God the church is addressing. They are praying from the winning side.

verseByVerse.quote: "for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place."
verseByVerse.commentary: The cross is named as the supreme example of human opposition meeting divine sovereignty: every party (Herod, Pilate, Gentiles, Israel) gathered against Jesus, and every action they took was simultaneously their free choice and God's predestined plan. The prayer does not explain the mystery; it simply affirms both realities side by side. And the church draws courage from this: if God's hand and plan governed the crucifixion, then his hand and plan govern the present opposition too. Nothing that happens to the church is outside his sovereignty (cf. Isa. 53:10; Luke 22:22).

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary: The prayer's request is remarkable for what it does not ask: it does not ask for the threats to stop, for the council to relent, or for protection from suffering. It asks for boldness to speak in the face of threats, and for the continued manifestation of God's healing power through the name of Jesus. The church's request is more mission than the authorities have threatened to suppress. This is the prayer posture of a community that has fully transferred its security from earthly protection to divine empowerment.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.
verseByVerse.commentary: God answers the prayer for boldness by filling them again with the Spirit who produces boldness. The physical shaking of the building is a theophanic sign — the presence of the divine response to prayer, recalling the earthquake at Sinai and the shaking of Isaiah's temple vision (Isaiah 6:4). The answer is immediate and unmistakable: the place shakes, the Spirit fills, and they speak the word of God with boldness. The boldness they asked for is the gift the Spirit gives, and the Spirit's gift is the answer to the prayer for the Spirit's gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'One heart and soul' (kardia kai psychē mia) — the deepest unity imaginable: a community of shared will and desire. This is what the Spirit produces in people who are fully yielded to him. The economic sharing flows from the spiritual unity: when people genuinely share one heart, the sharing of possessions follows naturally. 'With great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection' — the community's internal life of unity and generosity is the context in which the external proclamation of resurrection gains its credibility and its power (cf. John 17:21–23).

verseByVerse.quote: There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'There was not a needy person among them' — the church fulfills the Deuteronomic vision (Deuteronomy 15:4, 'there will be no poor among you') not by compulsion but by generosity. The laying at the apostles' feet and distribution according to need creates a community that embodies the kingdom's economics: from those who have, freely given; to those who lack, justly supplied. The apostles' role as distributors of the community's resources is temporary — the appointment of the Seven in ch. 6 will formalize a better arrangement — but the principle of need-driven generosity is permanent.

A word for Old Joe, since this is sometimes called 'Christian communism' and pressed into political service: it was nothing of the kind. It was wholly voluntary — Peter tells Ananias, 'while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?' (5:4) — so private property was kept and giving was free, never compelled. It was love-driven and Spirit-prompted, flowing from hearts made 'one,' not enforced by any state. And it was needs-based generosity ('as any had need'), not mechanical equalising. This is the very opposite of coercive collectivism: it is the free, glad open-handedness of people whom the Spirit had loosed from the grip of money. The abiding call is that same generosity and care for the needy among us; the particular form was one Spirit-filled moment's response.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke names Barnabas as the positive example of the community's generosity — the named illustration of an unnamed pattern. Barnabas ('son of encouragement') will reappear throughout Acts as the man who consistently sees potential where others see danger (9:27, 11:25–26, 15:39). His generosity here is the first glimpse of a character that will prove essential to the Gentile mission. The Levite who cannot own land in Israel (Numbers 18:20) but owns a field in Cyprus gives it away — his belonging is no longer to the tribe but to the community of the risen Christ.

4.theology: The Sovereignty of God and Mission. The prayer of Acts 4:24–30 is a theology lecture compressed into seven verses. God is addressed as despotēs — Sovereign Lord, absolute Master — who made heaven and earth and everything in them. Herod and Pilate and the nations, in their opposition to Christ, did “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.” This is not fatalism; it is the Reformed doctrine of providence applied to history’s darkest moment. And the implication for mission is not paralysis but boldness: if God was sovereign over the crucifixion, he is sovereign over every threat to the gospel. The church does not need favourable conditions to advance the kingdom. It needs the Spirit and the Word. God provides both.
4.examples:
Then: A church five weeks old, under arrest, before the same council that crucified their Lord, with no legal protection, no political allies, no plan B — and they prayed for boldness and were given it. The shaking of the place was God’s receipt: prayer received, boldness granted.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces the same fork: silence or speech, safety or boldness. The prayer of Acts 4 is still available. The God who shook that room has not grown quiet. He is still the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And he still grants boldness to those who ask for it — not because they deserve it, but because his Word must go out.

5.title: The Fear of the Lord
5.text: <sup>1</sup>But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, <sup>2</sup>and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet. <sup>3</sup>But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? <sup>4</sup>While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God.” <sup>5</sup>When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. <sup>6</sup>The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him. <sup>7</sup>After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. <sup>8</sup>And Peter said to her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” And she said, “Yes, for so much.” <sup>9</sup>But Peter said to her, “How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” <sup>10</sup>Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband. <sup>11</sup>And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things. <sup>12</sup>Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico. <sup>13</sup>None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem. <sup>14</sup>And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women, <sup>15</sup>so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter passed his shadow might fall on some of them. <sup>16</sup>The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed. <sup>17</sup>But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy <sup>18</sup>they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. <sup>19</sup>But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, <sup>20</sup>“Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life.” <sup>21</sup>And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council and all the senate of Israel and sent to the prison to have them brought. <sup>22</sup>But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, and they returned and reported, <sup>23</sup>“We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we did not find anyone inside.” <sup>24</sup>Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. <sup>25</sup>And someone came and told them, “Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.” <sup>26</sup>Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. <sup>27</sup>And when they had brought them, they set them before the council. And the high priest questioned them, <sup>28</sup>saying, “We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.” <sup>29</sup>But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. <sup>30</sup>The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. <sup>31</sup>God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. <sup>32</sup>And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.” <sup>33</sup>When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. <sup>34</sup>But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. <sup>35</sup>And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. <sup>36</sup>For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing. <sup>37</sup>After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. <sup>38</sup>So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; <sup>39</sup>but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!” So they took his advice, <sup>40</sup>and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. <sup>41</sup>Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. <sup>42</sup>And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
5.overview:
Two things happen in Acts 5 that seem to pull in opposite directions — and both are necessary. Ananias and Sapphira fall dead for lying to the Holy Spirit. And the apostles are beaten and leave the council rejoicing. The fear of God and the joy of the Lord are not opposites; they are the two poles of a life lived before the face of the Holy One. A church that has lost one will eventually lose both.

The sin of Ananias and Sapphira is not that they kept some of the money. Peter makes this explicit: the money was theirs to keep. The sin is the performance — the pretence of complete consecration while secretly holding back. They lied to the Holy Spirit. The God who fills his church with his presence will not be managed or deceived within his own house. The result: great fear came upon the whole church. This is the fear that is the beginning of wisdom. The church needed it then. The church always needs it.

Then the apostles are beaten. And they leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name. This is not stoicism; this is the freedom of those who have been so captured by the worth of Christ that physical suffering has become, in the light of his glory, a privilege they are grateful to share.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Holiness and Power in the Young Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The story of Ananias and Sapphira is the most disturbing episode in the early chapters of Acts — and it is meant to be. The church that was marked by grace and generosity now encounters the shadow of deception, and the result is swift, terrible, and instructive. Ananias and Sapphira do not steal from the community; they lie to the community. They keep part of the proceeds while presenting the whole as a gift. The sin is not the retention — Peter explicitly states that the money was theirs to keep (v. 4). The sin is the performance of generosity while practicing deception: the claiming of a holiness they did not possess.

The judgment is severe, but the lesson is mercy — mercy to the community being protected from the cancer of hypocrisy that, if unchecked, would have corrupted the one-heart-and-soul unity that was the church's defining mark. The God who will not share his glory with idols will not share his community with pretense. The holiness of the Spirit who fills the church is real, and those who lie to the Spirit discover what it means to be in the presence of the holy God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Holiness of God and the Danger of Hypocrisy

The death of Ananias and Sapphira is a New Covenant echo of the deaths of Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10) and Uzzah (2 Samuel 6) — episodes in which the holiness of God's presence is demonstrated by severe judgment on those who treat it carelessly. Reformed theology sees in these events not capricious divine anger but the necessary self-disclosure of the Holy One: a God who does not enforce his own holiness is not holy. The grace of the gospel does not diminish God's holiness; it satisfies it, so that those in Christ may approach the holy God with confidence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Great fear came upon all who heard of Ananias and Sapphira's deaths — a healthy fear that clarified the community's understanding of what it meant to live in the presence of the Holy Spirit. Now: The Ananias-and-Sapphira pattern is repeated wherever religious performance substitutes for genuine transformation — claiming a spiritual reality we are not actually living. The Spirit who knows hearts is not deceived by appearances.

verseByVerse.quote: But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, and with his wife's knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary: The 'but' that opens chapter 5 is one of the most ominous conjunctions in Acts — immediately contrasting the Spirit-filled generosity of Barnabas with the calculated performance of Ananias and Sapphira. Their sin is precisely calibrated: they sell the property (like Barnabas), they bring a portion to the apostles (appearing generous), but they present a partial gift as the whole. The conspiracy is between husband and wife ('with his wife's knowledge'), doubling the deliberateness of the deception.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's Spirit-given discernment exposes the sin immediately: the problem is not the retention of money (which was entirely their right — 'while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?') but the lie — presenting part as whole, claiming a generosity they were not actually practicing.

'Why has Satan filled your heart…?' — how does Peter mean this? Really and personally: Satan genuinely instigated the sin. The verb 'filled' (eplērōsen) is the dark mirror of being 'filled with the Spirit,' and it sets Ananias beside Judas, of whom Luke wrote that 'Satan entered into' him to betray Jesus for money (Luke 22:3; cf. John 13:2, 27). Behind the deceit stood the personal adversary, striking the newborn church from within at the very hour the gospel advanced with power (many hear an echo of Achan, whose secret sin defiled Israel at the threshold of the land, Josh. 7 — though Luke does not draw the parallel outright).

Yet Satan's hand is no excuse. In the same breath Peter asks, 'Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart?' (v. 4): both are true at once — Satan filled his heart, and Ananias schemed it in his own. Scripture holds these together everywhere (set Luke 22:3 beside Luke 22:22; cf. Gen. 50:20; Acts 2:23): the tempter does not override the will but inflames a heart already willing. As James says, 'each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire' (James 1:14) — Ananias's lie fed on his own covetousness and craving for praise, and Satan fanned the flame. 'The devil made me do it' is no excuse, and Peter offers none.

Is every sin, then, a special act of Satan like this? Scripture sets the proportions. Lying in particular bears his family likeness, for Jesus calls him 'a liar and the father of lies… when he lies, he speaks out of his own character' (John 8:44) — which is why his hand is so visible here; and in a broad sense all sin serves his kingdom (Eph. 2:2; 1 John 3:8). But the ordinary spring of sin is the human heart itself — 'out of the heart of man come evil thoughts… deceit' (Mark 7:21–23), 'his own desire' (James 1:14) — not, as here and with Judas, a direct 'filling' by Satan. The old shorthand names three sources that work together — the world, the flesh, and the devil — and we should neither blame every sin on demons nor pretend the devil has no hand in it.

And through it all Ananias remains fully responsible, for 'you have not lied to man but to God': the Spirit dwelling in the church is the living God, and to deceive his people is to lie to him. Where the text is silent we will not pretend — Luke says plainly that Satan filled the heart and that Ananias contrived the deed, but not how that 'filling' worked or how it compared to ordinary temptation. We rest in what is revealed: real satanic instigation, real human guilt, no excuse, and a holy God who will not be mocked. (cf. 1 Cor. 3:16–17; Heb. 10:26–31)

verseByVerse.quote: When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment is immediate and unannounced — Peter pronounces no sentence; he only exposes the sin. The death is God's response to the deception, not Peter's punishment. 'Great fear came upon all who heard' — the proper effect: the community grasps afresh that the Spirit among them is the Holy God himself, not a benevolent force that accommodates religious play-acting.

But why so severe — when nearly every liar, believer or not, walks away still breathing? God is plainly making a point, and the point comes clear once we notice a pattern across Scripture: again and again, when God inaugurates something new, the first sin against it is judged with startling swiftness.

Consider the line of them. At the very dedication of the priesthood and tabernacle worship, Nadab and Abihu offer 'unauthorized fire,' and fire from the LORD consumes them on the spot (Lev. 10:1–2). At Israel's first step into the promised land, Achan secretly takes devoted spoil, and the whole nation is defeated until he is judged (Josh. 7). As the ark is brought up to its new home in Jerusalem, Uzzah reaches out to steady it and is struck dead beside it (2 Sam. 6:6–7). And here, at the birth of the church, the first hypocrisy within it is met with instant death. (One might add the three thousand who fell as the covenant was first given at Sinai, Exod. 32; and, in the new-covenant age, Paul's sobering word that abuse of the Lord's Supper had left some in Corinth weak, ill, and even dead, 1 Cor. 11:30.)

Why does God deal so at these particular moments? Three reasons run through them all. First, to stamp the holiness of the new thing on the people's memory at its very outset — as God said at the priesthood's founding, 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified' (Lev. 10:3). Second, these are representative judgments — a single public sample of what all sin truly deserves, set down once so the rest are warned; 'great fear came upon the whole church' (5:11) is exactly the intended effect. Third, the formative danger: at the birth of something holy, one tolerated corruption could poison the whole — Achan's hidden sin defeated all Israel, and hypocrisy left unchecked could have rotted the newborn church at its core.

Why, then, do the rest of us not fall dead at every lie? Because these flashes of swift judgment are the exception, not the rule. God's ordinary way is patience — 'the riches of his kindness and forbearance,' meant to lead us to repentance (Rom. 2:4; 2 Pet. 3:9); 'if you, O LORD, should mark iniquities… who could stand?' (Ps. 130:3). The occasional sudden judgment is a lightning-flash that lights up the whole landscape for a moment, showing what every sin deserves and reminding us that the daily delay is mercy, not God's indifference or approval (Eccl. 8:11). One Ananias, recorded in Scripture, teaches the whole church age, so the lesson need not be written on every one of us. And for the believer the deepest answer is the cross: the judgment our sin deserves has already fallen on Christ, and the space God now gives is the room grace makes for repentance. (Whether Ananias was a true believer disciplined in body or a hypocrite exposed, Luke does not finally say; cf. 1 Cor. 11:30–32, where such discipline can be unto death yet not unto condemnation. His concern is not Ananias's eternal fate but the holiness of the church.)

verseByVerse.quote: After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. And Peter said to her, "Tell me whether you sold the land for so much." And she said, "Yes, for so much."
verseByVerse.commentary: The three-hour interval between Ananias's death and Sapphira's arrival means she does not know what has happened — she walks in without knowledge of her husband's fate. Peter's question gives her the opportunity to tell the truth: 'was this the price?' The answer she gives is the same lie her husband told. The conspiracy holds even when it no longer needs to — she maintains the deception not under pressure but out of the same calculated intent that motivated the original act. She is not lying to protect herself; she is lying because that is what she planned to do.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to her, "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out too." Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord' — the conspiracy between husband and wife is named as a testing of the Spirit, echoing Israel's testing of God in the wilderness (Exodus 17:2; Psalm 95:9). The same Spirit who knew Ananias's heart knows Sapphira's. Peter's announcement of her imminent death is not a sentence he is pronouncing but a fact he is revealing — the judgment belongs to God. Her death is immediate and final. The community that hosts the Spirit of the holy God cannot accommodate the deliberate performance of holiness alongside the practice of deception. As for why her sin, like her husband's, is judged so swiftly when sin is not normally repaid on the spot, see on vv. 5–6 — the pattern of immediate judgment at the founding of something new, and why God's ordinary way is patient forbearance.

verseByVerse.quote: When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband. And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Great fear came upon the whole church' — the holiness of God's presence is now established in the community's understanding with absolute clarity. This is the first use of the word 'church' (ekklēsia) in Acts — and it appears in the context of judgment, not triumph. The community that calls itself the church must reckon with the holiness of the God who dwells within it. The fear is not pathological terror but the reverential awe of those who now understand, viscerally, that they live and move in the presence of the holy God.

This ‘great fear’ opens one of Scripture’s deepest and most misunderstood themes: the fear of the Lord. People stumble at it in two opposite directions. Some empty it out, shrinking it to a polite ‘respect’ that no longer trembles at anything; others fill it with cringing, servile terror, as of a slave dreading a tyrant he longs to escape. The Bible means neither. The fear of the Lord is the reverent awe of a creature who has truly seen who God is — holy, majestic, the Judge of all the earth — and so takes him with deadly seriousness. It is ‘the beginning of wisdom’ (Proverbs 9:10), the soil all right living grows in; it ‘is hatred of evil’ (Proverbs 8:13); and far from being abolished by the gospel, it is deepened by it — ‘with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared’ (Psalm 130:4) — and the New Testament still bids us worship ‘with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire’ (Hebrews 12:28–29). Even Jesus said, ‘fear him’ (Luke 12:5).

For the believer this fear is not the terror that drives you away from God but the awe that draws you near and keeps you from trifling with him. The very chapter that records this dread also records the church multiplying (5:14), and Luke later sums up its healthy life as ‘walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit’ (Acts 9:31) — fear and comfort, side by side. Picture Old Joe at his hearth on a winter night. He loves the fire; he pulls his chair close for its warmth and light and would not want to be anywhere else. Yet he would never dream of putting his hand into it or treating it carelessly — he knows what it is. That is the fear of the Lord: to draw near to God in love, and at the very same moment to know he is holy and never, ever to be trifled with. ‘Our God is a consuming fire’ — and he bids his children sit by the hearth. What Ananias and Sapphira had lost was precisely this: they had grown casual with the fire. The church, seeing it, learned to fear again — and a church that rightly fears God is not a frightened church but a reverent, wise, and growing one.

verseByVerse.quote: Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon's Portico.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Signs and wonders' — the two words themselves reveal their purpose. A 'sign' (sēmeion) points beyond itself to something; a 'wonder' (teras) astonishes. They were never meant to be admired as ends in themselves but to authenticate the message and its messengers — God's own seal on the apostolic gospel. Scripture says so plainly: the miracles were 'the signs of a true apostle' (2 Cor. 12:12); God 'bore witness' to the gospel 'by signs and wonders and various miracles' (Heb. 2:3–4); the Lord 'confirmed the message by accompanying signs' (Mark 16:20) and 'bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands' (Acts 14:3). Even Jesus' own signs were written down 'so that you may believe' (John 20:31). The wonder was the wrapping; the word was the gift — which is why Jesus rebuked those who craved signs for their own sake (Matt. 12:39).

This authenticating purpose is also why the historic Reformed church has held that these apostolic sign-gifts have ceased — and the case is drawn from Scripture, not merely from observation. The signs marked out the apostles (2 Cor. 12:12), and the apostles were a foundation laid once and unrepeatably: the church is 'built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets' (Eph. 2:20) — and a foundation is laid only once. Their office could not be handed on (its men had to be eyewitnesses of the risen Christ and directly commissioned; Paul calls himself the 'last of all,' 1 Cor. 15:8). And the revelation those signs authenticated is now complete — 'the faith once for all delivered to the saints' (Jude 3). Once the foundation was laid and the message set down in Scripture, the credentials that had attested the foundation-layers had served their purpose, as scaffolding is taken down once the building stands.

Two honest qualifications. First, no verse says in so many words, 'miracles will cease when the apostles die.' The certain ground is the purpose of the signs, which Scripture states outright; the timing of their ceasing is a strong and reasonable inference from that purpose joined to the close of the apostolic age and the completing of the canon — not a single proof-text (1 Cor. 13:8–10 does say tongues and prophecy will 'cease' and 'pass away,' though believers differ over when 'the perfect' comes). Second, this does not mean God no longer works miracles: he remains entirely free to heal and to act wonderfully in answer to prayer, and often does. What ceased is the distinctive apostolic sign-gift as a standing credential of new revelation — not God's power, nor his nearness. (Bible-loving Christians do hold differing views here; this is the historic cessationist reading, and the one these notes follow.)

'Solomon's Portico' was a long, covered colonnade — a roofed walkway lined with great columns — running along the east side of the temple's outer court. Popular tradition linked it to Solomon, though it belonged to Herod's temple complex. It was a well-known public gathering and teaching place: Jesus had walked there (John 10:23), and Peter had preached there after healing the lame man (Acts 3:11). That the believers met there 'all together' is itself striking — not huddled in hiding, but gathered openly in the most public religious space in Jerusalem, in the very shadow of the temple. The holy, fearless church stood out in plain sight.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'None of the rest dared join them' — and 'the rest' raises a fair puzzle: it can hardly mean true believers (they had already gladly joined), yet plain unbelievers would not be 'joining' the church in any case. Who, then, are 'the rest'? The word 'join' (kollasthai) means to glue or fasten oneself to, to attach closely — and 'the rest' are best understood as the fringe: the half-hearted, the merely curious, the would-be hangers-on who, in an earlier and less sobered moment, might have casually attached themselves to so admired and powerful a movement for the prestige or the benefits of belonging. After Ananias and Sapphira, no one dared do that any more. The fearful holiness of the community (vv. 5, 11) had raised the cost of insincere belonging to terrifying clarity: you do not glue yourself to this people for mixed motives; you cannot come as a spectator or a social climber. So this verse and the next are two sides of one coin. Verse 13: the nominal and the false no longer dared press in. Verse 14: 'yet more than ever believers were added.' The fear screened out the pretenders while the Spirit kept adding the genuine — the church purified and multiplied at once. (Commentators do differ on the exact reference of 'the rest'; but this reading, flowing straight out of the Ananias episode, is the most natural.)

'But the people held them in high esteem' — and this is worth pausing over, because the church's public welcome runs hot and cold through Acts. Here they are esteemed; a few verses on they are arrested (5:17–18); later Stephen is stoned and a great persecution breaks out (chs. 7–8). Is there a pattern? Several real ones, though no rigid formula. First, the fault line often runs between the common people and the authorities: the crowds admired the apostles while the threatened rulers persecuted them — and the people's esteem actually shielded them, for the officers dared use no force 'for they were afraid of being stoned by the people' (5:26). Persecution in early Acts is mostly top-down. Second, public favour is real but fickle — the same city can cheer and then turn, as the crowds who cried 'Hosanna' soon cried 'Crucify.' Third, both favour and hostility serve God's purposes and come from his hand: he grants seasons of favour to open doors for the gospel (2:47, 'having favour with all the people, and the Lord added to their number'), and he permits persecution to scatter the seed and spread the word (8:1–4). So the believer should be neither intoxicated by esteem nor crushed by opposition. Scripture holds both honestly: 'when a man's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him' (Proverbs 16:7), and yet 'all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted' (2 Timothy 3:12). Esteem is a gift, to be received humbly and spent for Christ; persecution is the normal long-run lot of faithful witness (John 15:20). Both, in God's hands, advance the same kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women,
verseByVerse.commentary: 'More than ever' — the fear and the growth are simultaneous, not sequential. The church that takes holiness seriously is the church the Spirit is pleased to inhabit and to fill, and the Spirit-filled church draws people to the Lord it reflects. 'Added to the Lord' — the growth is not institutional recruitment but personal belonging: people are being added to the Lord himself, not merely to a community. And the growth is comprehensive: 'multitudes of both men and women,' fulfilling Joel's promise that the Spirit would be poured out on sons and daughters alike.

verseByVerse.quote: so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The healing ministry has reached a scale that draws the entire Jerusalem region and beyond. 'That at least his shadow might fall' — this is popular faith expressing itself in folk terms; Luke does not say the shadow healed anyone, but the faith that drove people to lay the sick in Peter's path was honored by God. 'They were all healed' — Luke's summaries of healing are consistently comprehensive. The kingdom has arrived; creation is being restored; the preview of the new creation is visible in the streets of Jerusalem.

'Those afflicted with unclean spirits' raises the hard subject of the demonic, and here we should say only what Scripture actually tells us. 'Unclean spirits' are real, personal, evil spirit-beings — what the Gospels equally call 'demons,' using the two terms interchangeably (e.g. Mark 5:2, 12–15; 7:25–26). They are not mere symbols, nor simply an ancient label for illness; the New Testament treats them as intelligent beings with will and speech, part of the kingdom of Satan (Matt. 12:24–26) and commonly understood as fallen angels (Rev. 12:9; 2 Pet. 2:4). 'Unclean' marks their nature: they are defiling, the very opposite of the holiness of God. They can oppress and torment, and at times control a person, with effects both physical (muteness, convulsions, even unnatural strength — Matt. 9:32–33; Mark 5:3–4; 9:18) and inward (the torment of mind and soul, Mark 5:5). Note, though, that Scripture does not blame every sickness on demons: it deliberately lists 'the sick' and 'those afflicted with unclean spirits' as two distinct groups (here, and Mark 1:32–34) — so we are neither to deny the demonic nor to see a demon behind every illness.

What Scripture stresses above all is their relation to Christ. The unclean spirits recognize him and tremble (Mark 1:24; James 2:19), are utterly subject to his authority and to his name on the lips of his servants (Luke 10:17; Acts 16:18), and flee before the advancing kingdom: 'if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you' (Matt. 12:28). At the cross he 'disarmed the rulers and authorities... triumphing over them' (Col. 2:15). So when Luke writes that here 'they were all healed,' he is displaying the kingdom's triumph: where Christ's gospel advances, the unclean spirits retreat. As for the rest — how exactly a spirit afflicts, the line between oppression and possession, why some and not others — Scripture is reticent, and we will not pretend to know more than it tells us. It gives us enough to take the reality seriously, never to fear it, and to look only to the Conqueror: 'he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world' (1 John 4:4).

On the purpose of such healings and exorcisms as 'signs and wonders' — given to authenticate the apostolic message rather than as ends in themselves, and the question of whether these sign-gifts continue today — see the commentary on v. 12.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second arrest of the apostles produces an angelic jailbreak, a second appearance before the Sanhedrin, and the most sustained declaration of apostolic independence from human authority in Acts. 'We must obey God rather than men' is the church's permanent answer to every attempt to silence the gospel by human authority. The Sanhedrin is enraged; Gamaliel counsels caution; the apostles are flogged and released and immediately return to teaching and preaching in the name of Jesus. The chapter ends where it began — with a community in the temple courts and in homes, every day, teaching and proclaiming Jesus as the Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gamaliel's Argument and Its Limits

Gamaliel's advice ('if this plan or undertaking is of human origin, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them') is often cited as a counsel of prudent tolerance. But it is not itself Christian reasoning — it is pragmatic patience that does not distinguish between truth and falsehood, only between durable and ephemeral movements. The apostles do not base their continued preaching on Gamaliel's argument; they base it on obedience to God. Gamaliel is a providential restraint, not a theological authority.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The apostles left the Sanhedrin 'rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name.' Flogging and shame became occasions of joy because the name they suffered for was the name above all names. Now: The willingness to suffer for the name of Jesus is not a sign of masochism but of joy — the joy of those who know that the name they bear is worth every cost the world can impose.

verseByVerse.quote: But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The party of the Sadducees' — a word on who they were, since they now become the apostles' chief persecutors. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy of Jerusalem: the wealthy, ruling, temple-controlling families, and the high priest himself was their head (hence 'the high priest... and all who were with him, that is, the party of the Sadducees'). The temple and its vast establishment were theirs; they dominated the priestly side of the Sanhedrin and, as the men who profited from the status quo, cooperated closely with Rome to keep their power. Theologically they accepted only the written Law of Moses (the first five books) as binding, rejected the oral traditions the Pharisees prized, and — crucially here — denied the resurrection of the dead, along with angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). Their name most likely derives from Zadok, Solomon's high priest (1 Kings 2:35; cf. the 'sons of Zadok,' Ezek. 44:15), marking them as the party of the old priestly line; they had emerged as a distinct group in the two centuries before Christ (the precise origins are not certain). All of which explains the heat of their reaction: the apostles were filling Jerusalem with the message of a risen Jesus — the very doctrine of resurrection the Sadducees denied (cf. Acts 4:1–2) — and were drawing the people's allegiance away from the temple establishment. The gospel struck at both their theology and their power.

'Filled with jealousy' — the motivation for the second arrest is stated explicitly. The apostles' growing influence and public esteem have provoked the envy of the religious establishment. The Sadducees who deny resurrection are watching a community built entirely on resurrection faith grow exponentially under their noses. The arrest is a response to success — every closure the authorities attempt is prompted by the gospel's advance. The world's opposition to the gospel is always, at root, a form of jealousy: the kingdom of God wins the allegiance that human institutions cannot command.

verseByVerse.quote: But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, "Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life."
verseByVerse.commentary: The angel's instruction is precisely what the council was trying to prevent — 'go stand in the temple and speak all the words of this Life.' The jailbreak is not for the apostles' safety or comfort; it is for the mission's continuation. 'All the words of this Life' — the gospel is the announcement of life itself, the life that death could not contain in the tomb of Jesus, the life that now flows to all who believe. The phrase captures the whole gospel: Jesus is life, his words are life, and the community that proclaims him is the community of this Life.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simple and stunning: they heard, they went, they taught. By daybreak they are back in the temple — the very building controlled by the men who imprisoned them — teaching exactly what they were imprisoned for teaching. No deliberation, no calculation of risk, no consultation about whether to obey the angel. The obedience is immediate and complete. This is the pattern of apostolic ministry throughout Acts: when God opens a door (literally or figuratively), the missionaries walk through it without hesitation.

Meanwhile the other half of the verse shows the establishment swinging into action: 'the high priest... called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.' The 'council' is the Sanhedrin (synedrion), the supreme ruling court of the Jewish nation — seventy members presided over by the high priest (seventy-one in all), drawn from the chief priests (Sadducees), the elders (the lay aristocracy and heads of leading families), and the scribes (the legal experts, largely Pharisees). It was the highest religious and judicial body in Israel, meeting in the temple precincts, with authority over Jewish law — though under Rome a death sentence still needed the governor's ratification (cf. John 18:31). 'All the senate of the people of Israel' (gerousia, the council of elders) is Luke piling term upon term to stress that they convened the entire official body in its most solemn, formal session — a term with deep roots, for a 'senate of elders' had governed the nation since the days of the Maccabees and before, and grew into the Sanhedrin. And here is the quiet irony Luke means us to feel: the full might of the establishment is ponderously assembled, and officers are sent to fetch prisoners — who are no longer there. The grandest court in Israel grinds into motion against men God has already set free and who are, at that very hour, teaching in the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, and they returned and reported, "We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside."
verseByVerse.commentary: The divine comedy of sovereign power: the prison is perfectly secure — locked doors, guards at their posts — and entirely empty. No human explanation is possible; the guards have been doing their job correctly. The report is a perfectly preserved miracle: everything that should have contained the apostles is in place; the apostles alone are absent. Luke records the detail with characteristic restraint, allowing the reader to feel the officers' bewilderment without editorializing. God has done what God always does: used locked doors to display his freedom.
