verseByVerse.quote: Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, "Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The perplexity of the authorities is genuine — they cannot explain the empty prison, and they have no strategy for what it means. 'Wondering what this would come to' — they sense that events are moving in a direction they cannot control. The interruption of someone's arrival with news is almost farcical: the men you imprisoned are back in the temple teaching. The cycle of arrest and proclamation is already completing its second revolution. The word that the authorities cannot silence is being proclaimed in the building they control.

A brief word on the two named here. The 'captain of the temple' (stratēgos; Hebrew sagan) was the chief officer of the temple, second in rank only to the high priest himself — a senior priest who commanded the Levitical temple guard, kept order in the precincts, held the power of arrest (it was he who helped seize Jesus, Luke 22:4, 52, and the apostles, Acts 4:1), and was often the high priest's deputy and next in line. The 'chief priests' (archiereis) were the priestly aristocracy at the top of the temple hierarchy: the high priest, former high priests who kept the title and influence, and the heads of the leading priestly families — a small, mostly Sadducean elite who controlled the temple administration and were prominent in the Sanhedrin. In short, this is the temple's entire ruling establishment — its head of security and its senior clergy — standing helpless and 'greatly perplexed' before an empty cell.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second arrest is conducted with notable timidity: 'not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people.' The council's authority over the apostles depends on the people's neutrality — the moment the community sides with the apostles, the council cannot enforce its will without triggering a riot. The apostles are brought before the council, but the authorities' fear of the people constrains their options from the beginning. The gospel's popularity is itself a form of protection, though the apostles are not counting on it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest questioned them, saying, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest's complaint is an inadvertent testimony: 'you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching.' The very thing they were trying to prevent has happened on a city-wide scale. 'You intend to bring this man's blood upon us' — the council's bad conscience about the crucifixion surfaces. They know what they did; they fear the crowd's reaction; and they cannot silence the ones who keep announcing it. 'This man's blood' — they will not speak the name. The refusal to name Jesus is the first of many failed attempts to suppress him by silence.

'To bring this man's blood upon us' uses an old Hebrew idiom for bloodguilt — to hold someone responsible for a death, to lay the guilt of it at his door (Lev. 20:9; Josh. 2:19; 2 Sam. 1:16; Ezek. 33:4). The council fears the apostles are publicly fastening on them the charge of having murdered Jesus — and they are quite right to fear it, for that is exactly what the apostles have been doing: 'you crucified and killed' him, 'whom you killed by hanging him on a tree' (Acts 2:23, 36; 3:15; 5:30). The irony is bitter: at Jesus' trial this same leadership had stirred the crowd to cry, 'His blood be on us and on our children!' (Matt. 27:25) — they once called the bloodguilt down on themselves; now they are terrified of being held to it. But notice where their fear is aimed — not at their guilt, but at the men who name it. They want to silence the accusation rather than be cleansed of the blood, and that is their tragedy. For there was a way to be rid of this man's blood, and it was not to muzzle the preachers but to be washed in the very blood they had shed. The blood that lay 'upon them' as guilt was being held out to them as atonement: 'repent... for the forgiveness of your sins' (Acts 2:36–38). The accusation and the cure were one and the same blood.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'We must obey God rather than men' — the church's permanent answer to the permanent question. This is not individualistic 'follow your conscience' — it is the recognition of a hierarchy of authority in which the command of the living God supersedes the command of human institutions. The apostles do not claim political immunity or special rights; they claim a higher obligation. And they immediately demonstrate what obeying God looks like: proclaiming that God raised Jesus, who was killed by hanging on a tree — citing Deuteronomy 21:23, which named crucifixion as a curse. Jesus bore the curse that we deserved. (cf. Dan. 3:16–18; Acts 4:19–20)

verseByVerse.quote: "God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Leader and Savior' (archēgon kai sōtēra) — the crucified one is now the Leader who blazed the trail through death to resurrection and the Savior who offers repentance and forgiveness. 'To give repentance to Israel' — repentance itself is God's gift, not human achievement; the same God who commands it supplies it through the exalted Jesus. Two witnesses testify to these things: the apostles (human eyewitnesses of the resurrection) and the Holy Spirit (divine confirmation given to those who obey). The council cannot refute either witness.

In what way is the Holy Spirit a 'witness'? Jesus had promised exactly this pairing: 'the Spirit of truth... will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness' (John 15:26–27) — two witnesses, as the Law required (Deut. 19:15). The Spirit testifies in several joined ways. By his very outpouring: the fact that God has poured out the Spirit is itself proof that the crucified Jesus is risen and enthroned, for only the exalted Christ could send him — 'having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves see and hear' (Acts 2:33). The Spirit's presence in the church is living evidence of the resurrection the apostles proclaim. By empowering their testimony: the Spirit emboldens and speaks through the witnesses themselves (Acts 1:8; 4:8, 31). By outward attestation: the signs, wonders, and the transformed, multiplying church are God bearing witness 'by gifts of the Holy Spirit' (Heb. 2:4). And by inward conviction: the Spirit presses the truth home on the conscience, convicting the world of sin and righteousness and judgment (John 16:8–11) and confirming the gospel within the believer (Rom. 8:16). So the council faces not merely the word of a few fishermen but the testimony of God himself: a witness they can imprison no more than they could keep the prison shut.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council's response to the apostolic declaration is rage — not refutation, not deliberation, but the visceral fury of those whose authority has been publicly and repeatedly defied. They 'wanted to kill them' — the same impulse that led to the crucifixion is now directed at his witnesses. But God's providential care for his messengers operates through an unlikely instrument: Gamaliel, the most respected Pharisee of his generation (Paul's own teacher, 22:3), whose caution and authority are sufficient to pause the council's murderous intent.

Beyond the New Testament, Jewish sources tell us a fair amount about Gamaliel — though it is best weighed as tradition rather than certified biography. He is remembered as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder (Gamaliel I), one of the most honoured sages of his age and, by Jewish tradition, a descendant (commonly, the grandson) of the famed Hillel and a leader of Hillel's school; he is traditionally reckoned the first to bear the exalted title 'Rabban' ('our master'), a rank above 'Rabbi.' The Mishnah pays him a striking tribute: 'When Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the glory of the Torah ceased, and purity and piety died' (Sotah 9:15). Tradition also credits him with several legal rulings (takkanot) made for the public good, including protections for women in the law of divorce (Mishnah Gittin 4). And, as Luke notes elsewhere, the young Saul of Tarsus — the future apostle Paul — was trained 'at the feet of Gamaliel' (Acts 22:3). (A much later Christian legend claimed Gamaliel secretly became a believer and that his remains were found in AD 415; but this has no historical foundation and should be set aside.)

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, followed him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary: Gamaliel's argument is pragmatic rather than theological: he offers historical precedents of messianic movements that collapsed when their leaders died. Theudas (and Judas the Galilean) rose, gathered followers, died, and their movements dissolved. If the Jesus movement is merely human, it will follow the same pattern — why risk the council's reputation and the people's anger for what will collapse on its own? Gamaliel's reasoning is provident without being evangelical: he is right about the outcome (the gospel will not fail) but wrong about the mechanism (it will not fail because Jesus rose).

verseByVerse.quote: "After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;"
verseByVerse.commentary: Judas the Galilean's revolt at the time of Quirinius's census (AD 6) was better known and more politically charged than Theudas's movement — the mention of it would have resonated deeply with the council. Gamaliel's principle ('if it is of man, it will fail') is the kind of wisdom that sounds profound but avoids the actual question: is it of God? His counsel is a deferral, not a judgment. But it serves God's purpose: the apostles are not killed, the mission continues, and Gamaliel himself is perhaps set wondering whether this movement is different from the ones he named.

verseByVerse.quote: "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" So they took his advice.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You might even be found opposing God' — the possibility Gamaliel raises is the one the reader knows is actual: the council is opposing God, precisely as Gamaliel feared. His warning contains more truth than he understands. 'They took his advice' — God uses the caution of a respected Pharisee to protect his messengers. The council cannot refute the gospel; they can only be restrained from murdering its proclaimers. Providence works through the wisdom of those who do not fully understand what they are being wise about.

verseByVerse.quote: and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council cannot kill the apostles (Gamaliel's counsel has prevented it) but they can punish them — and they do: forty lashes less one (the standard Jewish punishment for contempt of authority). The charge is repeated: 'not to speak in the name of Jesus.' The beating is meant to break the boldness; the charge is meant to silence the proclamation. Neither will succeed. The apostles emerge from the flogging not broken but unbowed, not silent but more vocal. Suffering for the name does not diminish their willingness to speak it.

A brief word for the everyday reader on what 'speaking in the name of Jesus' means. In the Bible a 'name' stands for the whole person — his identity, his character, and above all his authority. To do or say something 'in someone's name' is to act on his behalf, as his representative, by his authority — the way an ambassador speaks not his own mind but his king's, or a constable says 'stop, in the name of the law.' So when the apostles 'spoke in the name of Jesus,' they were not merely mentioning him; they were publicly proclaiming who he is — the crucified and risen Lord — and calling people to trust and obey him, and doing it as his authorized messengers, backed by his authority and not their own (as when the lame man was healed 'in the name of Jesus Christ,' 3:6, and 'there is salvation in no one else,' 4:12). That is exactly what the council wanted to stop: not idle talk, but the authoritative announcement that Jesus is Lord. To forbid the name was to forbid Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and proclaiming Jesus as the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name' — the flogging is not a tragedy but a privilege. The apostles understand what Paul will later articulate: 'it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake' (Philippians 1:29). The joy is not stoic endurance but genuine gladness — they have entered into the fellowship of Christ's sufferings. And the response is not retreat but advance: every day, temple and homes, teaching and proclaiming Jesus as the Christ. Nothing can stop this. (cf. Matt. 5:11–12; 1 Pet. 4:13–14)

5.theology: The Holiness of God in the New Covenant Community. The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are not anomalies — they have a precise parallel in Leviticus 10, where Nadab and Abihu are struck dead at the founding of the tabernacle worship. At every founding moment of a new covenant expression, God makes his holiness unmistakable. He did it at Sinai. He did it in the wilderness. He does it here, at the birth of the church. The message is the same: I am holy. You are dwelling in the presence of the Holy One. This is not a place for pretence. It is not that God is more severe in the new covenant than the old; it is that the new covenant community lives in an even closer proximity to the Holy Spirit than any previous generation, and proximity to holiness demands purity.
5.examples:
Then: A Jerusalem church five weeks old, discovering that the Spirit who fills them also searches them — and that the God of grace is also the God of holiness. The fear that fell on the church was not paralyzing; the next verse tells us that believers were added to the Lord in multitudes. Healthy fear of God does not drive people away from him; it drives away the casual, and draws in the sincere.

Now: The contemporary church has largely lost the category of the fear of God. We speak of grace, love, and welcome — and rightly so. But a church that never trembles before the holiness of God has not understood grace; it has domesticated it. Ananias and Sapphira remind every generation that the Spirit cannot be fooled, that the church is not a social club, and that God’s presence is still a consuming fire.

6.title: The Choosing of the Seven
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. <sup>2</sup>And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. <sup>4</sup>But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” <sup>5</sup>And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. <sup>6</sup>These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <sup>7</sup>And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. <sup>8</sup>And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. <sup>9</sup>Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen. <sup>10</sup>But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking. <sup>11</sup>Then they secretly instigated men who said, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” <sup>12</sup>And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council, <sup>13</sup>and they set up false witnesses who said, “This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, <sup>14</sup>for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.” <sup>15</sup>And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
6.overview:
The church is growing — and growth creates problems. The Hellenist widows are being neglected in the daily distribution. This is not a scandal; it is what happens when an organism grows faster than its structures can accommodate. The twelve could try to do everything. Instead they do something remarkable: they name the problem plainly, they define their own calling with precision (“we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the Word”), and they delegate to men of character and Spirit.

The result is instructive: “the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem.” When the church’s structures serve the Word rather than compete with it, the Word runs. Ministry organisation is not bureaucracy — it is stewardship of the mission.

But Luke also introduces Stephen, and with Stephen the chapter darkens. He is full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, full of grace and power. He does wonders no one can deny. He speaks with a wisdom the opposition cannot withstand. So they do what those who cannot win an argument always do: they lie. And Stephen, standing before the council with false witnesses arrayed against him, has a face like the face of an angel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Appointment of the Seven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first organizational crisis in the church is also the first demonstration of the church's Spirit-guided wisdom. A complaint arises: the Hellenistic Jewish widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The complaint is not theological but administrative — a failure of pastoral care that threatens the church's unity across its cultural divide. The apostles' response is both principled and practical: they will not abandon the ministry of the Word and prayer for table service, but they will ensure that table service receives Spirit-filled, wisdom-endowed leadership of its own.

The appointment of the Seven is not merely organizational efficiency; it is a theological act. Seven men, all with Greek names, all apparently from the Hellenistic Jewish community that felt overlooked, are set apart by prayer and the laying on of hands. The community that felt marginalized receives representation in leadership. And the result: the word of God continued to increase, the number of disciples multiplied greatly, and a large number of priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
Word and Service in the Church

The apostles' insistence that they must not 'give up preaching the word of God to serve tables' (v. 2) is not a hierarchy of dignity but a principle of vocation. Every member of the body is called to a specific ministry; the body is impoverished when people are given tasks that prevent them from fulfilling their God-given calling. The Seven are not 'junior ministers' — Stephen will prove to be one of the most theologically powerful figures in Acts. But their calling is to table service, and that calling is as Spirit-endowed as the apostolic calling to the word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The organizational problem threatened to divide the church along cultural lines (Hebrew vs Hellenistic Jews). The Spirit-guided solution served the marginalized community by placing them in leadership. Now: Every church must wrestle with the question of who is being overlooked in its pastoral care — and the answer always involves the Spirit-filled appointment of the right people to the right ministries.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables."
verseByVerse.commentary: The complaint surfaces at the intersection of rapid growth and cultural difference: Hellenistic Jewish widows (Greek-speaking, from the Diaspora) are being overlooked compared to Hebrew-speaking widows. The oversight may be unintentional — the product of language barriers and the expanding scale of the community — but its effect is to create a have and have-not division along ethnic lines. The twelve's response is principled: the ministry of the word cannot be sacrificed for administrative needs, but administrative needs cannot be neglected either. Both are genuine callings; neither can absorb the other.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this task. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."
verseByVerse.commentary: The qualifications the twelve require for table service — 'good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom' — are not lesser than the qualifications for preaching. Every ministry that represents Christ to the community requires the Spirit and wisdom; the only difference is the specific form the service takes. The apostles' insistence on their own 'prayer and the ministry of the word' is not a claim of superiority but a recognition of vocation: they are called to these specific ministries, and the community is impoverished if they abandon them for tasks others can fulfill. (cf. 1 Tim. 4:13; 2 Tim. 4:2)

verseByVerse.quote: And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All seven names are Greek — the community chose to address the Hellenistic complaint by placing Hellenistic leaders in charge of the distribution. This is practical wisdom guided by Spirit-sensitivity: honor the marginalized by entrusting leadership to them. The laying on of hands by the apostles is the public act of commissioning, setting apart, and praying for the Spirit's empowerment for this specific ministry. Stephen is immediately distinguished: 'full of faith and of the Holy Spirit.' He will not remain a table-server for long; the Spirit fills people to overflow.

'Full of faith and of the Holy Spirit' — but how could anyone tell that Stephen was full of the Spirit? Notice that the apostles had told the church to pick out such men (v. 3, 'men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom') — which means the fullness was not a hidden, private claim but something the congregation could actually recognise. The Spirit's fullness shows itself, and over time it is unmistakable. It shows in character — the fruit the Spirit grows: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, gentleness, self-control (Gal. 5:22–23), seen steadily enough to earn a man 'good repute.' It shows in wisdom — the way he speaks and handles matters (with Stephen, a wisdom his opponents 'could not withstand,' v. 10). It shows in faith, a settled trust and boldness; and in Stephen's case it would soon show in grace and power, in 'great wonders and signs' (v. 8), and even in a face that shone 'like the face of an angel' (v. 15). In short, the church needed no special revelation; they could see the Spirit in how Stephen lived, spoke, and served. This is Jesus' own rule: 'you will recognise them by their fruits' (Matt. 7:16, 20). And note the lovely ordinariness of it — these Spirit-filled men were being chosen to wait on tables and sort out a food dispute; fullness of the Spirit is proved first in faithful, humble, everyday service, not only in the spectacular.

'They prayed and laid their hands on them' — the laying on of hands is a gesture the Bible uses in several ways, and its weight here is best read against its Old Testament roots. It was used for blessing (Jacob over Ephraim and Manasseh, Gen. 48:14; Jesus over the children, Mark 10:16); for identifying with a sacrifice (the worshipper's hand on the animal's head, Lev. 1:4; the high priest's hands on the scapegoat, Lev. 16:21); and, closest to our verse, for commissioning a person to an office or task. The pattern text is Moses and Joshua: 'Take Joshua... a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him... and commission him in their sight' (Num. 27:18–20), so that afterward 'Joshua... was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him' (Deut. 34:9). That is just what happens here: the seven are publicly set apart and authorised for their ministry, with prayer that God would equip them by his Spirit. The New Testament keeps the practice for appointing to ministry — Barnabas and Saul are sent out the same way (Acts 13:3), and Timothy received his gift 'when the council of elders laid their hands on you' (1 Tim. 4:14; 2 Tim. 1:6). Two things to hold clear: the gesture is never magic — it is always joined to prayer, and it is the prayer that asks God to act; and it is a public act — the church openly recognising and commissioning those God has called, so all may see who is set apart and for what. (Scripture even warns it must not be done lightly: 'do not be hasty in the laying on of hands,' 1 Tim. 5:22.)

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary: The organizational solution produces spiritual fruitfulness: word increase, disciple multiplication, and — most dramatically — 'a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.' The priests who served in the temple at whose gates the lame man was healed, in whose courts the apostles taught, are now submitting themselves to the gospel. The word 'obedient' is significant: faith is not merely intellectual assent but the submission of the whole self to the authority of the risen Lord. The gospel is penetrating the very heart of the religious establishment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Stephen: The Man Who Couldn't Be Stopped
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Stephen refuses to stay in his lane. Appointed to distribute food, he moves immediately into public disputation and Spirit-powered signs and wonders — because the Spirit who fills him is the Spirit of proclamation, and no organizational category can contain him. The opposition he encounters is instructive: when his opponents cannot win the argument (they 'could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking'), they do what every movement that cannot defeat truth does: they manufacture false witnesses and drag him before the council on invented charges.

The false witnesses' accusation is a distorted version of a truth: Stephen has been speaking about Jesus changing the Mosaic customs and the temple. He has been — and he is right to do so. The old order of temple and Torah is giving way to the new order of the Spirit and the fulfillment of all that the temple and Torah pointed toward. Stephen's face shines like an angel: this is not allegory but theophanic reality — the man who is about to die for the gospel is already reflecting the glory of the Lord he is going to see.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cost of Prophetic Witness

Stephen's arrest and trial follow the exact pattern of Jesus's arrest and trial: false witnesses, charges of blasphemy against the temple and the law, the council's rage. This is not coincidence — it is the pattern of all prophetic witness that challenges entrenched religious power. The servant is not above the master. Reformed theology sees in Stephen's fate the confirmation that genuine gospel proclamation will always meet the resistance of those whose power depends on the maintenance of the status quo that the gospel overturns.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen's opponents could not withstand his wisdom but refused to yield to it — so they resorted to violence and false testimony. The gospel will not always win the argument in the short term; sometimes it wins the martyr's crown first. Now: The church is called to the same quality of Spirit-and-wisdom witness that Stephen embodied, knowing that the outcome is in God's hands and that even martyrdom is not defeat.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen refuses to stay in his administrative lane. The Spirit who fills him for table service is the Spirit of proclamation, and that Spirit cannot be contained by an organizational role. 'Full of grace and power' — the grace that marks his character and the power that accompanies his ministry are both gifts of the same Spirit who appointed him to distribute bread.

What does 'full of grace and power' mean? It is the third time Luke describes Stephen with 'full of...' (full of faith and the Spirit, v. 5; of the Spirit and wisdom, v. 3; now of grace and power) — he is a man saturated by God. Grace (charis) carries two notes that belong together: the favour of God resting richly upon him — his life freely enabled and blessed by God, nothing of it earned — and the graciousness that such favour produces, the winsome, Christlike attractiveness of a man shaped by grace (the same word lies behind Jesus' 'gracious words,' Luke 4:22, and 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14). Power (dynamis) is the Spirit's enabling might — the very power Jesus promised, 'you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you' (Acts 1:8) — here overflowing in 'great wonders and signs.' Note the order: grace first, then power. The favour and gracious character come first, and the power flows out of a life already full of grace; power without grace is a dangerous thing, but Stephen had both. And mark who this is: not an apostle, but one of the seven chosen to wait on tables (vv. 3–5) — yet full of grace and power and working wonders that Luke had until now reported of the apostles alone (2:43; 5:12). The grace and power of God were never the private property of the Twelve; they filled a humble table-servant who was wholly yielded to the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up and disputed with Stephen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the first mention of a synagogue in Acts, so a word on what it was. The synagogue (Greek synagōgē, simply 'a gathering') was the local Jewish assembly and meeting-house — not the temple (there was only one temple, in Jerusalem), but a community centre found in every town and city where Jews lived, for the reading and study of Scripture, prayer, and teaching. It arose after the Babylonian exile, when the temple lay in ruins and the people were scattered, and by Jesus' and Paul's day it was the heartbeat of Jewish life everywhere. (For its origins, how a synagogue service ran, and whether Jews still gather so today, see the fuller note at 13:15.) A great city like Jerusalem held many synagogues, often grouped by homeland or language — which brings us to this one.

'The synagogue of the Freedmen' — who were these opponents? 'Freedmen' (Libertinoi, a Latin word, libertini) means freed slaves and their descendants. The likeliest background is that these were Jews, or the children of Jews, who had been taken captive — many when the Roman general Pompey conquered Jerusalem in 63 BC — carried off to Rome as slaves, later set free, and whose families formed a distinct community; some settled again in Jerusalem with their own synagogue. Jerusalem held many such synagogues for Greek-speaking Jews of the diaspora, and Luke names several homelands here: Cyrene (North Africa), Alexandria (Egypt), and Cilicia and Asia (regions of Asia Minor). (Whether this means one synagogue or two or more is grammatically uncertain; the number is not the point.) Notice that these were all Hellenistic (Greek-speaking) Jews — the very group Stephen himself belonged to (6:1). So this first great clash is a debate among fellow Greek-speaking Jews, Hellenist against Hellenist.

And one homeland on the list should make the reader sit up: Cilicia — the province of Tarsus, and so the home region of Saul (Paul), who appears just a few verses later, standing by and approving Stephen's death (7:58; 8:1). Scripture does not say outright that Saul was among these particular disputants, but he was a zealous Cilician Pharisee, present at the scene; many think it likely he was in the thick of it. They 'rose up and disputed with Stephen' — and finding (v. 10) that they could not withstand his Spirit-given wisdom, they would soon abandon argument for false witness and violence. The synagogue debate is the arena of the church's first great apologetic confrontation — and, quite possibly, the place where the future apostle Paul first set himself against the name of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: But they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit' — the combination is invincible. Wisdom alone can be out-argued; Spirit alone can be dismissed as enthusiasm. Together they constitute an irrefutable witness: the logos of Scripture rightly handled and the dynamis of divine presence confirming it. When truth cannot be defeated by reason, those determined not to yield to it resort to other means. Stephen's opponents, unable to win the argument, will manufacture a legal case — the pattern of every human power that cannot refute the gospel. (cf. Luke 21:15; Matt. 10:19–20)

verseByVerse.quote: Then they secretly instigated men who said, "We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God." And they stirred up the people and the elders and the scribes, and they came upon him and seized him and brought him before the council,
verseByVerse.commentary: The mechanism of persecution when argumentation fails: secret instigation, manufactured charges, stirred-up crowds, and the arrest of the one who cannot be silenced by debate. 'Secret instigation' — they cannot make their case publicly, so they work in the shadows, priming witnesses to make claims they know are distortions. The charge of blasphemy against Moses and God is the most serious possible — it carries the death penalty. What cannot be refuted in open argument will be prosecuted in a closed council.

verseByVerse.quote: and they set up false witnesses who said, "This man never ceases to speak words against this holy place and the law, for we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and will change the customs that Moses delivered to us."
verseByVerse.commentary: The false witnesses' charge is a distortion of real teaching. Stephen has been speaking about Jesus as the fulfillment and transformation of temple and Torah — and he is right to do so. Jesus himself had spoken of the temple's destruction and the arrival of something greater (John 2:19; Matthew 12:6). The distortion lies in 'destroy' and 'change' framed as threats rather than fulfillments. The witnesses take genuine apostolic proclamation, remove its context and its hope, and present the residue as blasphemy. Truth, stripped of its framework, becomes a lie.

verseByVerse.quote: And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The council stares at the accused blasphemer and sees a face like an angel — the glory of God reflected in the face of his servant (2 Corinthians 3:18). Luke does not explain the phenomenon; he simply records it. Stephen already belongs to the world he is about to enter. The council that is about to pass judgment on him is sitting in the presence of a man upon whom the divine glory has already rested — and they do not recognize it. They will stone a face like an angel, as their ancestors stoned the prophets whose words they could not endure.

6.theology: Word and Deed, Order and Spirit. Acts 6 is the New Testament’s foundational text on church structure. It establishes that the body has different members with different callings; that no one person can or should do everything; that the criterion for all ministry, however practical, is character shaped by the Spirit; and that when ministry is rightly ordered, the Word — not the institution, not the ministers — is what grows. This is not a management manual; it is a theology of the church as the body of Christ, each member functioning according to its calling, all of it in service of the one mission: that the Word of God would run and be glorified.
6.examples:
Then: A rapidly growing Jerusalem church discovering that love without structure produces injustice — the widows being neglected are real women with real needs — and that structure without love produces dead religion. The seven are the church’s solution: Spirit-filled servants who bring both.

Now: Every growing church faces the tension of Acts 6: how do we care well for people without the leaders becoming so consumed with management that the Word is starved? The answer is not to choose between pastoral care and proclamation; it is to raise up men and women of Spirit and wisdom to share the load — and then to watch what God does with a church that is both devoted to the Word and devoted to its neighbours.

7.title: The Speech of Stephen
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the high priest said, “Are these things so?” <sup>2</sup>And Stephen said: “Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, <sup>3</sup>and said to him, ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred and go into the land that I will show you.’ <sup>4</sup>Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. <sup>5</sup>Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child. <sup>6</sup>And God spoke to this effect—that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave them and afflict them four hundred years. <sup>7</sup>But I will judge the nation that they serve, said God, and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.’ <sup>8</sup>And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs. <sup>9</sup>“And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him <sup>10</sup>and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. <sup>11</sup>Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. <sup>12</sup>But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit. <sup>13</sup>And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh. <sup>14</sup>And Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all. <sup>15</sup>And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, <sup>16</sup>and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem. <sup>17</sup>“But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt <sup>18</sup>until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph. <sup>19</sup>He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not be kept alive. <sup>20</sup>At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God’s sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father’s house, <sup>21</sup>and when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. <sup>22</sup>And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds. <sup>23</sup>“When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. <sup>24</sup>And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian. <sup>25</sup>He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. <sup>26</sup>And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?’ <sup>27</sup>But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? <sup>28</sup>Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ <sup>29</sup>At this retort Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. <sup>30</sup>“Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. <sup>31</sup>When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.’ And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. <sup>33</sup>Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. <sup>34</sup>I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.’ <sup>35</sup>“This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. <sup>36</sup>This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years. <sup>37</sup>This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.’ <sup>38</sup>This is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us. <sup>39</sup>Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, <sup>40</sup>saying to Aaron, ‘Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.’ <sup>41</sup>And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. <sup>42</sup>But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you bring to me slaughtered beasts and sacrifices, during the forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? <sup>43</sup>You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.’ <sup>44</sup>“Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. <sup>45</sup>Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David, <sup>46</sup>who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. <sup>47</sup>But it was Solomon who built him a house. <sup>48</sup>Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, <sup>49</sup>‘Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? <sup>50</sup>Did not my hand make all these things?’ <sup>51</sup>“You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you. <sup>52</sup>Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, <sup>53</sup>you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.” <sup>54</sup>Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. <sup>55</sup>But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. <sup>56</sup>And he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” <sup>57</sup>But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and ran together at him. <sup>58</sup>Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. <sup>59</sup>And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” <sup>60</sup>And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
7.overview:
Stephen’s speech is the longest in Acts and one of the most daring pieces of rhetoric in the New Testament. He does not defend himself. He puts Israel on trial. From Abraham to Solomon to the council before him, he traces a single thread through the whole of salvation history: God always moves forward, and Israel always resists. The patriarchs sold Joseph into Egypt — but God was with him. Israel rejected Moses — twice — but God used him to redeem them. Israel turned to idols in the wilderness. Israel refused to keep the law they received. And now the same pattern reaches its fullest expression: they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One himself.

The speech dismantles the two pillars of Jewish security: the temple and the law. The Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands — he never did. And the law you received from angels, you never kept. Strip away the temple and the law as sources of security, and what remains? Only the God who appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before there was any temple, before there was any law — the God who has been moving toward his people and through his people and despite his people, from the beginning.

Then Stephen looks up and sees what the council cannot see: the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. Standing — not seated. As if the Son of Man rose to his feet to receive his first martyr home. They stop their ears and rush at him. He dies praying his Lord’s own prayer for his killers. And at the edge of the scene, holding the coats, is a young man named Saul.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–50 — Stephen's Defense: Israel's History and God's Patience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin is the longest speech in Acts and one of the most important theological documents in the New Testament. It is not a defense in the legal sense — Stephen makes no argument for his innocence. It is a counter-indictment: a recital of Israel's history that demonstrates that the pattern of rejecting God's messengers, preferring Egypt to the promised land, worshipping idols while possessing the law, and trusting in a building more than in the God the building could not contain — this pattern has characterized Israel across its entire history. The council that is about to stone Stephen is simply the latest iteration of what Israel has always done to the prophets.

The speech moves through Abraham (the God who calls is not tied to a particular land), Joseph (the rejected one who became the savior of his brothers), Moses (the deliverer rejected by Israel twice), and the tabernacle/temple (which David wanted to build but Solomon built, even though 'the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands'). At each turn, Stephen is making the same point: God's presence and purpose are not limited to the institutions Israel has made central — and Israel has consistently resisted the God who exceeds those institutions.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Temple and the Transcendence of God

Stephen's climax in v. 48 ('the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands') is not anti-temple polemic in the abstract — it is the prophetic critique rooted in Isaiah 66:1–2 that the temple itself contained. Solomon himself acknowledged at the dedication that no building could contain God (1 Kings 8:27). The problem is not the temple but the reduction of God to a building: the belief that the presence of the temple in Jerusalem means the presence of God in a manageable, controllable form. Reformed theology sees in Stephen's critique the permanent warning against every institutionalization of God that substitutes the sign for the reality.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen recited Israel's history to demonstrate that rejection of God's messengers was Israel's characteristic pattern — and that the council was repeating it. The history of the church confirms that prophetic witness against institutional comfort is always costly. Now: The church must constantly examine whether it is trusting in its buildings, traditions, and structures more than in the living God who will not be contained by any of them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest said, "Are these things so?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The high priest's opening question is the briefest possible — 'Are these things so?' — and it hands Stephen the floor for the longest speech in Acts. The question expects a defense; what it receives is a counter-indictment. The man on trial becomes the prosecutor; the prosecutors become the defendants. This is what the Spirit does with an opportunity: he takes the space given and fills it with the truth that the questioners least want to hear but most need to.

verseByVerse.quote: And Stephen said: "Brothers and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, and said to him, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred and to the land that I will show you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The God of glory' — Stephen's opening phrase sets the theological agenda for the entire speech. God is glorious, and his glory is not tied to any place. God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia — outside the promised land, outside Israel's territory, before there was an Israel. The call of Abraham is the paradigm of Stephen's entire argument: God acts sovereignly, outside every institutional and geographical boundary his people will later mistake for his essence. The God of glory cannot be contained in any house, land, or establishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And after his father died, God removed him from there into this land in which you are now living. Yet he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his offspring after him, though he had no child.
verseByVerse.commentary: The gap between promise and possession is Stephen's first point: God promised Abraham the land of Canaan, then gave him 'not even a foot's length.' Abraham spent his entire life as a sojourner in the land of promise — owning none of it, living in tents, holding the promise by faith. The point for the council is subtle and devastating: if Abraham — the founding father of the covenant community — lived his entire life by faith in an unfulfilled promise, then land-possession and institutional establishment cannot be the essence of belonging to the God of glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke to this effect — that his offspring would be sojourners in a land belonging to others, who would enslave and afflict them four hundred years. 'But I will judge the nation that they serve,' said God, 'and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary: God not only promised land; he predicted exile and slavery before the promise would be fulfilled. The four hundred years of Egyptian bondage were not an accident interrupting the plan — they were part of it. 'I will judge the nation that they serve, and after that they shall come out and worship me in this place' — the 'this place' is Mount Sinai (Exodus 3:12), not the Jerusalem temple. God's people worshipped him in the wilderness, at a burning bush, before there was a temple. The Spirit's presence preceded the institution.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave him the covenant of circumcision. And so Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him on the eighth day, and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant sign of circumcision is given in this context of promise-without-possession: the seal of the covenant is not attached to land or temple but to the promise of God alone. Abraham circumcised Isaac; Isaac circumcised Jacob; Jacob's sons became the twelve patriarchs — the founding generation of Israel. The covenant is entirely portable, entirely personal, entirely dependent on the God who made it. Stephen's council audience bears the mark of a covenant that was designed from the beginning to be independent of any building.

Why call it 'the covenant of circumcision'? The phrase names the covenant by its sign. The covenant itself was God's promise to Abraham — a people, a land, and blessing for all nations (Gen. 12; 15; 17) — and when God formalised it he gave Abraham circumcision as its token in the flesh: 'This is my covenant... every male among you shall be circumcised... it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you' (Gen. 17:10–11). Sign and covenant became so bound together that the whole covenant could be called simply 'the covenant of circumcision' — the covenant whose seal was circumcision, much as we might name an agreement by its signature. Two things are worth holding here. First, the sign sealed a promise already received by faith: Abraham was counted righteous through faith (Gen. 15:6) before he was ever circumcised (Gen. 17), so circumcision was 'a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith' (Rom. 4:11) — the mark never earned the promise; it pointed to it. Second, the eighth-day circumcision of Isaac, then of Jacob's line down to the twelve patriarchs, shows the covenant people being marked out generation by generation — the family through whom, in the end, the blessing to all nations would come in Christ (cf. Gal. 3:8, 16).

verseByVerse.quote: "And the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him and rescued him out of all his afflictions and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household."
verseByVerse.commentary: Stephen's first explicit example of the pattern: Israel's own patriarchs — the founding twelve — sold their brother out of jealousy. The rejected one becomes the rescuer; the envied one becomes the savior. 'God was with him' — the presence of God did not leave Joseph when his brothers sold him; it accompanied him into Egypt, into Potiphar's house, into the prison, into Pharaoh's court. The God of glory is not tied to the land of Canaan; he is with his people wherever they are sent, even in slavery, even in prison.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there came a famine throughout all Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could not find food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers on their first visit."
verseByVerse.commentary: The famine that drives the patriarchs to Egypt is God's sovereign provision — the crisis that brings the rejected brother and the remaining brothers back together. The 'great affliction' of famine is the means by which God will accomplish the reunion and reconciliation that Joseph's rejection had interrupted. The first visit to Egypt is the beginning of the resolution: Jacob hears there is grain, he sends his sons, and they will unknowingly approach the one they sold. God's providential governance of history includes the famines as much as the harvests.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. And Joseph sent and summoned his father Jacob and all his kindred, seventy-five persons in all."
verseByVerse.commentary: The second visit is the turning point: Joseph reveals himself, and the family is reunited. The reunion is not achieved by human strategy but by divine orchestration — 'Joseph made himself known' at the moment God had prepared. The seventy-five persons who go down to Egypt represent the entire family of God's covenant people: they enter Egypt as a family and will emerge as a nation. The descent into Egypt is not a retreat from God's purposes; it is the path through which those purposes will be fulfilled.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jacob and the patriarchs die in Egypt — outside the promised land — and are carried back for burial. Their bones make the journey home that their lives could not complete. The purchase of the burial plot at Shechem by Abraham (Genesis 23; 33:19) is the only piece of the promised land that Abraham actually possessed: a grave. The patriarchs own the land in death before their descendants possess it in life. Even in death they are clinging to the promise — buried in the land that God swore to give them.

verseByVerse.quote: "But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had granted to Abraham, the people increased and multiplied in Egypt until there arose over Egypt another king who did not know Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The time of the promise drew near' — God's timing is exact; the four hundred years of sojourning (v. 6) are nearly complete. The very moment of preparation for the promise's fulfillment is also the moment of greatest danger: the new king who did not know Joseph is the instrument of the oppression that will make Israel cry out to God. The pattern repeats: as the promise approaches its fulfillment, the opposition intensifies. The darkness before the dawn is not a setback to God's plan but part of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "He dealt shrewdly with our race and forced our fathers to expose their infants, so that they would not survive. At this time Moses was born; and he was beautiful in God's sight. And he was brought up for three months in his father's house,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The decree of death against Israel's male infants is the backdrop against which Moses is born. 'Beautiful in God's sight' — the phrase points beyond physical appearance to divine election: this child is seen by God and destined for a purpose that the royal decree cannot prevent. Three months of concealment in his father's house — three months of faith and fear — prepare for the extraordinary rescue that follows. The God who preserved Israel in Egypt will preserve the deliverer whom Egypt is trying to destroy.

verseByVerse.quote: "and when he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter adopted him and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rescue of Moses through Pharaoh's own daughter is sovereign irony: the king who decreed death for Israel's sons ends up raising Israel's deliverer in his own palace. 'Instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, mighty in his words and deeds' — Luke uses the same description of Moses that he uses of Jesus in Luke 24:19. God prepares his deliverers in unexpected places: forty years of Egyptian court education producing the man who will lead Israel out of Egypt. The preparation takes place inside the very system being overcome.

What was 'the wisdom of the Egyptians'? Egypt was the great seat of learning in the ancient world — its name a byword for advanced knowledge (even of Solomon it is said his wisdom 'surpassed... all the wisdom of Egypt,' 1 Kings 4:30). It embraced mathematics and geometry (the skill behind the pyramids and the re-surveying of fields after each Nile flood), astronomy and the calendar, a famed medicine, architecture and engineering, the scribal art of writing, statecraft and administration, and a large body of moral 'instruction' literature — together with the lore of the priestly class. As Pharaoh's daughter's adopted son, raised in the royal court, Moses would have received the elite education of an Egyptian prince — the finest schooling the age could give, which left him 'mighty in words and deeds.' (The detail that he was trained in 'all' this wisdom is not stated in Exodus itself; it is the natural inference from his upbringing, preserved also in Jewish tradition — Philo and Josephus describe his education at length.) Stephen's deeper point soon follows: for all his Egyptian learning and natural greatness, Moses' first attempt to deliver Israel in his own strength failed (vv. 23–29), and he had to wait forty years in the desert for God's call. The world's finest wisdom equipped him, but it did not make him the deliverer — God did.

verseByVerse.quote: "When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended the oppressed man and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It came into his heart' — Moses acts from an impulse that Stephen characterizes as the beginning of a God-given calling: the desire to be with his people, to see them, to defend them. The defense of the oppressed Israelite is Moses's first act of solidarity with the people he was born to rescue. The violence is wrong in method even if right in motivation; God did not authorize this private act of vengeance. But the heart is already right: Moses's identification with the suffering Israelites against the Egyptian oppressor is genuine and costly.

verseByVerse.quote: "He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarreling and tried to reconcile them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why do you wrong each other?'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He supposed that his brothers would understand... but they did not understand' — the rejected deliverer is Stephen's second example of Israel's pattern. Moses came to his people with a God-given calling and a genuine desire to rescue them, and they did not recognize what God was doing through him. The parallel with Jesus is unmistakable: the one sent to rescue Israel is not recognized by those he comes to save. The second day's attempt at reconciliation ('you are brothers — why do you wrong each other?') is itself a portrait of the deliverer's heart: peacemaking before rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the man who was wronging his neighbor thrust him aside, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?' — the question thrown at Moses is the question Israel will throw at every prophet, and ultimately at Jesus himself (Luke 20:2). The challenge to authority is the characteristic response of those who want to be governed only by their own will. The taunt about the Egyptian killing exposes Moses's act and triggers his flight — but what actually drives Moses out is not the taunt but the recognition that Israel has rejected him. The first rejection of the deliverer prefigures every subsequent rejection.

verseByVerse.quote: "At this speech Moses fled and became an exile in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons."
verseByVerse.commentary: Forty years in Midian — forty years of exile as a result of being rejected by the people he came to save. Moses becomes an exile for the second time: first in Egypt (a Hebrew raised as an Egyptian), now in Midian (an Egyptian-trained Hebrew among a Midianite people). God's deliverers are consistently prepared in exile, away from the center of power and institutional prestige. The wilderness forms what the palace cannot: a man who has been stripped of everything except his dependence on God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and as he drew near to look, there came the voice of the Lord:"
verseByVerse.commentary: Forty more years pass in Midian before God speaks. The delay is not divine forgetfulness but divine timing: the Moses who flees Egypt in his own strength at forty is not yet the Moses who will lead Israel out with the staff of God at eighty. The wilderness of Sinai — remote, uninhabited, outside every institutional structure — is where God chooses to reveal himself to the one he will send to Egypt. 'A flame of fire in a bush' — fire is the sign of the divine presence (Exodus 19:18; Isaiah 6:4), and it burns here in a thornbush on a Midianite hillside.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob.' And Moses trembled and did not dare to look. Then the Lord said to him, 'Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I am the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob' — the voice identifies itself with the covenant God of the patriarchs, establishing continuity between the promise made to Abraham and the rescue about to be accomplished through Moses. Moses trembles and cannot look: the appropriate human response to the presence of the holy God is awe that makes one unable to sustain eye contact with the divine glory. 'Holy ground' — not the temple, not Jerusalem, but a patch of Midianite wilderness where God has chosen to be present. Holiness belongs to God, not to buildings.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you to Egypt.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I have surely seen... I have heard their groaning... I have come down to deliver them' — the three-fold divine initiative: observation, hearing, action. God is not absent from the suffering of his people; he sees, he hears, he acts. 'And now come, I will send you' — the sending of Moses is the form God's coming-down takes. The divine action and the human mission are inseparable: God delivers Israel by sending Moses. Stephen's council should be hearing the echo: God has come down to deliver his people again, and has sent Jesus — the prophet like Moses — to accomplish it.

verseByVerse.quote: "This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt and at the Red Sea and in the wilderness for forty years."
verseByVerse.commentary: The parallelism is devastating: the Moses Israel rejected ('who made you a ruler and a judge?') is the very Moses God sent as ruler and redeemer. The one they despised became the one they needed. The wonders and signs — in Egypt, at the Red Sea, in the wilderness — span the entire exodus and wilderness narrative: forty years of sustained miraculous ministry by the one Israel rejected at the beginning. Stephen is holding a mirror to the council: the pattern you enacted with Moses, you have now enacted with Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.' He is the one who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us."
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses himself predicted the prophet-like-Moses who would follow him (Deuteronomy 18:15) — and Moses is the one who 'received living oracles to give to us.' The law given at Sinai was received by the rejected-and-restored deliverer, mediated through an angel, given as 'living oracles' — not dead letters but the living word of the living God. The law is a gift from the same Moses who was rejected by Israel; rejecting the prophet-like-Moses (Jesus) is therefore a repetition of the original rejection of the law's own mediator.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt, saying to Aaron, 'Make for us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: At the height of Moses's ministry — while he was at Sinai receiving the living oracles — Israel made a golden calf and said 'we do not know what has become of him.' The people who have the deliverer abandon him at the moment of his greatest work. Stephen cites the golden calf episode not as a historical curiosity but as the defining demonstration of Israel's characteristic pattern: the tendency to 'turn to Egypt' in heart even after being delivered from it. The council that is judging Stephen has ancestors who worshipped an idol while Moses held the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol and were rejoicing in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets:"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Rejoicing in the works of their hands' — idolatry is always the worship of human production: the creature worshipping something it has made rather than the Creator who made it. And God's response to persistent idolatry is judicial abandonment: 'he gave them over' (Romans 1:24, 26, 28 — Paul draws on the same principle). The worship of the host of heaven that followed the golden calf was not Israel's choice alone; it was God's judgment on Israel's rejection of his provision and presence. The nation that would not worship the Lord was given idols to satisfy its preference.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images that you made to worship; and I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amos 5:25–27 provides the prophetic indictment: Israel's wilderness worship was never as pure as nostalgia imagined. The tent of Moloch and the star of Rephan were carried even in the wilderness — the idolatry was present from the beginning, not merely a later corruption. And the consequence is named: 'I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.' The Babylonian exile was not a historical accident but a divine judgment on the persistent pattern of rejecting God's messengers and worshipping man-made idols. Stephen's council inherits both the pattern and the warning.

Who were these two? Moloch (Molech) was a pagan deity, named as 'the abomination of the Ammonites' (1 Kings 11:7) and notorious across the region for child sacrifice — children 'passed through the fire' to him (Lev. 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10; Jer. 32:35). The name is tied to the Hebrew melek, 'king' — 'the King'-god (Hebrew scribes seem to have pointed it with the vowels of bosheth, 'shame,' a deliberate jab). The 'tent of Moloch' is a portable idol-shrine carried in procession — a grim parody of the tabernacle, God's own tent. Rephan (also spelled Remphan/Rompha) is 'the star of your god' — an astral deity, almost certainly the planet Saturn worshipped as a god; this is star-worship, the bowing to 'the host of heaven' that Scripture repeatedly condemns (Deut. 4:19; 2 Kings 21:3–5).

An honest word on the names: Stephen is quoting the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) of Amos 5:25–27, and its wording differs from the Hebrew, which at this point is genuinely obscure. Where the Hebrew has 'Sikkuth' and 'Kiyyun' (Chiun) — themselves probably names of Mesopotamian astral gods (Saturn again) — the Greek rendered them 'Moloch' and 'Rephan.' So the exact identifications are the best scholarly reconstruction, not certainty; but the sense is plain and that is Stephen's point: even in the wilderness — the very generation that carried God's tabernacle — Israel was also carrying the shrines of pagan star-gods. The idolatry his temple-proud accusers would rather forget ran right through their history from the start.

verseByVerse.quote: "Our fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as he who spoke to Moses directed him to make it, according to the pattern that he had seen. Our fathers in turn brought it in with Joshua when they dispossessed the nations that God drove out before our fathers. So it was until the days of David,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The tabernacle was divinely designed — 'according to the pattern that he had seen' (the heavenly archetype shown to Moses on Sinai, Exodus 25:9, 40) — and therefore genuinely sacred. Stephen is not dismissing it. But the tabernacle was portable, moveable, designed for a people on pilgrimage. It accompanied Israel into Canaan under Joshua, adapting to the geography of conquest and settlement. The tent of meeting traveled with the people of God, not the people of God with the tent. The tabernacle pointed beyond itself to something the land could not contain.

verseByVerse.quote: "who found favor in the sight of God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him."
verseByVerse.commentary: David found favor with God — David, the man after God's own heart (Acts 13:22; 1 Samuel 13:14). And what David wanted was to build a dwelling for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built the house, not David — because God told David his son would build it (2 Samuel 7:13). The distinction matters: David's desire was right (devotion to God's honor), but God redirected the timing and the builder. Even the best human initiatives for God's honor must be submitted to God's sovereign direction. The temple was God's gift, not Israel's achievement.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands, as the prophet says, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands' — the title 'Most High' (hypsistos) is itself an argument: the God who is Most High cannot be housed by what is lowest. Isaiah 66:1–2 places the decisive limit on every building: heaven is his throne and earth his footstool — what possible house could contain the God who fills both? The question is rhetorical and devastating. Solomon built the temple; Isaiah prophesied within sight of the temple; and Isaiah declares that the God whose presence the temple claimed to house cannot be contained by it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Did not my hand make all these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The closing rhetorical question answers itself: God made everything. The temple was made by human hands from materials that God made; the God who made all things cannot be contained in one of those things. Stephen's point is not that temples are wrong but that the confusion of the sign with the reality — treating the temple as the indispensable dwelling of a God who fills heaven and earth — is the theological error that the council's murderous defense of 'this holy place' represents. The God of glory exceeds every building, every institution, every establishment his people can construct.

For Old Joe there is a sweet turn here. If God never truly dwelt in the building, where is his dwelling now? The New Testament answers: in Christ first of all (Jesus called his own body 'this temple,' John 2:19–21, 'in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,' Col. 2:9), and then, through him, in his people — 'you are God's temple and God's Spirit dwells in you' (1 Cor. 3:16; 6:19; Eph. 2:21–22). The God too great for any house made of stone has chosen to make his home in the hearts of ordinary believers. Stephen's point is not that buildings are wrong, but that we must never trap the living God in a place or a thing while missing him where he truly dwells.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Stephen's sermon ends not with a conclusion but with an accusation — directed, for the first time in the speech, at the council itself. 'You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you.' The speech has been building to this: the entire recital of Israel's history was a mirror held up to the council so they could see themselves in it.
