They are the latest generation of prophet-killers; they have done to Jesus exactly what their ancestors did to the prophets who foretold him.

Stephen's vision at the moment of death is the most extraordinary detail in the entire passage: he sees the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. Not seated — standing, as if risen in welcome, or risen as a witness, at the right side of the Father. Stephen dies with his eyes open, seeing the one who died first. His last words are the words of Jesus on the cross, in reverse order: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' (cf. Psalm 31:5; Luke 23:46) and 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' (cf. Luke 23:34). The first martyr dies in the exact posture of his Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stephen and the Pattern of Martyrdom

Stephen's death establishes the pattern of Christian martyrdom for all subsequent generations: bearing witness to the truth regardless of the cost, seeing Christ in the moment of dying, forgiving the persecutors in the spirit of the crucified Lord. The word 'martyr' (martys) means 'witness' — and Stephen's death is witness in its most complete form: testimony sealed by blood. Reformed theology sees in martyrdom not heroic human achievement but the Spirit's sustaining grace taking the witness to the ultimate expression of their testimony.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Saul of Tarsus stood watching the coats of those who stoned Stephen, approving. The very man who would become the greatest missionary in history began as a persecutor. Stephen's prayer — 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' — may have been the first word of grace that Saul heard spoken toward him. Now: The prayer of the dying martyr for his killers is the most Christlike act a human being can perform — and the most powerful witness available to the church in the face of persecution.

verseByVerse.quote: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Stephen's abrupt turn from narrative to accusation marks the sermon's climax. 'Stiff-necked' (Exodus 32:9; 33:3) — the wilderness generation's characteristic description applied to the council. 'Uncircumcised in heart and ears' — the prophets' indictment of Israel's spiritual deafness (Jeremiah 4:4; 9:26; Ezekiel 44:9) applied to the men who pride themselves on their circumcision. 'You always resist the Holy Spirit' — not occasionally, not in some generations, but always. The resistance is the defining pattern of the history Stephen has just recited. (cf. Isa. 63:10; Heb. 3:7–8)

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it."
verseByVerse.commentary: The indictment reaches its zenith: every prophet who announced the Messiah was persecuted by the ancestors of the men now sitting in judgment on Stephen; and the council itself has 'betrayed and murdered' the Righteous One the prophets announced. The final accusation lands with double force: 'you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it.' They boast of the law; they killed its fulfillment. They received the most privileged communication from God and used it to justify the murder of the one to whom every law and prophet pointed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him. But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council grinds their teeth in fury; Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, sees heaven opened. The contrast is absolute: those who resist the Spirit are blinded by rage; the one filled with the Spirit sees the glory of God. The Spirit's fullness opens the eyes of the martyred witness to see what faith has always seen but now is confirmed beyond all doubt: the throne of God and Jesus at his right hand. 'Standing' — not the seated Lord of Psalm 110:1 but the Lord who stands to welcome his first martyr, or to rise as a witness in Stephen's defense before the divine court. (cf. Dan. 7:13–14; Heb. 12:2)

What does Luke mean by 'full of the Holy Spirit' here? It is a phrase he loves (he has already used it of Stephen at 6:3, 5, 8 — on how such fullness is recognised, see there), and it means a person so wholly yielded to and possessed by the Spirit that the Spirit's presence and power are manifest in and through him. But notice what it introduces at this moment. First, spiritual sight: filled with the Spirit, Stephen 'gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.' The Spirit gives him eyes for the unseen reality — 'the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God' and reveals what no eye could otherwise see (1 Cor. 2:9–10). Second, strength for the supreme test: this filling comes at the hour of his death, and it makes him able to die like his Lord — committing his spirit to Jesus (v. 59, as Jesus did to the Father) and forgiving his killers (v. 60, as Jesus did from the cross). This is exactly what Jesus had promised his witnesses — when dragged before councils, 'the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say' (Luke 12:11–12).

So this is not a sudden, first reception of the Spirit (Stephen was already 'full,' 6:5) but a fresh, heightened filling for a decisive moment — the same pattern as Peter 'filled with the Holy Spirit' just before he answered the council (4:8). The Spirit who abides in every believer also fills afresh for the crises of witness and suffering. And mark the point worth carrying away: being 'full of the Spirit' is not first about ecstatic feelings; its truest evidence is a man who sees Christ clearly and dies like Christ graciously. The Spirit did not spare Stephen the stones — he filled him to face them, fixing his eyes on the glory of God and on Jesus risen to receive him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The Son of Man' — the only occurrence of this title on anyone's lips other than Jesus's own in all four Gospels and Acts. Stephen quotes Jesus's own description of himself at his trial (Mark 14:62; Luke 22:69), applying it now as the testimony of an eyewitness: Jesus is the Son of Man of Daniel 7:13, approaching the Ancient of Days and receiving dominion, glory, and a kingdom. The council that condemned Jesus for claiming this title is now hearing Stephen confirm it from a vision of heaven. The evidence against the council's verdict is being given from the courtroom of God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him. Then they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Stopped their ears' — the physical enactment of the spiritual condition Stephen named: uncircumcised ears. They cannot bear to hear the claim that Jesus is the exalted Son of Man at God's right hand. The execution is outside the city (following the law of Leviticus 24:14) — and at the feet of the witnesses' garments stands a young man named Saul. Luke introduces the future apostle as the consenting guardian of the executioners' coats — a detail he will return to in 22:20, where Paul himself remembers it with grief and gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were stoning Stephen, he called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And falling to his knees he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' — the prayer of Psalm 31:5, addressed to Jesus directly as Lord. Stephen does not pray to the Father through Jesus; he prays to Jesus himself — testimony to his unambiguous conviction about Jesus's divine identity. 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' — the echo of Jesus's own prayer from the cross (Luke 23:34) is unmistakable and deliberate. The first Christian martyr dies in the exact posture of his Lord: witnessing to the glory of God, forgiving his killers, surrendering his spirit. 'He fell asleep' — death for those in Christ is sleep before resurrection. (cf. Luke 23:34, 46; 1 Pet. 4:19)

7.theology: The Pattern of Rejection and Vindication. Stephen’s survey of Israel’s history reveals God’s way in the world: the one God sends is always rejected first. Joseph, Moses, the prophets, the Righteous One himself. And in each case, God vindicates the rejected one and uses that rejection as the means of redemption. This is not historical accident; it is divine pattern — the pattern of the cross. The grain of wheat must fall into the ground and die (John 12:24). The stone the builders reject becomes the cornerstone. And the martyr who follows the rejected-and-vindicated Lord shares the same arc: killed by men, received by God, his prayer answered in the conversion of his chief persecutor. Saul of Tarsus is Stephen’s greatest vindication.
7.examples:
Then: Stephen stands before the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets, and preaches them their own history. He is the first Christian martyr, and he dies as he lived — full of the Holy Spirit, full of faith, his face like an angel’s. His death scatters the seed further than his life could have planted it.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces Stephen’s question: what do you do when you cannot be silenced by argument and so are silenced by violence? Stephen shows us: you look up, you see the glory of God, you commend your spirit to Christ, and you pray for those who kill you. This is not heroism; it is the overflow of a life lived so close to Christ that even death cannot separate you from him — and cannot stop the gospel.

8.title: The Scattered Gospel
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. <sup>2</sup>Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. <sup>3</sup>But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison. <sup>4</sup>Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. <sup>5</sup>Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. <sup>6</sup>And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. <sup>7</sup>For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. <sup>8</sup>So there was much joy in that city. <sup>9</sup>But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. <sup>10</sup>They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.” <sup>11</sup>And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic. <sup>12</sup>But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. <sup>13</sup>Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. <sup>14</sup>Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, <sup>15</sup>who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, <sup>16</sup>for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>17</sup>Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit. <sup>18</sup>Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, <sup>19</sup>saying, “Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” <sup>20</sup>But Peter said to him, “May your money perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! <sup>21</sup>You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. <sup>22</sup>Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. <sup>23</sup>For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.” <sup>24</sup>And Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.” <sup>25</sup>Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. <sup>26</sup>Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert place. <sup>27</sup>And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure and had come to Jerusalem to worship <sup>28</sup>and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. <sup>29</sup>And the Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” <sup>30</sup>So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” <sup>31</sup>And he said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. <sup>32</sup>Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. <sup>33</sup>In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.” <sup>34</sup>And the eunuch said to Philip, “About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?” <sup>35</sup>Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. <sup>36</sup>And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?” <sup>38</sup>And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. <sup>39</sup>And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. <sup>40</sup>But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
8.overview:
Persecution was meant to silence the gospel. Instead it scattered it. The death of Stephen, the ravaging of the church by Saul, the flight of believers from Jerusalem — all of this was intended to put out the fire. But you do not put out a fire by scattering the embers. You only spread it further. Those who were scattered went about preaching the Word. Not the apostles, who remained — the ordinary believers, the unnamed men and women who had heard Peter preach and Stephen argue, and who could not stop telling the story wherever their flight took them.

Philip goes to Samaria — enemy territory by centuries of Jewish reckoning — and the crowds pay attention, and there is much joy in that city. Then the Spirit pulls him away from the revival to a desert road, to one man in a chariot reading Isaiah 53. The divine calculus is instructive: the sovereign God who fills a city with the gospel also directs one evangelist to one seeker on one road. Every soul matters to him.

The Ethiopian eunuch was an outsider twice over: a foreigner, and a eunuch, barred from the assembly of Israel (Deuteronomy 23:1). He had come to Jerusalem to worship the God of Israel and had found, in a sense, no entry. Now, on a desert road, he encounters the one who tears down every dividing wall — and he goes on his way rejoicing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Persecution, Scattering, and the Gospel in Samaria
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The stoning of Stephen does not silence the gospel — it scatters it. 'There arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria.' What the authorities intend as extermination becomes the mechanism of expansion: the church cannot be contained in Jerusalem because Jesus said it would reach the ends of the earth, and persecution is the instrument God uses to push his people toward that horizon. Philip goes to Samaria — a half-step toward the Gentile world — and the mission Jesus promised in 1:8 begins its second movement.

Philip's ministry in Samaria is remarkable: signs and wonders, unclean spirits cast out, the lame and paralyzed healed, and great joy in the city. But the Jerusalem apostles send Peter and John to Samaria, and their arrival produces something Philip's preaching and baptizing had not: the Holy Spirit falls on the Samaritans. This sequence raises a genuine theological question — why did the Spirit not come with Philip's preaching? — and Luke's narrative suggests that the Spirit's delayed coming ensured that the Samaritan expansion was apostolically authorized and connected to the Jerusalem mother church, not a breakaway sect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Scattering as Mission Strategy

Reformed theology sees in Acts 8 the confirmation that God's sovereign purposes are not thwarted by human wickedness — they are advanced through it. The persecution that Saul superintends becomes the means by which the gospel reaches Samaria, fulfilling Jesus's commission (1:8). God uses the church's worst moments (martyrdom, persecution, exile) to accomplish the church's primary task (witness to the ends of the earth). The scattering of the Jerusalem church is the kingdom's advance disguised as defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Philip preached Christ in Samaria, where Jews had no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9). The gospel demolished the ethnic barrier before any doctrinal argument was made. Now: The gospel continues to cross barriers that human prejudice maintains — not because Christians are naturally free of prejudice, but because the Spirit who fills the church pushes its witness toward the people and places its human members would most naturally avoid.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The persecution begins with Saul's approval of Stephen's death and immediately expands into something systematic and city-wide. The scattering fulfills Jesus's command (1:8): the church that might have remained comfortable in Jerusalem is driven outward by the very opposition that was meant to destroy it. The apostles stay — their staying in Jerusalem is perhaps their ministry of stabilization; the scattered believers become the missionaries. The 'great lamentation' over Stephen is the grief of those who have lost a brother — genuine, theological grief, not mere sentimentality. (cf. Matt. 10:23; John 15:20)

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house by house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Ravaging' (elymaineto) — the word is used of animals tearing prey. Saul's persecution is not bureaucratic enforcement but violent destruction: house by house, men and women alike, dragged to prison. The detail that he targets 'men and women' equally is notable — the gospel's community is not protected by gender; the Spirit's presence marks every member for the persecutor's attention. The man who will become the greatest missionary begins as the most ferocious persecutor. The grace that reaches Saul on the Damascus road will be proportionate to the violence he is doing now.

verseByVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Those who were scattered went about preaching the word' — the persecution produces exactly what it was designed to prevent. Every fleeing believer becomes a gospel-carrier; every city they reach becomes a mission field. Philip (one of the Seven, appointed to distribute food) goes to Samaria and proclaims the Christ. The Samaritans were half-Jewish and deeply despised by mainline Judaism; Philip's going to them is not the natural choice but the Spirit's choice. The gospel reaches those the Jerusalem establishment would have preferred to ignore.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Samaritans' response is striking: 'with one accord' — the same unity that characterized the Jerusalem church now marks the Samaritan audience. The signs authenticate the message: unclean spirits cast out, paralytics healed. The kingdom's arrival in Samaria looks exactly like its arrival in Jerusalem — the same Lord, the same Spirit, the same power over sickness and demonic oppression. There are no second-class recipients of the gospel's power; the Samaritans receive the same signs as the Jerusalem thousands at Pentecost.

On what 'unclean spirits' actually are — real, personal, evil spirit-beings, the same the Gospels call 'demons,' and what Scripture does and does not tell us about them — see the fuller note on 5:15–16. Here the point is simply this: the same authority over them that marked the kingdom's arrival in Jerusalem now appears in Samaria. At the preaching of Christ they cry out and come out; the gospel advances and the unclean flee.

verseByVerse.quote: So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the nation of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Much joy in that city' — the gospel always produces joy when it genuinely arrives, because it announces the arrival of the king whose presence is fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11). The contrast Luke immediately introduces is sharp: Simon Magus, the great magician who had amazed the Samaritans with his powers and cultivated a following that regarded him as divine. The juxtaposition is deliberate — Philip's proclamation and Simon's magic are about to collide, and the collision will reveal what the gospel is and what it is not.

verseByVerse.quote: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
verseByVerse.commentary: Simon's hold on the Samaritans was based on amazement — the same amazement that attended Philip's miracles. But the source and character of the two kinds of power are entirely different: Simon's magic served Simon's reputation ('this man is the power of God called Great'), while Philip's signs served the proclamation of Christ. Power exercised for self-exaltation is the characteristic mark of the demonic; power exercised for the proclamation of the crucified Lord is the mark of the Spirit. The Samaritans are about to discover the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip, amazed even he was at the signs and wonders performed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip's preaching displaces Simon's hold on the Samaritans: they believe the good news of the kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ and are baptized. The comprehensive scope — 'both men and women' — mirrors the Jerusalem community. Simon himself believes and is baptized — but Luke's narrative tracks his ongoing fascination with 'the signs and wonders performed.' Simon is amazed by the miracles rather than transformed by the message; his baptism will prove to be a profession without possession.

What does it mean that Philip 'preached the kingdom of God'? The kingdom of God is God's saving reign — his kingly rule breaking into the world through Jesus the Messiah to rescue and to rule. And notice that Philip preached 'the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ' in one breath: you cannot proclaim the kingdom without proclaiming the King. To preach the kingdom is to announce that God's long-promised reign has arrived in Christ, who died, rose, and reigns, and to call people to repent, believe, and bow to him as Lord — entering his kingdom now and forever (so Paul, too, 'proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ,' Acts 28:31; on the kingdom as both 'already' here and 'not yet' consummated, see also on Col. 4:11).

Why, though, is 'the kingdom of God' on nearly every page of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, yet rare in John and in the letters? Not because the truth fades, but because the vantage point and the vocabulary shift. The first three Gospels record Jesus' own preaching to Jewish audiences, and 'the kingdom of God' was his characteristic summary of it ('repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand,' Matt. 4:17) — language steeped in Israel's hope (Dan. 7:13–14). They preserve his very idiom. John, writing later and more reflectively, names the kingdom only twice (John 3:3, 5) but says the same thing with a different word: 'eternal life.' Compare how Mark 10 uses 'inherit eternal life,' 'enter the kingdom,' and 'be saved' interchangeably in a single passage — for John, to 'enter the kingdom' simply is to 'have life,' and that word spoke more directly to his wider readership.

The Epistles were written after the resurrection and enthronement, to mostly Gentile churches — and now the focus falls on the King himself. Because Jesus has come, died, risen, and been seated at God's right hand, the apostles' shorthand becomes 'Jesus is Lord' (Rom. 10:9; Phil. 2:11), 'in Christ,' and 'Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet' (1 Cor. 15:25) — which is kingdom-preaching centred on the reigning King. So the term grows less frequent while the reality saturates everything (and Paul still uses it plainly enough — Rom. 14:17; 1 Cor. 6:9–10; Col. 1:13; 1 Thess. 2:12). A likely added reason: in the Roman world, announcing 'another king' and 'another kingdom' sounded seditious (Acts 17:7), so 'Lord' and 'Christ' were often the more natural words. Same kingdom throughout — announced by Jesus in Israel's language, rendered by John as 'life,' and proclaimed by the apostles through the lordship of the risen King.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary: The Jerusalem apostles' response to the Samaritan revival is to send their two most prominent members — Peter and John — not to inspect or control but to pray for the Samaritans. The apostolic visit is an act of fellowship, not supervision: they come to complete what Philip's ministry has begun. The prayer is specific: 'that they might receive the Holy Spirit.' The Samaritans have believed and been baptized but have not yet received the Spirit — a sequence that departs from what happened at Pentecost and raises the question of why.

verseByVerse.quote: for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke's note that the Spirit had not fallen on any of them despite genuine faith and baptism is theologically significant. The most likely explanation: the Spirit's delayed arrival until the Jerusalem apostles came ensured that the Samaritan believers were visibly incorporated into the one apostolic community, not a parallel and separate sect. The laying on of hands by Peter and John is the visible sign of apostolic blessing and fellowship, and the Spirit's arrival confirms that the Samaritan mission is continuous with the Jerusalem church, not a competing movement.

This delay — genuine believers, baptized, on whom the Spirit had 'not yet fallen' until the apostles came — is one of the most discussed passages on receiving the Spirit, and godly Christians read it in different ways. Pentecostal and charismatic brothers often see here a distinct 'baptism in the Spirit' subsequent to conversion, a normative second stage (and read Acts 19 likewise). The sacramental traditions (Roman Catholic, Anglican) find here the root of confirmation, the Spirit given through the laying on of hands after baptism. The Reformed reading — taken above — sees this as a unique, transitional hinge in redemptive history rather than a pattern for every believer: just as the gospel crossed each great barrier (Jews at Pentecost, ch. 2; Samaritans here; Gentiles in ch. 10), God marked each crossing with a visible outpouring of the Spirit, so that the long-estranged Samaritans would be openly joined into the one apostolic church, not begin a rival Christianity. On this view the regular doctrine of how we receive the Spirit is taught in the letters, not drawn from these one-time narratives — and there the answer is plain: the Spirit is given to all who believe, at conversion ('anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him,' Rom. 8:9; 'when you believed, you were sealed,' Eph. 1:13; Gal. 3:2). So Old Joe need not fear he is a half-Christian awaiting a second gift: if he belongs to Christ, he already has the Spirit. The point is said with respect for brothers who differ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary: Simon's request unmasks what his 'belief' was: he wants the Spirit-conferring power as a commodity, something he can acquire with money and deploy for his own ministry. 'Give me this power also' — the word 'power' (exousia) reveals his framework: he thinks in terms of power-transfer, not personal transformation. Money can buy what magicians sell; but the Spirit of God is not for sale, and the apostles are not vendors. Simon's request is the paradigmatic error of treating the gifts of God as products in an economy of religious exchange.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's response is severe and clear: 'may your silver perish with you.' The condemnation is not of wealth but of the attempt to commodify what is freely given by God. 'You have neither part nor lot in this matter' — Simon's offer reveals that he has no share in what he is trying to buy. His heart is 'not right before God' — not aligned with the truth of the gospel, not transformed by the grace he has professed. The word 'simony' (purchasing church offices) derives from this episode, naming the perennial temptation to treat God's gifts as marketable goods.

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter does not give up on Simon — he calls him to repentance. The 'if possible' of v. 22 is not uncertainty about God's forgiveness but an honest recognition that Simon must actually repent, not merely regret the rebuke. 'The gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity' — Peter diagnoses Simon's spiritual condition: a heart that has not been liberated by the gospel but is still bound by its own agenda and bitterness. The call to repentance is still open; Simon is not beyond grace. His response (vv. 24–25) is ambiguous — he asks Peter to pray for him but makes no visible turn.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary: Simon's response focuses on the consequences rather than the repentance: 'that nothing of what you have said may come upon me.' He does not say 'I repent' or 'forgive me'; he asks for intercession against judgment. Luke leaves his story unresolved — a warning to readers not to mistake religious amazement and formal baptism for genuine faith. Peter and John, their apostolic mission complete, return to Jerusalem — but not before 'preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.' The Spirit who uses persecution to scatter the church uses the apostles' journey home to seed an entire region.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit who called Philip to Samaria now calls him away from the most successful revival he has ever experienced, to a desert road, to meet a single man — one of the most deliberately provocative scenes in Acts. An Ethiopian eunuch, a Gentile court official of the queen of Ethiopia, returning from worship at Jerusalem with a scroll of Isaiah in his hands, cannot understand what he is reading. Philip is sent to explain it. The explanation leads to baptism, to joy, and to the eunuch's departure — and Philip is immediately transported to another city. The encounter is over almost before it begins.

The eunuch is reading Isaiah 53 — the Servant Song that describes the suffering and death of the one who bore the sins of the many. Philip begins with this very text and preaches Jesus from it. The question the eunuch asks — 'Who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?' — is the hermeneutical question that unlocks the entire Old Testament. The answer is Jesus, and from that answer, faith flows, the gospel is confessed, baptism follows, and joy fills the Ethiopian official on his way home to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the Substitutionary Atonement

Philip begins with Isaiah 53 and 'told him the good news about Jesus.' Isaiah 53 is the clearest Old Testament anticipation of substitutionary atonement: 'he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed' (Isaiah 53:5). The Reformed tradition has always seen here the doctrinal heart of the gospel: the innocent Servant bearing the punishment deserved by the guilty, so that the guilty might go free. Philip preaches the crucified and risen Jesus from the text that most clearly explained why he had to die.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: An Ethiopian eunuch — excluded from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1 — is baptized and welcomed into the community of Christ. The gospel dismantles the exclusions of the old covenant in its very first Gentile encounter. Now: The gospel continues to reach those who have been told they are too far away, too different, too excluded. No distance is too great, no background too foreign, no exclusion too definitive for the Spirit who pursues the one.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel's instruction is geographically precise and apparently impractical: leave Samaria's revival for a desert road. Philip's obedience is immediate and unquestioning: 'he rose and went.' The eunuch's identity is carefully established: Ethiopian (the end of the known world), eunuch (excluded from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1), court official (a man of power and privilege), pilgrim to Jerusalem (a God-fearer drawn to Israel's worship). He is simultaneously a man of privilege and a man of exclusion — and the gospel is about to address both dimensions of his identity.

'An angel of the Lord said to Philip' — and many a believer today quietly wishes God would guide him so directly. Why was this kind of thing common then but not now? First, an honest correction to the question: angelic appearances were never an everyday matter even in Scripture. The Bible spans two thousand years, yet angels speaking to people cluster at a handful of pivotal moments — the patriarchs, the Exodus, the prophets here and there, the birth of Christ, the empty tomb, and the launching of the church in Acts. The vast majority of godly saints across most of biblical history never saw or heard an angel. They appear often in the narrative because Scripture records the turning points, not the ordinary years.

And Acts is exactly such a turning point: the once-for-all launch of the gospel out from Jerusalem to Samaria, to this Ethiopian, to Cornelius the Gentile (ch. 10), to the ends of the earth. For that foundational breakout God used extraordinary, direct steering — angels, visions, the Spirit speaking by name (10:3; 13:2; 16:9) — to drive the apostles into territory they would never have entered on their own. Like the authenticating signs and wonders (see on 5:12), this belonged to the laying of the foundation (Eph. 2:20), which by its nature is laid once.

Today God ordinarily guides his people by settled and sufficient means — and we are not less supplied but more. We hold what the early church was still receiving: the completed Scripture, 'a lamp to my feet' (Ps. 119:105), able to make us 'complete, equipped for every good work' (2 Tim. 3:16–17); the indwelling Spirit who illumines it; and prayer, wisdom, godly counsel, and providence. Indeed Scripture positively warns against craving angelic encounters: it cautions against those puffed up by 'the worship of angels' who do not hold fast to Christ the Head (Col. 2:18); it notes that Satan himself 'disguises himself as an angel of light' (2 Cor. 11:14); and it says that even 'if an angel from heaven' preached another gospel, he is to be rejected (Gal. 1:8) — for no angelic experience stands above the written Word. Deepest of all, God 'has in these last days spoken to us by his Son' (Heb. 1:1–2), who is far superior to the angels (Heb. 1:4); to ask for an angel when we hold the word of the Son is, in truth, to ask for something lesser. We 'walk by faith, not by sight' (2 Cor. 5:7), and 'blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed' (John 20:29).

Two honest qualifications. This does not mean angels are idle: they remain 'ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation' (Heb. 1:14), often unseen — God has not lost his freedom to use them. And no single verse says outright, 'angels will stop speaking after the apostles'; that they no longer do so as our normal guidance is a reasonable inference from the foundational character of the Acts era, the completion and sufficiency of Scripture, and the Bible's own warnings against seeking such things. The settled point for Old Joe is this: do not hanker after an angel — you have the finished Word of God, the Spirit of God, and the Son of God himself. That is more, not less, than a voice from the desert road.

What was a 'eunuch'? In the plain sense, a man who had been castrated. In the ancient royal courts such men were deliberately employed — above all to guard the king's or queen's household and women, since a man who could neither father children nor pose a sexual or dynastic threat was reckoned uniquely safe and loyal. Far from being lowly, eunuchs often rose to the highest posts of trust — chamberlains, advisers, treasurers — exactly as this man, who was 'in charge of all the treasure' of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. (The word could also be used more loosely as a title for a high court official, whatever his physical state — Potiphar is called a 'eunuch' in Genesis 39:1 though he was married; and Jesus speaks of three kinds in Matt. 19:12, those born so, those made so by men, and those who choose celibacy for the kingdom. Here, given both his office and the exclusion noted below, he is most likely a literal eunuch holding high office.)

And this is the poignancy of the scene. Under the law of Moses, 'no one whose... male organ is cut off shall enter the assembly of the LORD' (Deut. 23:1) — a eunuch was, by his very body, barred from full membership in Israel's worship, however earnestly he sought God. So here is a man who has travelled the length of the known world to worship in Jerusalem, only to remain a permanent outsider, shut out at the door. Yet he is reading Isaiah — the very book where God had promised that day when the eunuch who holds fast his covenant would be given 'a name better than sons and daughters... an everlasting name that shall not be cut off' (Isa. 56:3–5). The gospel Philip is about to preach to him is the fulfilment of that promise: in Christ the excluded outsider is brought all the way in.

verseByVerse.quote: and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit directs Philip with specific precision: 'Go over and join this chariot.' Not 'go to that general area' but 'go to that chariot, that man, that scroll.' Divine providence has arranged the encounter: the eunuch is reading Isaiah at the exact moment Philip arrives; the Spirit gives Philip the exact instruction he needs. The Spirit's personal, specific direction of Philip to the eunuch is the pattern of all genuine mission: the Spirit goes ahead, prepares the heart, and then sends the messenger with exact timing.

verseByVerse.quote: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Philip runs — the urgency of the Spirit's direction expressed in physical movement. The question 'Do you understand what you are reading?' is both honest and winsome: it acknowledges the difficulty of the text without condescension. The eunuch's response is the most teachable answer in Acts: 'How can I, unless someone guides me?' He knows his need; he welcomes help; he invites Philip into his chariot. Humility about one's understanding of Scripture is the posture that opens the door to genuine encounter with Christ in the text.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah 53:7–8 — the center of the Servant Song that describes the one who dies silently, unjustly, and vicariously. 'He opens not his mouth' — the silence of the Servant before his accusers is the silence of the one who has accepted the cup the Father has given him. 'In his humiliation justice was denied him' — the death of the Servant is a miscarriage of justice by human courts; but it is the perfect justice of God, who is punishing the sins of others in the Servant. The eunuch is reading the text that explains the cross before Philip arrives to show him the text is about Jesus. (cf. Isa. 53:7–8; 1 Pet. 2:22–25)

verseByVerse.quote: And the eunuch said to Philip, "About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" And Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The eunuch's question is the hermeneutical question that unlocks the entire Old Testament: is the Servant someone in particular, or is this a general picture? Philip's answer begins 'with this Scripture' — Isaiah 53 — and from it preaches Jesus. The christological interpretation of the Servant Songs is not imported into Isaiah but drawn from Isaiah: the Servant's silence, humiliation, vicarious suffering, and death by injustice are fulfilled in Jesus's passion in a way that no other figure in history has fulfilled them. Jesus is not a projection onto Isaiah; Isaiah is a prophecy of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘What prevents me from being baptized?’ — a remarkable question, given that the eunuch’s own body was the legal answer under the old covenant (Deuteronomy 23:1). But Philip’s question in response (‘if you believe with all your heart, you may’) establishes the gospel’s single condition: faith. The eunuch’s confession — ‘I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God’ — is the earliest baptismal confession in Acts and one of the most comprehensive: he affirms both the messianic identity (‘Christ’) and the divine identity (‘Son of God’) of Jesus. Nothing prevents his baptism.

The Isaiah 56 fulfilment: What makes this scene so charged is where the eunuch has been reading. He has a scroll of Isaiah open to chapter 53 when Philip arrives — the Servant’s vicarious suffering and death. But just three chapters later, Isaiah 56:3–5 makes the eunuch a figure of prophetic promise: ‘Let not the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” For thus says the LORD: to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant, I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters.’ The very book the eunuch is reading contains the prophecy that he — the excluded one — will be gathered. He is not merely reading Isaiah 53; he is inhabiting Isaiah 56. Luke wants his readers to feel the precision of Providence: the Spirit does not just send Philip to the right road but to the right man reading the right book at the right passage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary: The baptism is complete, and Philip is immediately transported by the Spirit — the encounter is over, and the human intermediary departs. The eunuch's response is the same as the crowd at Pentecost's response, the same as Samaria's response: joy. The gospel always produces joy in those who genuinely receive it, because it announces the arrival of the one who is the fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11). The eunuch returns to Ethiopia with no church, no Bible in his language, no pastor — only the Spirit and the risen Christ. And tradition says the Ethiopian church began with him.

verseByVerse.quote: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
verseByVerse.commentary: Philip is transported to Azotus (the ancient Philistine city of Ashdod) and continues evangelizing up the coastal plain to Caesarea, the major Roman port city where he will eventually settle (21:8). The Spirit who removes him from the eunuch sends him immediately into new mission territory. Philip's life is a model of Spirit-directed mission: obedient to sudden redirections, faithful in revival and in desert encounter, content to disappear from one story so the next chapter of God's mission can begin.

8.theology: The Gospel Breaks Every Barrier. Acts 8 is the chapter in which the gospel crosses its first major boundary — from Jews to Samaritans, and then from Israel to Africa. This is not accidental; it is the working out of Acts 1:8: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, ends of the earth. The Ethiopian eunuch is the first representative of the “ends of the earth” in the book — geographically distant, ethnically foreign, ritually excluded. And the gospel reaches him on a desert road through a text he happened to be reading. This is the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling in action: the Spirit directs the preacher, opens the Scriptures, and draws the seeker. Nothing is left to chance. The God who elects a people from every tongue and tribe and nation uses the ordinary means — a man, a chariot, a scroll — to accomplish his extraordinary purposes.
8.examples:
Then: Scattered believers, fleeing for their lives, who could not stop preaching. A deacon pulled off a city-wide revival and then redirected to one man on a road. An African official who came to Jerusalem seeking God and left having found him in the most unexpected way. The gospel in chapter 8 is gloriously uncontrollable.

Now: The church tends to think of mission in terms of programs and strategies. Acts 8 shows God doing his best work through disruption — persecution that scatters, divine direction that redirects, a Scripture passage that raises exactly the right question. The lesson is not that we should abandon planning, but that we must hold our plans loosely enough that we can hear “go over and join this chariot” when the Spirit speaks it.

9.title: The Road to Damascus
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest <sup>2</sup>and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. <sup>3</sup>Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. <sup>4</sup>And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” <sup>5</sup>And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. <sup>6</sup>But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do.” <sup>7</sup>The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. <sup>8</sup>Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. <sup>9</sup>And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. <sup>10</sup>Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” <sup>11</sup>And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying, <sup>12</sup>and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.” <sup>13</sup>But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” <sup>15</sup>But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. <sup>16</sup>For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.” <sup>17</sup>So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized; <sup>19</sup>and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.” <sup>21</sup>And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” <sup>22</sup>But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. <sup>23</sup>When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, <sup>24</sup>but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him, <sup>25</sup>but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. <sup>26</sup>And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. <sup>27</sup>But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. <sup>28</sup>So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. <sup>29</sup>And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him. <sup>30</sup>And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. <sup>31</sup>So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. <sup>32</sup>Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. <sup>33</sup>There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. <sup>34</sup>And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. <sup>35</sup>And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. <sup>36</sup>Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. <sup>37</sup>In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. <sup>38</sup>Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.” <sup>39</sup>So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. <sup>40</sup>But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. <sup>41</sup>And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. <sup>42</sup>And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. <sup>43</sup>And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
9.overview:
No conversion in history has been more dramatic, more sovereign, or more consequential. Saul of Tarsus is not seeking God. He is hunting God’s people — breathing threats and murder, armed with letters of arrest, heading to Damascus to drag more believers to prison. And the risen Christ stops him on the road. A light from heaven. A voice. “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” Not them — me. To touch the church is to touch Christ. The head and the body are one.

What happens to Saul on the Damascus road is not the result of prior openness, spiritual preparation, or moral readiness. It is pure, sovereign, unilateral grace — the kind that stops a man in the middle of his worst act and makes him a new creature. Saul does not choose Christ; Christ chooses Saul. “He is a chosen instrument of mine.” The word is skeuos eklogēs — vessel of election — and it is the language of sovereign divine appointment. The most violent persecutor of the church becomes its most prolific apostle. Only God could write that story.

And then there is Ananias — a small man in a small house on a street called Straight, who hears the Lord say “go to Saul of Tarsus” and who goes, against every instinct of self-preservation, and calls the man who had come to arrest him “Brother Saul.” Two words that cost everything and mean everything. Grace in the mouth of a frightened disciple.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The conversion of Saul of Tarsus is the most dramatic reversal in the New Testament outside of the resurrection itself. The man who superintended Stephen's execution and was 'ravaging the church' (8:3) is arrested by the risen Christ on the road to Damascus, blinded, led into the city helpless, and three days later emerges as the most committed missionary the world has ever seen. Luke tells the story three times in Acts (here, in Paul's defense before the crowd in ch. 22, and before Agrippa in ch. 26) because it is the event that shapes everything that follows: the Gentile mission, the theology of grace, and the entire second half of Acts.

The encounter on the Damascus road is stark and absolute: 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' The risen Christ identifies himself with the church he is persecuting — to persecute the church is to persecute Jesus. And then the identification in reverse: 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.' The Christology is radical: the exalted Lord so thoroughly identifies with his people that violence against them is violence against him personally. Saul's three days of blindness, fasting, and prayer are his death and resurrection before baptism: the old Saul — the Pharisee, the persecutor, the man confident in his own righteousness — dies in the darkness, and the new creation emerges when Ananias restores his sight.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of Grace in Conversion

Saul's conversion is the purest demonstration in the New Testament of the sovereignty of grace. He was not seeking Christ; he was hunting Christians. He had no inclination toward the gospel; he was destroying the church. He was not moving toward faith; he was moving toward Damascus to imprison believers. And then the risen Christ stopped him — entirely, unilaterally, sovereignly. Reformed theology sees in Saul's conversion the paradigm of all conversion: every person who comes to faith is someone who was, in one degree or another, moving away from God when God arrested them. The grace that reached Saul reaches all who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ananias was asked to go to 'the man who has done much evil to your saints in Jerusalem.' He went — and addressed him as 'Brother Saul.' The man who could have been his executioner became his brother. Now: The gospel creates family out of former enemies. The church's testimony to the grace that reached Saul is its most powerful argument for the gospel's transforming power: if Christ can reach the chief of sinners, he can reach anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Still breathing threats and murder' — the participle conveys that Saul's hostility is his constant condition, not an occasional impulse. He has not moderated since Stephen's stoning; he has intensified. The request for letters to the Damascus synagogues reveals both the geographical reach of his persecution and the legal structure through which he operated: the high priest's authority extended to Jewish communities throughout the Diaspora. 'The Way' — the earliest self-designation of the Christian movement, emphasizing that following Jesus is a path, a manner of life, not merely a set of beliefs.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Suddenly a light from heaven shone around him' — the glory of the risen Christ, brighter than the Syrian midday sun (26:13). Saul falls to the ground: the posture of prostration before overwhelming divine presence. The double name — 'Saul, Saul' — echoes the divine address of Abraham (Genesis 22:11), Moses (Exodus 3:4), and Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10): the urgent, personal summons of God to a specific individual at a turning-point moment. 'Why are you persecuting me?' — Jesus does not ask why Saul is persecuting the church; he asks why Saul is persecuting him. The identification is total. (cf. 1 Cor. 15:8–10; Gal. 1:15–16)

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who are you, Lord?' — Saul addresses the voice as Lord before he knows whose voice it is; the light and the fall have already produced a posture of submission. The answer is the most important sentence in Saul's life: 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.' The Jesus he has been persecuting is alive, is Lord, is the risen Christ. In a moment, everything Saul has built his life on — the law, the Pharisaic tradition, his own righteousness — is overturned. 'Rise and enter the city' — the sovereign Lord who has arrested him now directs his next steps. Saul will be told what to do: his autonomy is over.

verseByVerse.quote: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The companions hear the voice but see no one — they are witnesses to the supernatural character of the event without being recipients of its content. Their speechlessness is the appropriate response to a theophany they cannot interpret. Saul's blindness is the physical enactment of his spiritual condition: the man most certain he could see clearly — the zealous Pharisee, righteous by the law's standards — now sees nothing and is led by the hand like a dependent child. The reversal is total and immediate.

verseByVerse.quote: And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three days without sight, food, or drink: the posture of one in crisis, in prayer, at the end of himself. The three days anticipate the death-and-resurrection pattern of baptism: the old Saul — the Pharisee, the persecutor — is dying in the darkness, and the new creation will emerge when Ananias comes. Fasting intensifies prayer; the darkness forces inward the attention that had previously been turned outward in confident self-reliance. God is at work in Saul's three-day night.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The risen Christ is orchestrating the encounter from both ends simultaneously. Ananias's response — 'Here I am, Lord' — is the posture of Isaiah (6:8) and Samuel (1 Samuel 3:4): the servant available for whatever the Lord assigns. The precision of the directions — street, house, name, city — is characteristic of the Spirit's guidance throughout Acts. The Lord tells Ananias what Saul is doing: praying. The man who entered Damascus in authority to arrest believers is now a blind man in prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Lord has already shown Saul in a vision that Ananias is coming — the healing has been previewed for the one who will receive it. This double orchestration — directing Ananias to Saul, and showing Saul that Ananias is coming — ensures that both participants understand they are being brought together by divine arrangement, not human coincidence. When Ananias arrives, Saul will be expecting him. The Spirit's work in preparation always exceeds the missionary's awareness of what has been prepared.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary: Ananias's objection is reasonable and understandable: Saul's reputation has preceded him. 'How much evil he has done to your saints' — the saints, the holy ones, the community to which Ananias himself belongs. And Saul is not only a past persecutor; he has authority to arrest 'all who call on your name' — including Ananias himself. Going to Saul is, by any rational calculation, walking into the arms of the man who is hunting you. Ananias's honesty with God is itself a form of faith: he raises the objection, but he will go when the Lord answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Lord's answer to Ananias's objection contains the two most important facts about Saul's future: he is a 'chosen instrument' (divine election, not human decision) to carry the name before Gentiles, kings, and Israel (the scope of Acts 9–28); and he 'must suffer' (his suffering for the name will be proportionate to his former infliction of suffering in the name's suppression). The call to mission and the call to suffering are inseparable in Acts and in Paul's own letters (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). The Lord does not conceal the cost from the one he is calling. (cf. Rom. 1:1; 2 Cor. 11:23–27)

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Brother Saul' — the first word Ananias speaks is 'brother.' The man who came to arrest members of the Way is welcomed by one of them as family. This is the gospel's social miracle: the persecutor becomes the brother. The healing and the Spirit come together: sight returns, the Spirit fills, and Saul is baptized. The three days of blindness, prayer, and fasting are over; the new creation emerges from the baptismal water. Paul will later call his conversion a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17) and a participation in Christ's death and resurrection (Galatians 2:20).

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, He is the Son of God.' — the theological content of Saul's first proclamation is the highest possible christological claim: 'Son of God.' This is not a gradual dawning of insight; it is the immediate consequence of meeting the risen Christ. The man who was going to the Damascus synagogues to arrest believers goes to the Damascus synagogues to preach the faith he had been destroying. The reversal is total and instant. The christology that will undergird all of Paul's letters is already fully formed: Jesus is the Son of God. (cf. Gal. 1:16; 2 Cor. 5:17)

What did Saul mean by 'Son of God'? The title gathers up two streams of Scripture into one confession. First, it is a claim to full deity. To call Jesus God's own Son, in the unique sense, is to say he shares the very nature of God — which is exactly how his hearers understood it: Jesus was charged with 'making himself equal with God' because he called God his own Father (John 5:18; 19:7). 'Son' here speaks not of a beginning or of a lesser rank but of sameness of nature and eternal relation: as an earthly son shares his father's humanity, the divine Son shares the Father's deity, eternally — of one substance with him, 'begotten, not made.' Second, 'Son of God' was a royal, messianic title: the promised king of David's line was called God's son (2 Sam. 7:14; Ps. 2:7), so to say 'Jesus is the Son of God' is also to say he is the Christ, the anointed King — which is just where Saul's preaching goes next, 'proving that Jesus was the Christ' (v. 22). In Christ the two meet: the true Davidic King who is himself truly God.

One guard against misunderstanding. Scripture calls angels and even believers 'sons of God' (Job 1:6; John 1:12) — but those are sons by creation or by adopting grace. Jesus is the Son, the 'only-begotten' (monogenēs, John 3:16), Son by eternal right and by nature, not made a son and not adopted. We become sons only through him. So this short sentence is the gospel in miniature: the man Jesus, crucified and risen, is God the Son and the royal Messiah, worthy of all trust, worship, and obedience — and it is the very confession that saves, 'that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name' (John 20:31; cf. 1 John 4:15). And here is the wonder of the moment: the man who had set out to destroy everyone who made this claim is now the first in Damascus to make it.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound to the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Damascus synagogue's bewilderment is understandable: Saul is doing the opposite of what he came to do. 'Increased all the more in strength' — the opposition that should have silenced him energizes him. 'Confounded' — the word implies a complete defeat in argument; Saul's combination of rabbinic training, personal encounter with the risen Christ, and Spirit-given understanding of Scripture makes him effectively unanswerable. The persecutor has become the most formidable advocate for the faith he once destroyed.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary: Saul's first experience of persecution is at the hands of the same community he once served. The plot mirrors the plots against Jesus and Stephen: when the message cannot be refuted, violence is the next resort. 'Watching the gates day and night' — the siege is thorough, the intent murderous. Paul will later mention this episode in 2 Corinthians 11:32–33 with an additional detail: the governor of Damascus was also involved, under the Nabataean king Aretas, whose ethnarch watched the city gates.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary: The escape in a basket through the city wall is both humiliating and providential. Paul will later cite it as his first 'boast' in weakness (2 Corinthians 11:30–33) — the episode that established the pattern of his entire apostolic career: not triumph but survival, not power but endurance, the treasure carried in a clay jar. The disciples who lower him over the wall are the Damascene community he has just spent time building — their care for him is the first concrete expression of the church's solidarity with its most controversial new member.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Jerusalem church's fear of Saul is entirely rational: his reputation for destroying the church is intact, and his conversion claim might be a ruse. Barnabas — the 'son of encouragement' who first appeared selling his field in chapter 4 — again demonstrates his characteristic gift: seeing what others fear to see, trusting where others hesitate. His advocacy for Saul before the apostles is the bridge between the persecutor and the community he persecuted. Without Barnabas, Saul might never have been integrated into the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul's pattern in Jerusalem mirrors his pattern in Damascus: bold proclamation in the name of Jesus, disputation with the Hellenists (the very group that had disputed with Stephen, whose martyrdom Saul had approved), and a plot to kill him. The Hellenists cannot refute him any more than they could refute Stephen — so they resort to the same response. Saul has stepped into Stephen's role, advocating before the same opponents with the same Spirit and, apparently, the same mortal danger.

A word on who 'the Hellenists' were (their fuller profile is at 6:1 and 6:9): the term (Hellēnistai) means Greek-speaking Jews — men of the diaspora, raised in the Greek language and culture, many with synagogues of their own in Jerusalem (such as the Synagogue of the Freedmen, 6:9). The word names a person's language and culture, not his faith: in 6:1 it labels Greek-speaking Jewish believers, whereas here — as with Stephen's opponents — it means unbelieving Greek-speaking Jews. And there is a sharp irony in Saul disputing with them: a man of Tarsus in Cilicia (6:9), he was himself a Hellenist, very likely once standing with this same circle against Stephen — and now he turns to plead the name of Jesus among his own former camp, and meets the very answer Stephen met.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Jerusalem brothers act to protect their most controversial member: they route him through Caesarea to Tarsus, his hometown. The period in Tarsus (covering what Galatians 1:17–21 suggests was at least three years in Arabia and Syria-Cilicia) is the hidden preparation time — years of obscurity in which Paul was being formed for the mission he will carry. God does not rush his instruments; he prepares them in silence before deploying them in public. Barnabas will retrieve Saul from this obscurity in 11:25 when the Antioch church needs a teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke's summary statement covers the period of relative peace after Saul's departure from Jerusalem. The church's growth is described in terms of its spiritual character: 'fear of the Lord' (the reverential awe that marks a community conscious of God's presence) and 'the comfort of the Holy Spirit' (the paraklēsis — the consoling, strengthening, encouraging work of the Spirit). These two together produce multiplication: a community that fears God and is filled with the Spirit's comfort is a community the world finds both sobering and attractive.

On 'walking in the fear of the Lord,' see the fuller treatment at 5:11 — the reverent awe that draws near to God in love while never trifling with his holiness (Old Joe at the hearth, who loves the fire and pulls his chair close, yet would never put his hand in it). Here it is worth dwelling on its companion phrase, 'the comfort of the Holy Spirit.' The word 'comfort' (paraklēsis) is far richer than our modern notion of soothing ease. It belongs to the same family as paraklētos — the name Jesus gave the Spirit, the 'Helper' or 'Comforter' he promised: 'I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever' (John 14:16). The root means to be 'called alongside' to give aid, and it sounds three notes at once: to console the troubled, to encourage the faint-hearted, and — as the old word 'comfort' (from the Latin for 'with strength') tells us — to make strong. So 'the comfort of the Holy Spirit' is no cosy ease; it is the personal presence of God's own Spirit coming alongside his people to console them in trouble, embolden them to witness, and strengthen them to stand and grow. And mark the lovely pairing Luke sets down: fear and comfort, side by side — trembling reverence before the holy God, and the strong consolation of his Spirit. They are not rivals but partners; the same church that fears God is upheld by his Helper — and out of the two together it 'multiplied.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Saul is in Tarsus preparing for his mission, Peter is extending the Jerusalem church's reach through the coastal plain — the territory Philip had evangelized between Azotus and Caesarea. Two healing miracles frame this section: Aeneas, paralyzed for eight years, told to rise and make his bed; and Tabitha (Dorcas), a woman full of good works and acts of charity, raised from the dead. Both miracles are performed explicitly 'in the name of Jesus Christ' or by calling on his name — the authority behind every apostolic act is the authority of the risen Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha (vv. 36–43) deliberately echoes Jesus's raising of Jairus's daughter (Luke 8:49–56): the mourners sent outside, the command 'rise,' the taking of the hand, the presentation to the community. Peter is not performing his own miracles; he is ministering in the power of the one who raised Jairus's daughter and who was himself raised from the dead.
