Every healing and resurrection in Acts is a preview of the final resurrection, a foretaste of the new creation in which all that sin and death have broken will be permanently restored.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Tabitha was known for 'good works and acts of charity,' and when she died, the widows she had served showed Peter the coats and garments she had made for them. Her resurrection was the answer to the prayers of a community she had served. Now: The church's ministry of practical love — clothing the poor, caring for widows, serving the marginalized — is the soil in which the witness of the gospel grows. Tabitha's deeds were the evidence of the faith that the resurrection confirmed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's itinerant ministry through the coastal communities is the apostolic equivalent of the scattered believers' missionary work — both are extending the church's reach through the movement of God's servants. Lydda (ancient Lod) is in the Shephelah region southeast of the port of Joppa. Aeneas represents the kind of need that the gospel always finds: a man defined by his condition, bedridden for a period longer than the church has existed, whose restoration will proclaim the gospel's power more effectively than a sermon.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Jesus Christ heals you' — the healing is attributed immediately to its actual source; Peter is explicit that he is not the healer. Eight years of paralysis ended with a word spoken in the name of Jesus — 'immediately he rose.' The healing is not private: all the residents of Lydda and the Sharon plain saw Aeneas and turned to the Lord. The restored body is the sermon; the miracle is the proclamation. In every healing in Acts, the physical restoration is a concrete manifestation of the gospel's claim that Jesus is Lord over everything that sin and death have broken.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary: Tabitha's description — 'full of good works and acts of charity' — is the portrait of a disciple whose faith was expressed in practical love for the community's most vulnerable. Her name is preserved in both Aramaic (Tabitha) and Greek (Dorcas), suggesting a bilingual community that treasured her in two languages. Her death is a community catastrophe: the widows she served depended on her, and her absence leaves a gap that no organizational arrangement can fill. Luke's note that her body was washed and laid in an upper room follows Jewish burial custom and preserves the historical detail of what Peter will enter.

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples' urgent summons — 'please come without delay' — is not mere hope but prayer expressed in action: they have seen what Jesus did for Jairus's daughter and Lazarus, and they dare to believe that the power that raised the dead is still at work in his church through his apostle. The geography matters: Lydda is close enough to Joppa that an urgent summons can reach Peter in time. The disciples' faith is expressed not in passive waiting but in active seeking — they go to find the person through whom God is working.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary: The widows' exhibition of the garments Tabitha made is both a tribute to her and an implicit prayer: this is what will be lost if she does not return. Peter kneels in prayer first — the miracle is not the result of apostolic authority exercised independently but of prayer addressed to the Lord who raises the dead. The scene deliberately echoes Jesus's raising of Jairus's daughter: the mourners put outside, the command 'arise,' the immediate response. 'Tabitha, arise' is almost identical in Aramaic to Jesus's 'Talitha cumi' (Mark 5:41). Peter acts in his Lord's authority and his Lord's pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her to them alive.
verseByVerse.commentary: The taking of her hand echoes Jesus's raising of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:41) — Peter is not merely following a technique but participating in the same redemptive action his Lord performed. 'He presented her to them alive' — the presentation is the proclamation: the community that had come to grieve receives instead the occasion of joy. The raising of Tabitha is the gospel enacted: the one who was dead is alive, the one who was lost is restored, the community that mourned now celebrates. The resurrection of Jesus has practical consequences in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary: The raising of Tabitha, like the healing of Aeneas, produces widespread faith: 'many believed in the Lord.' The miracles are not ends in themselves but proclamation in visible form; the community responds to what it has seen by turning to the one who did it. Peter's lodging with Simon the tanner is a detail Luke preserves with significance: tanners worked with dead animals and were considered ritually unclean — Peter's comfort with a tanner's hospitality hints at the attitude shift that the vision of chapter 10 will make explicit.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest portrait of unconditional election and effectual calling. There is nothing in Saul that would attract God’s grace — he is actively persecuting the church, violently opposed to Christ, supremely confident in his own righteousness (Philippians 3:4–6). God chose him anyway. Not because of anything foreseen in him, but according to his own sovereign purpose — to display the fullness of his grace in the most unlikely vessel imaginable. Paul himself will later write that his conversion was designed to be a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. That is the point. The doctrine of election is not a closed door; it is the foundation of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother. Understandably, they were afraid. It took Barnabas — son of encouragement — to stand between the suspicious church and the new apostle and vouch for the reality of his conversion. The church that had prayed for boldness now needed faith to receive the answer.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person who seems most violently opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to apprehend. This is not a reason for naivety; it is a reason for prayer — the kind of prayer that believes God can stop any Saul on any road at any time. The church’s task is to be ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
The tenth chapter of Acts is one of the pivotal moments in the history of redemption. God has been preparing two men simultaneously: a Roman centurion who prays and gives alms and fears the God of Israel, and a Jewish apostle on a rooftop in Joppa having a vision that overturns a lifetime of religious instinct. The God who governs all things is coordinating these two lives across thirty miles — because the gospel is about to cross the border that mattered most.

Peter’s vision is not primarily about food. It is about people. “What God has made clean, do not call common.” The dietary laws that had kept Israel separate from the nations were always pointing toward something — a people set apart for God. Now that people is being redefined around the Messiah, and the old boundary markers are being transformed. God is not lowering his standards; he is declaring that Gentiles, received through faith in Christ, are clean. They always could be. The wall between Jew and Gentile was never in God’s ultimate plan; it was a temporary steward until the seed came (Galatians 3:24).

The Spirit falls while Peter is still preaching. Not after an altar call. Not after theological instruction is complete. The sovereign Spirit comes when and where he wills, and what he produces in the house of Cornelius is praise. The Jewish believers who came with Peter are amazed. God is not. He planned this before the foundation of the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Acts 10 is the theological center of the book. The conversion of Cornelius — a Roman centurion, a Gentile, uncircumcised — is the event that breaks open the gospel's trajectory toward the ends of the earth. Peter needs a vision from heaven before he will cross the threshold of a Gentile home; God needs to tell him three times that what he has made clean is not unclean. The resistance is not personal prejudice alone but centuries of Torah observance that drew sharp lines between Israel and the nations. To cross those lines required a direct word from God — and God gives it.

What happens in Cornelius's house is unmistakable: as Peter is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear the word, and they speak in tongues and praise God. The circumcised believers who came with Peter are astonished — the Spirit has been 'poured out even on the Gentiles.' The Spirit does not wait for circumcision, for full Torah compliance, or for the completion of Peter's sermon. He falls on those who hear the word and believe, confirming that faith in Jesus Christ is the only condition of receiving the gift. This is the Gentile Pentecost, and it makes the mission to the nations not merely possible but divinely commanded.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean: The Gospel Dismantles Food Laws as Ethnic Barriers

The vision of the sheet containing all kinds of animals (vv. 9–16) uses the food laws as a symbol for the ethnic separation they enforced: if God has made all foods clean, he has made all peoples accessible. Reformed theology sees here the fulfillment of the old covenant's shadow-function: the food laws distinguished Israel from the nations as a temporary measure, pointing toward the day when the gospel would break down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14–16). Cornelius's conversion is not the abandonment of God's covenant purposes but their fulfillment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter entered a Gentile home and preached the gospel, something the Torah-observant Jew in him resisted with his whole being. He needed a vision from heaven to override his cultural conditioning. Now: The church continues to need the Spirit's override of its cultural conditioning — the instinct to preach the gospel only to people like us requires the same divine interruption that Peter received.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Cornelius's characterization is carefully drawn: Roman (centurion of the Italian Cohort, a Gentile soldier), devout (a God-fearer, one who worshipped the God of Israel without full conversion), generous (almsgiving to the Jewish people), and prayerful (continually). He is the best possible Gentile from a Jewish perspective — everything that Gentile piety could be — and it is not enough. His prayers and alms are noticed by God (v. 4), but he still needs the gospel. Religious sincerity and moral generosity do not produce salvation; the gospel of Jesus Christ does.

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary: The ninth hour (3pm) is the hour of prayer in Judaism, and Cornelius is in prayer at that very hour when the angel appears. 'He stared at him in terror' — the appropriate response to a genuine divine messenger: the fear of the Lord that is the beginning of wisdom. 'Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God' — the language of the temple offering (Leviticus 2:2, 9) applied to prayer and charity: these have come before God as a fragrant offering, not in themselves salvific, but noticed and responded to by the God who hears prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary: The angel's instruction is remarkably specific: not just 'find a preacher' but 'find Simon called Peter, lodging with Simon the tanner, at a house by the sea in Joppa.' God is not sending Cornelius a private revelation but directing him to a human preacher — the means of grace (the apostolic word) remains God's ordinary channel of saving faith. The specificity confirms divine orchestration: the angel knows exactly where Peter is because God has arranged the convergence. Cornelius will send men before he knows why; Peter will receive them before he knows who sent them.

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having explained everything to him, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary: Cornelius acts immediately and completely on the angel's instruction — the mark of genuine responsiveness to God. He explains everything to his servants and the devout soldier: not just the errand but the divine context, so that those he sends understand the gravity and the source of the commission. The three men sent represent three days' journey: they will arrive at Peter's lodging on the day that God has arranged for Peter's vision to prepare him to receive them. Two divine visions are converging on a single moment of mission breakthrough.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's trance arrives in the context of prayer and hunger — the physical and spiritual combined in the moment God uses for revelation. The sixth hour (noon) and the hunger create the natural condition for what follows: a vision involving food. God's timing is sovereign even in Peter's stomach; the hunger that prompts thoughts of food prepares him to receive a vision about food laws that is actually about people. Divine revelation always meets us in the ordinary circumstances of embodied life.

verseByVerse.quote: and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The heavens opened — the same language used at Jesus's baptism (Luke 3:21) and Stephen's vision (Acts 7:56): divine initiative breaking through the boundary between heaven and earth. The sheet let down by its four corners suggests universality — the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:12; Revelation 7:1), hinting that what is descending concerns the entire inhabited world. The vision arrives from above, from God, making clear that what Peter is about to hear is not human wisdom but divine revelation overriding human convention.

verseByVerse.quote: In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All kinds of animals' — the sheet contains the full catalogue of the Levitical food lists: clean and unclean together, the comprehensive range of creatures that the Torah had divided into permitted and forbidden. 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat' — the command is direct and unambiguous, and it cuts directly across a lifetime of Torah observance. The divine voice is not asking Peter's opinion; it is issuing an instruction. The instruction is about food, but the application, Peter will discover, is about people — the food laws were always symbolic of the ethnic separation they enforced.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By no means, Lord' — the phrase contains an unresolved tension: you cannot say 'no' to someone you acknowledge as 'Lord.' Peter's resistance is genuine and deeply rooted: his entire life has been organized around these dietary boundaries, and the voice is asking him to cross them in a single moment. The tension between his acknowledgment of divine authority and his resistance to the divine command is itself the vision's point: the commandment he is most certain cannot be overridden is exactly the one God is overriding. What the Lord declares clean cannot be called common by those who follow the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'What God has made clean, do not call common' — the divine declaration overrides the Levitical categories. This is not the abrogation of God's word by a new word; it is the fulfillment of the old word by the new reality. The food laws were given to Israel to mark its distinctness from the nations; that function has been fulfilled in Christ, who is himself 'the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes' (Romans 10:4). Three times the vision is repeated — the number of confirmation, the number that Peter needs for something this radically counter-intuitive. Then it is taken up, leaving Peter to ponder. (cf. Mark 7:18–19; Col. 2:16–17)

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's perplexity is the space in which the Spirit will explain the vision. He has received a revelation from God that he cannot yet interpret; the interpretation will arrive through the three men at the gate. God's revelations often work this way: the vision precedes the understanding, the experience precedes the theology. Peter is 'pondering' — the word implies active reflection, not passive confusion. He knows something important has happened; he is working to understand what it means when the convergence of events provides the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit's explicit direction — 'I have sent them' — is the key to the chapter: the men at the gate are not random visitors but divinely dispatched messengers. 'Without hesitation' (or 'making no distinction') — the same word that Peter will use in 11:12 when he reports to Jerusalem: 'the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction.' The Spirit is removing the instinctive hesitation that Peter's cultural conditioning would produce, replacing it with the certainty that divine authorization has been given. The conversation with Cornelius is God's idea, not Peter's.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter went down to the men and said, "I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?" And they said, "Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say."
verseByVerse.commentary: The three men's description of Cornelius is carefully framed for a Jewish audience: upright (morally excellent), God-fearing (religiously sincere), well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation (socially respected). They frame the invitation in terms that minimize the cultural barrier: Cornelius is the most respectable Gentile Peter could possibly visit. The angel's direction is explicitly mentioned to confirm divine authorization. Every word of their description is designed to make it easier for Peter to say yes to what the Spirit has already told him to do.

verseByVerse.quote: So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's hospitality to the Gentile messengers — inviting them in as overnight guests — is itself a significant step across the cultural barrier the vision has been dissolving. He takes Jewish brothers from Joppa as witnesses: he knows this encounter will need to be accountable to the Jerusalem community. The foresight is pastoral and ecclesiological — not just 'what should I do?' but 'how will I explain this?' The brothers from Joppa will become the witnesses to the Cornelius conversion who later confirm Peter's account in Jerusalem (11:12).

verseByVerse.quote: And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Cornelius has gathered his extended household for this moment — not just his family but his close friends, the community that will receive Peter's proclamation together. The gospel's first Gentile convert immediately thinks corporately: this is too important to receive alone. His prostration at Peter's feet is an act of reverence toward the one he sees as God's authorized agent. The gesture reveals both the depth of his preparation and the character of his piety: a devout man accustomed to reverence before what he perceives as holy.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter lifted him up, saying, "Stand up; I too am a man."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Stand up; I too am a man' — the proper apostolic response to misplaced worship: deflection of the honor that belongs to Christ alone. Peter's correction is immediate and theologically essential. The contrast with Herod in chapter 12 is pointed: Herod accepts divine acclamation and dies; Peter refuses it and lives. The apostle who speaks most boldly for Christ is the apostle most insistent that he himself is only a man — the vessel, not the treasure; the messenger, not the Lord. Every ministry that endures maintains this distinction.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of a different nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's opening statement is remarkable for its transparency: he names the barrier before crossing it. 'You know it is unlawful for a Jew to associate with a Gentile' — he does not pretend the barrier does not exist or has always been negotiable. He acknowledges the cultural reality, then announces the divine override: 'God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean.' The vision was about food; the application is about people. Peter has correctly interpreted the vision: the categories 'clean' and 'unclean' applied to persons have been abolished by the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I came without objection' — Peter attributes his presence entirely to the Spirit's instruction: he has no personal inclination to be in a Gentile home, but the Spirit sent him and he came. His question — 'why did you send for me?' — is not ignorance but the protocol of an orderly encounter: he wants Cornelius to explain the divine arrangement from his end, so that both parties understand this meeting has been orchestrated from above. The mutuality of the divine preparation is itself the first element of the gospel that Cornelius needs to hear: God sought him before he could seek God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Cornelius said, "Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Cornelius tells Peter his side of the story with precision: four days ago, the ninth hour, the house, the angel's appearance. The angel's message is the gospel before the gospel: your prayer has been heard; your alms have been remembered before God. The God who notices Cornelius's piety is not indifferent to those outside the covenant; he is drawing them toward the Savior who is the fulfillment of all that their piety was seeking. The prayer and alms do not save Cornelius; they are the preparation of a heart ready to receive the one who does.

verseByVerse.quote: "Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.' So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'We are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord' — no preacher has ever faced a more receptive congregation. Assembled by divine instruction, aware of God's presence, explicitly ready to hear whatever God has sent the preacher to say. Cornelius has done the work of preparation — gathering his household, instructing them about what to expect — and now he presents them to Peter as an audience that has been prepared by God himself. This is the fruit of prayer: a community ready to hear the word.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'God shows no partiality' (prosopolēmptes) — the word used in the LXX for showing favoritism based on external appearance. Peter's opening declaration is the theological revolution compressed into a single sentence: the God of Abraham and Israel does not play favorites based on ethnicity. 'In every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him' — this is not universalism (Cornelius still needs the gospel) but the statement that God's grace is not ethnically limited. The Gentile who genuinely seeks the living God will be found by him — through the gospel that Peter is about to preach. (cf. Rom. 2:11; Gal. 3:28)

One clarification, since 'anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable' is sometimes taken to mean that sincere people of any religion are saved without Christ. The passage itself rules that out. The point is that God plays no favourites by nation — he welcomes seekers from every people, not Jews only. But 'acceptable' does not mean 'already saved apart from the gospel': devout, praying Cornelius still needed to hear and believe, for the angel said Peter 'will declare to you a message by which you will be saved' (11:14; 10:43, 'everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness'). God 'accepted' Cornelius's God-fearing search by sending him the gospel, not by counting him saved without it. The precious missionary truth here is that the honest seeker in any nation, God will see to it that the gospel reaches him — yet salvation remains through Christ alone, received by faith. (Inclusivists read 'acceptable' more broadly; Cornelius's own story — a seeker who still had to hear and believe — tells against it.)

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He is Lord of all' — the parenthetical christological declaration is the foundation of everything else Peter will say. 'Lord of all' is not 'Lord of Israel' but pantōn kyrios — Lord of every person, every nation, every power. The gospel that began in Israel was never intended for Israel alone; it was the word of peace for the whole world, sent first to Israel and now arriving at Cornelius's door. The universality of the lordship of Christ is the theological basis for the universality of the gospel's reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's kerygma begins with the baptism of John — the publicly known starting point of Jesus's ministry that even Cornelius's household can be expected to know. 'Anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power' — the messianic anointing (Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18). 'Doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil' — the ministry of Jesus is summarized as a comprehensive assault on the works of the evil one: liberation, healing, restoration. 'For God was with him' — the simplest possible christological claim, and the one that best fits the audience: this man lived and worked in the conscious presence of God.

'All who were oppressed by the devil' — the word for oppressed (katadynasteuō) means to be tyrannized, held down under a cruel power. Peter is summing up Jesus' whole ministry of healing and deliverance as a rescue operation: he was prising people loose from the devil's grip. The phrase reaches wider than the cases of open demon-possession (on the nature of those 'unclean spirits,' and the caution that not every illness is a direct demonic act, see on 5:15–16). It gathers up all whom the devil's dark dominion held — for behind the whole reign of sickness, bondage, and death in a fallen world stands, ultimately, 'the works of the devil,' and 'the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy' them (1 John 3:8). Jesus himself could call a crippled woman one 'whom Satan bound for eighteen years' (Luke 13:16).

So every healing was a liberation, and a preview of total victory. Jesus came as the stronger man who binds the strong man and plunders his house (Mark 3:27), invading the devil's territory to set the captives free — 'if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you' (Matt. 12:28). And he pressed it to the very end: at the cross he 'disarmed the rulers and authorities' (Col. 2:15) and through death destroyed 'the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil' (Heb. 2:14). For Old Joe the comfort is plain — whatever cruel power has held a person down, Jesus is the great Liberator, mightier than the devil, who rescues us 'from the domain of darkness' into his own kingdom (Col. 1:13; Acts 26:18). 'He went about doing good' — and the good he did was to break the oppressor's chains.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'We are witnesses' — the apostolic testimony is grounded in historical eyewitness, not religious experience or theological deduction. 'They put him to death by hanging him on a tree' — Deuteronomy 21:23 (the curse of the law) frames the cross as the bearing of the curse that humanity deserved; Paul will develop this explicitly in Galatians 3:13. 'But God raised him on the third day' — the divine reversal that vindicates the crucified one. The resurrection is always God's act, never merely the disciples' interpretation. Between the cross and the resurrection stands the sovereign action of God.

verseByVerse.quote: "not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses' — the resurrection appearances were not public spectacles but personal encounters with those God had designated as the authorized witnesses. The apostolic circle is not self-selected but divinely appointed. 'Who ate and drank with him after he rose' — the physicality of the resurrection appearances is emphatic: this is not a vision or a spiritual impression but a person who shared meals with his disciples, recognizably and bodily present. The risen Lord's eating is the guarantee of the bodily nature of the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
verseByVerse.commentary: The kerygma reaches its two poles: judgment and forgiveness. Jesus is 'the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead' — the cosmic judge before whom all humanity will stand. And simultaneously: 'everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.' The judge is the savior; the one who will evaluate all humanity at the end of history is the same one who offers forgiveness of sins to all who believe now. 'All the prophets bear witness' — the entire prophetic tradition of Israel has been pointing toward this dual reality: the one who judges and saves through faith in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'While Peter was still saying these things' — the Spirit does not wait for the invitation, the altar call, or the completion of the argument. He falls while the word is being preached, as the Spirit falls on those who hear and believe. 'Even on the Gentiles' — the amazement of the circumcised witnesses is genuine and theologically significant: they have believed intellectually that the gospel is for all, but now they are watching the Spirit confirm it with undeniable evidence. The Spirit's arrival on uncircumcised Gentiles is the end of the old covenant's ethnic categories. (cf. Acts 2:17; Rom. 10:12–13)

verseByVerse.quote: For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Gentile believers speak in tongues and praise God — the Pentecost sign repeated, confirming in the most direct possible way that what has happened to these Gentiles is identical to what happened to the Jewish believers at Pentecost. The circumcised witnesses cannot say 'they received a different, lesser gift' because the evidence is the same: tongues, praise, the Spirit's unmistakable presence. The sign serves the argument that Peter will need to make in Jerusalem: 'the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning' (11:15). The Pentecost of the Gentiles is as complete as the Pentecost of the Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Peter declared, "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Can anyone withhold water?' — the question is rhetorical and its answer drives everything that follows in Acts. The Spirit has made the decision: these Gentiles have received the same gift as the Jewish believers at Pentecost. To refuse them baptism would be to contradict the Spirit's own declaration. Peter commands baptism in the name of Jesus Christ — not merely water baptism but entry into the community of the risen Lord. Their invitation for Peter to stay 'for some days' is the beginning of the Gentile church: a community gathering around the word and the table in Caesarea.

'Baptized in the name of Jesus Christ' — the apparent tension with Jesus' own command to baptize 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matt. 28:19) is treated more fully at 2:38 (including why the 'Jesus Only' / Oneness reading goes wrong). In brief: Luke is not recording the exact words spoken over the candidate; he is describing the baptism's character — it was Christian baptism, baptism that belongs to Jesus and marks a person out as now his, as distinct from John's baptism or any other washing. To be baptized 'into the name of Jesus' is to be baptized into the whole triune God, for you cannot have the Son without the Father who sent him and the Spirit he gives — and this very scene proves it, with the Father anointing (10:38), the Son saving, and the Spirit falling on the household (10:44).

So, as to 'the way we should do it': we follow Jesus' own explicit instruction and baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19) — the words the Lord himself gave, and the church's practice from the earliest days (the Didache, around AD 100, already prescribes them). The Acts phrase 'in the name of Jesus' does not compete with that formula; it simply names whose baptism it is. The two say one thing from two angles: those baptized belong to Jesus, and to belong to Jesus is to belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

10.theology: Election and the Nations. Acts 10 is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham: “in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). The blessing always intended to reach the Gentiles; what Acts 10 shows is the mechanism — the proclamation of Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and the sovereign gift of the Holy Spirit to all who believe. The Gentile mission is not an emergency plan devised when Israel rejected the Messiah. It is the ancient plan of the God who chose Abraham in order to bless the world through him. Peter’s visit to Cornelius is, in the deepest sense, the arrival of what Genesis 12 promised. The God who shows no partiality has always intended a people from every nation. Acts 10 is that intention breaking into history.
10.examples:
Then: A Roman soldier who prayed toward Jerusalem and a Jewish fisherman who would never have entered a Gentile home — brought together by two visions, thirty miles apart, orchestrated by the God who wastes nothing and plans everything. The Spirit fell. The barriers fell. The church was never the same.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to build walls that God has torn down. The divisions that seem most natural — racial, cultural, economic, denominational — are the ones most likely to be the new versions of the Jewish-Gentile divide. What God has made clean, do not call common. The community of the Spirit is wider than our instincts, and deeper than our categories.

11.title: The Church at Antioch
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. <sup>2</sup>So when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcision party criticized him, saying, <sup>3</sup>“You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.” <sup>4</sup>But Peter began and explained it to them in order: <sup>5</sup>“I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me. <sup>6</sup>Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>7</sup>And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ <sup>8</sup>But I said, ‘By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’ <sup>9</sup>But the voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’ <sup>10</sup>This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven. <sup>11</sup>And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. <sup>12</sup>And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man’s house. <sup>13</sup>And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, ‘Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; <sup>14</sup>he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.’ <sup>15</sup>As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. <sup>16</sup>And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ <sup>17</sup>If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” <sup>18</sup>When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, “Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.” <sup>19</sup>Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews. <sup>20</sup>But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. <sup>21</sup>And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. <sup>22</sup>The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, <sup>24</sup>for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord. <sup>25</sup>So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, <sup>26</sup>and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. <sup>27</sup>Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. <sup>28</sup>And one of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius). <sup>29</sup>So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. <sup>30</sup>And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
11.overview:
The Jerusalem church is disturbed. Peter has eaten with Gentiles. In the world of first-century Judaism this was not a minor breach of etiquette; it was a fundamental transgression of the boundaries that defined the covenant people. And so Peter explains — not defending himself, but laying out the sequence of God’s action: vision, voice, Spirit, Gentiles praising God. And the argument that silences the critics is the simplest and most devastating: “who was I that I could stand in God’s way?” When God moves, the only question is whether you will move with him.

Meanwhile, two hundred miles to the north, the scattered believers who fled Stephen’s death are doing something unprecedented. Some of them — unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene — begin speaking to Gentiles in Antioch about the Lord Jesus. Not Peter. Not the twelve. Unknown disciples, obeying the impulse of the Spirit, doing what had never been done before. “And the hand of the Lord was with them.” A great many believed and turned to the Lord.

Antioch becomes the first truly multi-ethnic church, the first church not rooted in a synagogue, the birthplace of the word “Christian” — and the sending base from which the whole Gentile mission will be launched. The church that began in a frightened upper room in Jerusalem is now planting itself in the third largest city of the empire. God is moving with speed and surprise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The news of Cornelius's conversion reaches Jerusalem before Peter does, and the circumcised believers are waiting for him with a complaint: 'You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them.' The objection is not to Peter's preaching but to his table fellowship — the deepest expression of social equality in the ancient world. To eat with Gentiles was to declare them social equals; the Jewish believers in Jerusalem are not yet ready for the implications of what God has done in Caesarea.

Peter's response is to tell the entire story, step by step, from the vision in Joppa to the falling of the Spirit in Caesarea. When he reaches the climax — 'the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning' — he poses the question that cannot be answered: 'Who was I that I could stand in God's way?' The Jerusalem community's response is silence and praise: 'Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.' The theological revolution is complete: the gospel is for all nations, and God himself has declared it so.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel's Universal Reach and Human Resistance

Peter's account of Cornelius's conversion reveals the pattern by which God expands the church's missional imagination: direct divine intervention overriding human cultural limitation. The Jewish believers in Jerusalem were not wicked or small-minded; they were genuinely uncertain whether the promises of Israel extended to uncircumcised Gentiles. God answered their uncertainty not with a letter or a decree but with the undeniable fact of the Spirit's falling. Reformed theology sees here the sovereignty of the Spirit over every human boundary that would limit the gospel's reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church praised God and acknowledged that 'to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.' The praise was real — and the implications took years to work out (Acts 15). Now: The church continues to discover the implications of the gospel's universality — that no culture, no people, no individual is beyond the reach of the grace that reached Cornelius's household.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the apostles and the brothers who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. And when Peter went up to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision criticized him,
verseByVerse.commentary: News travels faster than Peter: the Gentile mission report has already reached Jerusalem before he arrives. 'Those of the circumcision' — Jewish believers who held that circumcision was still required of converts. Their criticism anticipates the Jerusalem Council debate of chapter 15; the question of Gentile inclusion and the conditions for it will occupy the church for years. The criticism is not of Peter's preaching but of his social practice — the issue is fellowship, not doctrine, though the two are inseparable in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them' — the complaint names the specific offense: table fellowship with Gentiles. In the ancient world, to share a meal was to declare social equality and communal belonging. For a Torah-observant Jew to eat with an uncircumcised Gentile was to declare that the boundary between clean and unclean — enforced in part by dietary laws — had been dissolved. The critics are not wrong about what Peter did; they are wrong about what it means. Peter's explanation will show that what looks like boundary violation is actually divine fulfillment.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter began and explained it to them in order: "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision, something like a great sheet descending, being let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came down to me."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter 'explained it to them in order' — a careful, sequential account that will not allow selective objection. He begins at the beginning: Joppa, prayer, the trance. The prayer context is important: this vision was not received in idle curiosity but in the posture of dependence on God. The sheet descending from heaven 'by its four corners' is the detail that hints at universality — the four corners of the earth — even before Peter understands the vision's full meaning. He is reporting faithfully what he received, not interpreting in advance of his audience's readiness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Looking at it closely, I observed animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air. And I heard a voice saying to me, 'Rise, Peter; kill and eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's retelling emphasizes the comprehensive scope of what was in the sheet: 'animals and beasts of prey and reptiles and birds of the air' — the full range of creatures, including those most clearly forbidden by the Levitical code. The command ('rise, kill, eat') was therefore maximally offensive to a Torah-observant Jew: it explicitly included the forbidden categories. Peter is not softening the story for his Jerusalem audience; he is telling them exactly what God said, including the parts most likely to provoke their objection, because the vision's authority depends on its exact content.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said, 'By no means, Lord; for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.' But the voice answered a second time from heaven, 'What God has made clean, do not call common.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter includes his own resistance in the retelling — an act of honesty that validates his account. He did not comply immediately; he objected with exactly the objection his Jerusalem audience would have made. And God's response — 'what God has made clean, do not call common' — is addressed equally to the Jerusalem critics through Peter's retelling: if God has declared it clean, their calling it common is a contradiction of divine declaration. The vision's authority overrules the tradition's classification.

verseByVerse.quote: "This happened three times, and all was drawn up again into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary: The triple repetition — three times the vision appeared, three times the voice spoke, three times Peter resisted and was corrected — is the number of confirmation: what God has declared three times cannot be dismissed as coincidence or misinterpretation. By the third repetition, the message is unmistakable. The drawing up of the sheet into heaven closes the vision: its content has been delivered and will not be repeated. Now Peter must act on what he has received — and the three men at the gate provide the immediate occasion.

verseByVerse.quote: "And behold, at that very moment three men arrived at the house in which we were, sent to me from Caesarea. And the Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered the man's house."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'At that very moment' — the divine timing is Peter's evidence of sovereignty: the three men arrived while the vision was still being pondered. 'The Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction' — the Spirit's explicit instruction is Peter's authorization for the boundary-crossing that follows. 'These six brothers accompanied me' — Peter brought witnesses, not merely for protection but for accountability. He understood that what he was about to do would require corroboration, and he provided it in advance. The six brothers are the evidence that the Jerusalem critics cannot dismiss.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he told us how he had seen the angel stand in his house and say, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon who is called Peter; he will declare to you a message by which you will be saved, you and all your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Cornelius's vision confirms the divine orchestration from his end: the angel named Peter specifically, and promised that the message Peter would bring would be the means of salvation — 'by which you will be saved, you and all your household.' The word 'saved' (sōthēsē) is the gospel's central term, and the angel uses it of what has not yet happened: the future salvation that the word about Jesus will bring. Peter's preaching is the ordained means; the Spirit's work is the enabling power; the outcome ('you will be saved') is the divine promise.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them just as on us at the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Just as on us at the beginning' — the identification of the Cornelius outpouring with the Pentecost event is Peter's most powerful argument: the Spirit who fell on these Gentiles is the same Spirit who fell on the Jerusalem community at Pentecost, producing the same evidence. The citation of Jesus's own word about Spirit-baptism (1:5) provides the interpretive key: the Spirit's falling on Cornelius's household is the fulfillment of the same promise that was fulfilled at Pentecost. What happened there has happened here — identically.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who was I that I could stand in God's way?' — the question that ends every legitimate objection to what God has done. Peter does not claim authority for what he did; he claims deference to what God did. The rhetorical question places the real choice before the Jerusalem critics: do they want to stand in God's way? The sovereignty of the Spirit's action is Peter's entire argument. He did not decide to include the Gentiles; God included them. To object to their inclusion is to object to God's sovereign decision, confirmed by the evidence of the Spirit's gift. (cf. Rom. 9:19–20; Gal. 2:14)

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things they fell silent. And they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." Now those who were scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'They fell silent... they glorified God' — the Jerusalem community's resistance is overcome not by argument but by the undeniable evidence of the Spirit's action. 'Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life' — the theological conclusion is drawn with precision: repentance is a gift that God grants, not an achievement that humans produce. Luke's transition in v. 19 connects the Cornelius episode to the broader scattering: the persecution that produced Stephen's martyrdom is also producing the gospel's expansion, though initially only to Jews.

One small but useful lesson in how to read the Bible lies in that phrase, 'God has granted repentance.' Notice that only repentance is named here, not faith — yet faith is plainly implied, for these Gentiles had believed the gospel (vv. 17, 21). Scripture constantly speaks this way, naming one part of a thing to stand for the whole (a figure of speech called synecdoche). Repentance and faith are simply the two sides of one single turning to Christ: repentance is turning from sin, faith is turning to the Saviour, and you cannot truly do one without the other. So Scripture sometimes names both — 'repent and believe in the gospel' (Mark 1:15), 'repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus' (Acts 20:21) — sometimes only repentance (here; Luke 24:47; Acts 3:19), and sometimes only faith ('believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved,' Acts 16:31; John 3:16). Whichever one is mentioned, the other comes with it. The whole gospel response can be summed up under any of its facets — 'call on the name of the Lord' (Rom. 10:13), 'confess... Jesus is Lord' (Rom. 10:9) all mean the same conversion.

Two cautions follow. First, never build a doctrine on the absence of a word: it would be a serious mistake to read this verse as though faith were unnecessary, or to read Acts 16:31 as though repentance were. Each statement is to be read in the light of the whole of Scripture, which everywhere joins the two. Second, savour what the verse actually says: God granted repentance. The very turning is his gift — as faith is also called 'the gift of God' (Eph. 2:8; cf. 2 Tim. 2:25; Phil. 1:29). So when Old Joe reads 'repent' or 'believe' standing alone, he should hear the whole: turn to Christ, from sin and unto the Saviour — and give thanks that even the turning was granted him from above.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Antioch becomes the second great center of the early church — and in some ways the more important one for the mission that follows. It is in Antioch that the gospel first crosses the ethnic barrier in a sustained way, not because of a divine vision (as with Peter and Cornelius) but because some unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene begin speaking to Greeks as well as Jews. It is in Antioch that believers are first called 'Christians.' It is from Antioch that the first missionary journey is launched. And it is to Antioch that Barnabas brings Saul of Tarsus from his long obscurity in Tarsus — the beginning of the partnership that will take the gospel to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Antioch Church as Mission Base

The Antioch church embodies the pattern that Reformed missiology has identified as the apostolic model: a church rooted in the word ('Barnabas taught a great many people'), committed to prayer and fasting (13:2–3), generous in its care for other churches (the famine relief of vv. 29–30), and willing to send its best leaders on mission. Antioch does not hoard Barnabas and Saul; it commissions them. The church that is most willing to release its best resources for mission is the church most shaped by the Spirit's priorities.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Antioch church was built by unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene who spoke to Greeks. The great mission advance was often made by anonymous believers, not recognized leaders. Now: The most significant missionary work in any generation may be done by people whose names do not appear in any history — those who simply speak the word to whoever is in front of them.

verseByVerse.quote: But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who on coming to Antioch spoke to the Hellenists also, preaching the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Men of Cyprus and Cyrene' — the great mission breakthrough in Antioch is made by unnamed believers, not by the Jerusalem apostles or Philip or Barnabas. They simply spoke the gospel to Greeks as well as Jews, apparently because it seemed the natural thing to do. 'The hand of the Lord was with them' — divine power accompanying human witness, producing a 'great number' of conversions. The expansion of the gospel to Gentiles in Antioch is organic and Spirit-driven, not the result of a council decision or an apostolic strategy. The unnamed missionaries of Antioch are among the most consequential figures in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: The report of this came to the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose,
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He saw the grace of God' — Barnabas's theological perception is itself a mark of spiritual maturity: he recognizes what he is seeing not as a sociological phenomenon (a growing movement) but as the work of God's grace. His response is joy. The Jerusalem church's decision to send Barnabas rather than an inspector is itself significant: Barnabas is the son of encouragement (4:36), not a son of suspicion. His exhortation — 'remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose' — addresses the primary danger facing a young church: wavering, compromise, the loss of the first love under the pressures of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were added to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke's characterization of Barnabas — 'a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith' — is the New Testament portrait of effective pastoral character. Not primarily gifted or strategic or well-connected, but good, Spirit-filled, and faithful. Under this kind of ministry 'a great many people were added to the Lord' — not to the church as an institution but to the Lord himself. The growth is organic, Spirit-driven, and continues the pattern established throughout Acts: genuine pastoral presence produces genuine community growth, because the Spirit is pleased to fill and work through those who embody these qualities.

'Full of the Holy Spirit' — it is, as you say, a description we rarely hear on people's lips today, yet it is one of the loveliest things Scripture ever says of anyone. (On how such fullness shows itself, and how the early church could actually recognise it, see the fuller treatment at 6:5.) In brief, Luke uses the phrase not for a momentary 'filling' for a single task — Acts has those too, a sudden filling for boldness or speech (4:8, 31; 13:9) — but for a settled, habitual condition: a man so yielded to the Spirit that the Spirit pervades and governs his whole life, his character and words and deeds. It is the same thing said of Jesus himself ('full of the Holy Spirit,' Luke 4:1) and of Stephen (6:5) — so to be full of the Spirit is simply to be deeply like Christ. And notice how concrete it is in Barnabas: it is paired with 'a good man... and of faith,' and we have watched it in action — the generous giver who sold his field (4:36–37), the big-hearted man who vouched for the feared new convert Saul when others would not (9:27), the encourager who 'was glad' to see God's grace in Antioch (11:23). That is what a Spirit-full life looks like: goodness, faith, generosity, courage, and an eye quick to rejoice in grace.

And it is not meant to be a rare distinction reserved for a Barnabas. The New Testament commands every believer, 'be filled with the Spirit' (Eph. 5:18) — a continuous filling, sought by yielding to him: letting the word of Christ dwell richly (Col. 3:16), praying, obeying, walking in step with the Spirit rather than grieving or quenching him (Gal. 5:16; Eph. 4:30; 1 Thess. 5:19). It is a phrase worth recovering, and a thing worth coveting — for the highest compliment that could be paid to Old Joe is not that he is clever or capable, but that those who meet him meet something of God, because he is full of the Holy Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: So Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.
verseByVerse.commentary: Barnabas goes to Tarsus to find Saul — a search that implies Saul was not easily located, perhaps itinerating in the Cilician region. Barnabas's retrieval of Saul is his second great act of advocacy for the man others feared: the first was introducing Saul to the Jerusalem apostles (9:27); now he brings him to Antioch to teach the church that Barnabas himself has planted. A year of teaching produces a community mature enough to be called 'Christians' — the first use of the name, given apparently by outsiders who noticed that this community was distinctively marked by its allegiance to Christ. (cf. 1 Pet. 4:16; Isa. 62:2)

verseByVerse.quote: Now in these days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. One of them named Agabus stood up and foretold by the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the world (this took place in the days of Claudius).
verseByVerse.commentary: The prophets who travel from Jerusalem to Antioch represent the continuing ministry of Spirit-given prophecy in the early church — not prophecy that adds to Scripture but prophecy that gives specific guidance and warning for the community's practical life. Agabus's prophecy of the coming famine is the first of two appearances in Acts (cf. 21:10–11). The famine under Claudius (c. AD 46–47) is historically verifiable; the Spirit's forewarning allows the church to prepare a response rather than merely react to the crisis.

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples determined, every one according to his ability, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Every one according to his ability' — the Antioch relief collection is a model of proportionate, voluntary generosity: not equal amounts but each person giving in proportion to their means. The collection for the Jerusalem church from the Gentile Antioch church is itself an enacted theology: the Gentiles who have received the spiritual blessings of Israel's Messiah share their material resources with the Jewish mother church. Paul will use exactly this argument in Romans 15:27. The Barnabas-and-Saul relief mission is their first joint mission and a foretaste of the partnership that will launch the Gentile mission.

11.theology: Repentance as Gift. Acts 11:18 contains one of the clearest biblical statements of the Reformed doctrine of monergism in conversion: “God has granted repentance that leads to life.” Repentance is not a human achievement that God rewards with salvation; it is itself a divine gift, granted by God to those he is drawing to himself. This does not eliminate human responsibility — the Gentiles in Cornelius’s house genuinely repented, genuinely believed, genuinely turned to Christ. But behind their turning was God’s giving. This is the grammar of all true conversion: God grants, the sinner turns, and God receives the glory. Antioch is not merely a sociological phenomenon — it is a theological one: God giving repentance to people who had no claim on him, because he is the God of all grace.
11.examples:
Then: Anonymous men from Cyprus and Cyrene, whose names are not recorded in Scripture, who crossed the ethnic boundary no one else had thought to cross, and started the church in Antioch. The hand of the Lord was with them. History turned on their obedience.

Now: The church at Antioch is the model of a healthy sending church: multi-ethnic, Spirit-filled, taught by gifted teachers, responsive to need (the famine collection), and willing to send its best people out on mission. Every local church must ask whether it looks more like the fearful circumcision party in Jerusalem or the glad, generous, outward-facing church at Antioch.

12.title: The Prison and the Providence
12.text: <sup>1</sup>About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. <sup>2</sup>He killed James the brother of John with the sword. <sup>3</sup>And when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. <sup>4</sup>And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. <sup>5</sup>So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. <sup>6</sup>Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentinels before the door were guarding the prison. <sup>7</sup>And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, “Get up quickly.” And the chains fell off his hands. <sup>8</sup>And the angel said to him, “Dress yourself and put on your sandals.” And he did so. And he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.” <sup>9</sup>And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. <sup>10</sup>When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him. <sup>11</sup>When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting.” <sup>12</sup>When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. <sup>13</sup>And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. <sup>14</sup>Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate. <sup>15</sup>They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they kept saying, “It is his angel!” <sup>16</sup>But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed. <sup>17</sup>But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. <sup>18</sup>Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter. <sup>19</sup>And after Herod searched for him and did not find him, he examined the sentinels and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there. <sup>20</sup>Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. <sup>21</sup>On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them. <sup>22</sup>And the people were shouting, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” <sup>23</sup>Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last. <sup>24</sup>But the word of God increased and multiplied. <sup>25</sup>And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
12.overview:
Herod Agrippa is playing to the crowd. He has killed James the son of Zebedee with the sword — the first of the twelve to be martyred — and it pleased the Jews, so he arrests Peter. The calculation is purely political. Herod is not a theological opponent; he is a man who will do whatever secures his power. And in the background, the church is praying.

The contrast Luke draws in this chapter is stark and deliberate: Herod’s power on one side, God’s providence on the other. Sixteen soldiers, chains, iron gates, maximum security — and Peter sleeping so peacefully that the angel has to strike him on the side to wake him. The man who is about to be executed is asleep. This is the peace that passes understanding — the peace of a man who knows that his life is in hands that Herod cannot reach.

The liberation is almost comic in its details: Peter thinks he is dreaming, Rhoda is too astonished to open the gate, the praying church refuses to believe their prayers are answered. But the most important moment in the chapter may be the shortest sentence: “But the word of God increased and multiplied.” Herod is dead, eaten by worms, and the Word is alive and growing. This is the verdict of history on every power that has set itself against the gospel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — Herod's Persecution and God's Deliverance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 12 is one of the most dramatic in Acts, structured around a stark contrast: the power of Herod against the power of God, with the church's praying community as the pivot between them. Herod Agrippa I kills James the son of Zebedee with the sword — the first apostolic martyrdom — and proceeds to arrest Peter, intending the same fate. The church's response is prayer, continuous and corporate. And while the church prays, an angel wakes a sleeping prisoner, leads him through locked gates, and deposits him in the street outside. Peter arrives at Mary's house while the community is still praying, and the servant girl who answers the door is so astonished she leaves him standing on the street.

The contrast sharpens in the chapter's conclusion: Peter escapes and disappears to 'another place'; Herod accepts the crowd's acclamation as a god and is immediately struck down by an angel and eaten by worms. The man who killed James and arrested Peter dies a grotesque death for accepting divine honors; the man who was chained between two soldiers is alive and free. The word of God continues to increase and multiply. The calculus of human power and divine sovereignty has been demonstrated once more, irrefutably.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Praying Church and the Sovereign God

The prayer meeting in Mary's house (v. 12) is the context in which the miraculous deliverance occurs. Reformed theology does not see this as magic — prayer does not force God's hand. Rather, prayer is the expression of the community's dependence on God, and God, in his sovereignty, works through the prayers of his people to accomplish his purposes.
