Peter's escape is God's sovereign act; the community's prayer is the means God has appointed for expressing their trust in his sovereignty. The two belong together: sovereign God and praying church.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rhoda's announcement that Peter was at the door was met with 'you are out of your mind' from the very people who had been praying for his release. The gap between what we pray for and what we believe God will do is the church's perennial challenge. Now: The church prays for revival, healing, deliverance, transformation — and is sometimes too surprised when it receives them. Genuine prayer includes genuine expectation.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword,
verseByVerse.commentary: Herod Agrippa I's targeting of the church is explicitly motivated by political opportunism — 'it pleased the Jews' (v. 3). James, the son of Zebedee and brother of John, becomes the first of the Twelve to die for his faith, fulfilling Jesus's word to the brothers that they would indeed drink the cup he would drink (Mark 10:38–39). The martyrdom is reported with stark brevity: no speech, no defense, no dramatic final scene. James is killed with a sword, and the kingdom of God advances. Martyrdom does not interrupt the mission; it is part of it.

verseByVerse.quote: and when he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread. And when he had seized him, he put him in prison, delivering him over to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary: The timing is deliberately ironic: during the days of Unleavened Bread, the week of Israel's liberation from Egypt, the one who proclaimed the greater Exodus is imprisoned. Herod's security arrangements — four squads of four soldiers each, rotating through night watches — represent the maximum containment that Roman military organization can provide. Peter is chained between two soldiers; sentries guard the doors. Every precaution that human power can devise is in place. And while Herod prepares his public execution, the church prepares its prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was being made to God by the church. Now when Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentinels before the door were guarding the prison.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But earnest prayer for him was being made to God by the church' — the 'but' is the theological hinge of the chapter: against Herod's power, the church's prayer. 'Earnest' — stretched out, sustained, intense: not casual intercession but the concentrated corporate prayer of a community that knows its only resource is God. Peter sleeps between his guards — a peace that can only be explained by the Spirit who gives peace beyond understanding (Philippians 4:7). On the night before his expected execution, Peter sleeps. (cf. Matt. 18:19–20; James 5:16)

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, an angel of the Lord stood next to him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell off his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary: The angel's arrival is described with precise economy: the light, the struck side, the command, the chains falling. Each element of Herod's security is overcome in sequence: first the chains (the immediate constraint), then the guards (passed without notice), then the iron gate (which opens of its own accord). The power that raised Jesus from the dead makes short work of Roman iron. The chains do not unlock — they fall off. The miracle is not a prison break; it is a divine statement that what God has commissioned cannot be contained by what humans have built.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to him, "Dress yourself and put on your sandals." And he did so. And he said to him, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me." And he went out and followed him. He did not know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision.
verseByVerse.commentary: The angel's instructions are almost mundane: dress yourself, put on your sandals, wrap your cloak. Even in the miraculous, God's care extends to the practical details of his servant's wellbeing — Peter will need his clothes in the night air outside the prison walls. Peter follows without fully understanding: 'he thought he was seeing a vision.' The man who had seen the vision of the sheet in Acts 10 is apparently accustomed to divine visions and cannot yet distinguish this liberation from another one. The grace of God sometimes arrives in forms we cannot initially process as real.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had passed the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord, and they went out and went along one street, and immediately the angel left him.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It opened for them of its own accord' (automatē) — the same word used in ancient texts of miraculously self-opening city gates, perhaps echoing Isaiah 45:1–2 where God opens gates before Cyrus. The iron gate, the strongest barrier, poses no obstacle. They walk one street, and then the angel departs — the divine assistance given for the necessary duration, no longer. Providence does not over-provide; it gives exactly what is needed when it is needed. Peter stands alone on the street of Jerusalem, free, alive, and about to discover that the church was praying him out while he slept.

verseByVerse.quote: When Peter came to himself, he said, "Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all that the Jewish people were expecting." When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John whose other name was Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When Peter came to himself' — the return of full consciousness, the recognition of what has happened. 'Now I am sure' — the certainty of deliverance becomes the certainty of praise. Peter immediately goes to the community that has been praying for him — the house of Mary, the mother of Mark, who will become the author of the Gospel of Mark. 'Many were gathered together and were praying' — the night-long prayer meeting that God has been answering while the community prayed, not knowing the answer was already walking through the streets toward them.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he knocked at the door of the gateway, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Recognizing Peter's voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and reported that Peter was standing at the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary: Rhoda's response is the comic heart of the passage and its most humanly recognizable moment. She identifies Peter's voice — she knows him well enough to recognize it through a closed door — and is so overwhelmed by joy that she abandons him on the street and runs to tell the others. The joy precedes any rational processing of what the joy means; she forgets the door entirely. Peter stands knocking outside the gate of the house where his community has been praying for his release. The gap between the answer to prayer and the community's capacity to receive it is Rhoda's closed door.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to her, "You are out of your mind." But she kept insisting that it was so, and they said, "It is his angel!" But Peter continued knocking, and when they opened, they saw him and were amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The prayer community tells the servant who announces the answer to their prayer that she is out of her mind. Then they suggest it must be his angel — a guardian spirit, a common Jewish belief about the doubles that sometimes appeared to represent the living. The earnest prayers of chapter 12's night meeting are, apparently, attended by earnest doubt about whether God will actually answer them. Luke preserves the comedy without condemnation: the church's surprise at answered prayer is its perennial challenge. Peter stands knocking while they debate theology. He continues knocking — patient, realistic, entirely alive.

verseByVerse.quote: But motioning to them with his hand to be silent, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, "Tell these things to James and to the brothers." Then he departed and went to another place. Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's debrief is brief and purposeful: he describes the Lord's action (not his own escape), directs that James and the brothers be informed, and departs immediately for safety. 'Tell James' — James the Lord's brother, now the leader of the Jerusalem church, needs to know; the leadership must be informed even when Peter cannot stay to inform them personally. The 'no little disturbance' among the soldiers is understandable: they are responsible for a prisoner who has vanished from maximum security, and the consequences for Roman soldiers who lose a prisoner are severe.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Herod had searched for him and did not find him, he examined the soldiers and ordered that they should be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and spent time there.
verseByVerse.commentary: Herod's investigation produces no explanation and therefore no recourse except to execute the guards — the brutal logic of Roman military accountability: the soldiers are responsible for the prisoner regardless of how the escape occurred. Their deaths are a dark footnote to Peter's liberation: human lives paying the price of divine sovereign action. Herod's retreat to Caesarea is the political consequence of his public failure: the execution that was meant to please the Jerusalem crowd cannot proceed, and the king who played politics with the church's lives has been embarrassed by the God he does not acknowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, and they came to him with one accord, and having persuaded Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king's country for food. On an appointed day Herod put on his royal robes, took his seat upon the throne, and delivered an oration to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The setting is a public assembly at Caesarea — probably the festival games or a formal diplomatic occasion. Herod in his royal robes on his throne delivering a speech is the picture of human power at its most magnificent: the king in full display, speaking to dependent peoples who need his favor. The description of the Tyrians and Sidonians seeking peace because their country 'depended on the king's country for food' provides the political context: this is a moment of maximum royal authority and maximum human vulnerability before that authority.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were shouting, "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" And immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast with Peter's angel could not be more complete. The same order of beings that freed Peter now execute Herod. The crowd's acclamation — 'the voice of a god, not of a man' — is the sin: Herod accepted divine honors that belong to God alone. 'Because he did not give God the glory' — the explicit reason for the judgment. The man who killed James and tried to kill Peter dies of a grotesque disease, eaten by worms. The power that he wielded against the church is shown, in the most visceral possible way, to be entirely dependent on the permission of the God he refused to acknowledge. (cf. Isa. 40:6–8; 1 Pet. 1:24–25)

verseByVerse.quote: But the word of God increased and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem when they had completed their service, bringing with them John, whose other name was Mark.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But the word of God increased and multiplied' — Luke's summary statement stands against the narrative of Herod's power: the king who tried to suppress the gospel is dead; the word of God flourishes. The formula appears three times in Acts (6:7; 9:31; 12:24) as a refrain marking the gospel's advance despite opposition. Barnabas and Saul return from Jerusalem with John Mark — the cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), son of Mary whose house was the prayer meeting, and future author of the Gospel that bears his name. The team is assembled for the mission to come.

12.theology: Providence, Prayer, and the Sovereignty of God over Kings. Acts 12 is a meditation on what it means to live under the providence of a God who governs kings and councils, who opens prison gates and strikes down tyrants, and who is not moved by the calculations of the powerful. James dies; Peter lives — both by divine appointment. The church prays; the answer comes — and still takes them by surprise. Herod grasps at divine honour; he is given worms and silence. This is the world the New Testament describes: not a world where God occasionally intervenes, but a world where God is always governing — every chain, every gate, every angel, every worm. The appropriate response is not to explain his ways, but to pray, to trust, and to keep speaking the Word that outlasts every king.
12.examples:
Then: A church under a murderous king, with no political recourse, no legal protection, and no army — meeting in a house and praying with everything they had. Their prayers opened a prison door thirty miles from where they sat. They did not know it would happen that way. They prayed because there was nothing else to do, and because the God they prayed to had not changed.

Now: The church in every hostile political environment must learn the same calculus: Herod has soldiers; God has angels. Herod has chains; God has the Word. The appropriate response to power arrayed against the gospel is not despair and not political calculation — it is earnest, persistent, expectant prayer to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And then, when the knock comes at the door, to open it.

13.title: The First Missionary Journey Begins
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. <sup>2</sup>While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” <sup>3</sup>Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off. <sup>4</sup>So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. <sup>5</sup>When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them. <sup>6</sup>When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. <sup>7</sup>He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God. <sup>8</sup>But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. <sup>9</sup>But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him <sup>10</sup>and said, “You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? <sup>11</sup>And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. <sup>12</sup>Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord. <sup>13</sup>Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup>but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. <sup>15</sup>After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.” <sup>16</sup>So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. <sup>17</sup>The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it. <sup>22</sup>And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, ‘I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ <sup>23</sup>Of this man’s offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. <sup>26</sup>Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation. <sup>27</sup>For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. <sup>28</sup>And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed. <sup>29</sup>And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>But God raised him from the dead, <sup>31</sup>and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. <sup>32</sup>And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, <sup>33</sup>this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, ‘You are my Son, today I have begotten you.’ <sup>38</sup>Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, <sup>39</sup>and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. <sup>40</sup>Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: <sup>41</sup>‘Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.’” <sup>42</sup>As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. <sup>43</sup>And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. <sup>44</sup>The next Sabbath almost the whole city came together to hear the word of the Lord. <sup>45</sup>But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him. <sup>46</sup>And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. <sup>47</sup>For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’” <sup>48</sup>And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. <sup>49</sup>And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region. <sup>50</sup>But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. <sup>51</sup>But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium. <sup>52</sup>And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
13.overview:
The first missionary journey begins not with a committee decision but with the Holy Spirit speaking in a worship service: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” The church at Antioch is worshipping and fasting — attending to God — and God speaks. This is always the order: first the consecration, then the commission. The church that is too busy to fast and pray will miss what God is saying. The church that waits on him will find that he is the one who sends.

Paul’s sermon at Pisidian Antioch is his great synagogue address — the same structure as Peter’s sermon at Pentecost: the sweep of Israel’s history, the fulfilment in Jesus, the resurrection, the call to repentance. But Paul adds something Peter did not stress: “by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses.” The law cannot save. The law could never save. It was never designed to save. Only Christ can do what the law could only demand.

Then verse 48, which has caused theologians to argue for twenty centuries and which the text itself presents without apology: “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed.” Election precedes faith. The believing is real; the appointment is prior. Both are true. Luke sees no contradiction.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The First Missionary Journey Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The launching of the first missionary journey is simultaneously the most significant moment in Acts after Pentecost and the most ordinary: a community fasting, worshipping, and praying hears the Spirit speak through the assembled prophets and teachers. 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.' The call is divine, the authorization is corporate, and the method is prayer and fasting and the laying on of hands. The mission to the nations that will occupy the rest of Acts begins in a prayer meeting in Antioch.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missionary Call and Corporate Discernment

The Spirit speaks the call through the assembled prophets and teachers — not to Barnabas and Saul alone but to the worshipping community. The sending is corporate: the church that set apart, fasted, prayed, and laid on hands is as much the sender as the Spirit is. Reformed ecclesiology sees here the model of missionary commissioning: the individual's call confirmed by the corporate community, the community's discernment confirmed by the Spirit. Neither the individual alone nor the institution alone determines the mission; the Spirit speaks to the church about the person, and the church responds.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Elymas the magician tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith and was struck blind. Paul's response — 'you son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness' — reveals what genuine mission encounters: not merely intellectual opposition but spiritual resistance to the gospel's advance. Now: The missionary enterprise always faces both human and spiritual opposition. The Spirit who struck Elymas blind is the Spirit who gives missionaries the discernment to recognize and the authority to name spiritual opposition when it appears.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Antioch leadership team reveals the breadth of the church's social and ethnic composition: a Cypriot Jew, an African (Niger suggests dark skin, and Lucius of Cyrene is North African), a childhood companion of Herod Antipas (who beheaded John the Baptist), and the former persecutor from Tarsus. The Spirit speaks the call during corporate worship and fasting — the posture of the community most fully yielded to God. 'Set apart for me' — the mission belongs to the Spirit; Barnabas and Saul are being allocated from the community to the Spirit's specific purposes.

'Fasting' — a word worth pausing on, since many believers today, like Old Joe, have never done it. Biblically, to fast is voluntarily to go without food (sometimes for part of a day, a day, or longer) for the sake of seeking God. It is not dieting, nor a hunger strike to twist God's arm, nor the grim self-punishment Scripture actually warns against (Col. 2:23). The empty stomach is meant to drive the soul to God — to say with the body what the heart means: 'Lord, I want you more than my daily bread.' In Scripture it goes hand in hand with earnest prayer, and attends the great seekings of God: guidance and the sending of missionaries (here, and 13:3; 14:23), repentance and humbling before God (Joel 2:12; Jonah 3), grief (2 Sam. 1:12), crisis and intercession (Esther 4:16; Ezra 8:21–23), and steady devotion (Anna, 'worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day,' Luke 2:37). Jesus himself fasted forty days before his ministry (Matt. 4:2).

Is it commanded of Christians — and is it in the Epistles? Here we should be honest: fasting is nowhere laid on believers as a law, and the letters mention it only sparingly (the references in 2 Cor. 6:5; 11:27 may even be involuntary hunger from hardship). So no one is in sin for not fasting, and no one earns a thing by doing it. And yet — and this is the key — Jesus plainly assumed his people would fast. He taught, 'WHEN you fast' (not if), warning only against doing it for show (Matt. 6:16–18); and when asked why his disciples did not fast, he answered that the wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, 'but the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and THEN they will fast' (Matt. 9:15) — that is, in this present age between his ascension and his return. So fasting is not a rule to keep under compulsion, but a privilege and a means of grace that the Lord expects his church to use.

So should Old Joe fast? Gently, yes — not out of guilt or to score points with God, but as a gift worth taking up; he is missing a help his Master plainly meant him to have. Why? Because there are seasons — a weighty decision, a heavy burden in prayer, sorrow over sin, a longing to seek God afresh — when setting aside even a good thing like food, to give that time and hunger to God, focuses and humbles the heart and intensifies prayer; and because the very hunger preaches to us that 'man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God' (Matt. 4:4). How? Start small and simple — skip a meal or two, or a day, and spend the time you would have spent eating in prayer and the Word; always tie the fast to a purpose and to prayer (fasting without praying is merely going hungry); keep it secret, between you and your Father, never paraded (Matt. 6:17–18). Two cautions: guard the heart against pride — the Pharisee boasted, 'I fast twice a week' (Luke 18:12), and Isaiah 58 shows God despising a fasting joined to self-righteousness and hard-heartedness; and use ordinary wisdom about health (those who are unwell, pregnant, or on medication should take care, and abstaining from water is only ever for very short periods). Fasting earns nothing; but as a humble, hungry way of seeking the God who satisfies, it is a means of grace Old Joe would do well to recover — for out of one such fast at Antioch the Spirit launched the gospel to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
verseByVerse.commentary: The commissioning is corporate and prayerful: fasting, prayer, the laying on of hands. The church does not merely affirm the Spirit's call — it participates in the sending through the formal act of commissioning. The laying on of hands is not the conferral of new authority (the Spirit has already called) but the community's blessing, solidarity, and public identification with the mission. Antioch is sending its best leaders — Barnabas was the church's founder, Saul its most gifted teacher — into the unknown. The generosity of sending is itself an act of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Sent out by the Holy Spirit' — Luke uses the same verb (apostellō) as for the apostles themselves: these missionaries are sent, authorized, commissioned by the Spirit who called them. The natural first stop is Cyprus — Barnabas's home island (4:36), familiar territory that provides a base for the mission. The pattern established here will repeat throughout the journey: beginning in the synagogue, where Scripture is read and the Messiah is expected, then moving outward. John Mark serves as a helper, carrying supplies and perhaps providing practical support for the team.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet, named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The traverse of Cyprus from east (Salamis) to west (Paphos) represents a sustained evangelistic campaign across the entire island. At Paphos — the Roman administrative capital — they encounter both the highest human authority (the proconsul) and the spiritual opposition that attends every genuine mission advance. Sergius Paulus's description as 'a man of intelligence' is notable: the gospel is not only for the simple; it addresses the cultivated mind. His desire to hear the word of God is genuine curiosity that is about to become genuine faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary: Elymas's opposition reveals the nature of spiritual warfare in mission: when someone of influence is genuinely seeking the gospel, the adversary works through proximate persons to prevent their hearing it. The magician's tactic is relational — he has the proconsul's ear. His goal is explicit and personal: 'to turn the proconsul away from the faith.' He does not engage the missionaries in debate; he tries to shut down the encounter before it produces faith. The opposition of darkness to light is always most intense when light is about to penetrate significant darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's first use of 'Paul' marks the shift to the Gentile mission focus that will occupy the rest of Acts. 'Filled with the Holy Spirit' — the filling that produces prophetic insight and authority. Paul's denunciation of Elymas is severe because the spiritual stakes are severe: a man standing between an intelligent seeker and the word that can save him. 'Son of the devil' — the source of Elymas's opposition is named; he is doing the adversary's work. 'Making crooked the straight paths of the Lord' — the image of Isaiah 40:3, applied to one who undoes the way the Lord has prepared.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time." Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: The blindness that falls on Elymas is a miniature echo of Paul's own Damascus road blindness — perhaps Paul recognizes in Elymas the man he himself once was: opposing the gospel, confident in his own power, about to be confronted with his own helplessness. The judgment is specifically 'for a time' — it is corrective, not final. The proconsul believes when he sees what has happened: the miracle confirms the word. 'Astonished at the teaching of the Lord' — the content of the teaching, not merely the miracle, is what moves Sergius Paulus. The word and the sign together produce faith.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–52 — Paul's Sermon in Pisidian Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The synagogue sermon in Pisidian Antioch is the first major speech of Paul's missionary career in Acts and a theological masterpiece. Luke preserves it as the representative example of Paul's apostolic preaching, structured identically to Peter's Pentecost sermon: a recital of God's redemptive history with Israel (vv. 17–25), the proclamation of Jesus's death and resurrection as the fulfillment of that history (vv. 26–37), and a call to response with warning (vv. 38–41). But Paul's sermon has characteristic emphases that distinguish it: the prominent place of David, the explicit statement of justification by faith apart from the law of Moses, and the citation of Habakkuk as warning against unbelief.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith in Paul's First Sermon

Paul's climactic statement in vv. 38–39 is the first explicit statement of justification by faith in Acts: 'let it be known to you that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses.' The law cannot justify; faith in the crucified and risen Jesus frees from everything the law could not free from. This is the heart of Paul's theology, already fully formed in his first recorded sermon — the gospel that will generate the letters to the Galatians and Romans.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God.' The widespread hunger for the gospel was met with jealousy from the Jewish leaders, who spoke against Paul. Their opposition drove the explicit turn to the Gentiles. Now: The pattern repeats whenever the gospel meets institutional religion: those who should be most receptive are sometimes least so, while those outside the religious establishment respond with open hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia.
verseByVerse.commentary: John Mark's departure at Perga — without explanation in Luke's account — will become a source of serious conflict between Paul and Barnabas (15:36–41). Paul will regard the departure as desertion from the work; Barnabas will see it as a recoverable failure. The journey from Perga to Pisidian Antioch crosses the Taurus Mountains — a difficult and dangerous route. The missionaries' willingness to make this crossing after John Mark's departure shows their commitment to the mission regardless of reduced team size. The mission's difficulty does not deter them; it refines them.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down. After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sabbath synagogue service provides the natural platform: after the readings from Torah and the Prophets, visiting teachers were invited to speak. The synagogue rulers' invitation — 'if you have any word of encouragement' — is gracious and open; they do not know what they are inviting. Paul will give them a 'word of encouragement' that interprets everything they have just heard from the Law and the Prophets in light of the risen Jesus — a word that will divide their congregation by the following Sabbath.

A word on the background of 'the reading from the Law and the Prophets,' since it shaped the whole scene. The synagogue service centred on two Scripture readings: one from the Law (the five books of Moses, the Torah) and one from the Prophets (a chosen passage — what the Jews call the Haftarah; this is the reading Jesus stood to give from Isaiah in Luke 4:16–20). After the readings came a 'word of exhortation,' a teaching, to which any competent man present might be invited — which is exactly the door opened to Paul here. Where did it all begin? The roots run back to Moses, who commanded the Law be read aloud to the assembled people (Deut. 31:10–13), and especially to Ezra after the exile, who read the Law to the gathered nation 'and gave the sense, so that the people understood' (Neh. 8:8). The synagogue itself (the word means simply 'gathering') grew up during and after the Babylonian exile (sixth century BC): with the temple gone and the people scattered, Jews assembled locally to hear and study God's Word. (The precise origins are uncertain, but by Jesus' day every town of any size had one.) The Law was read in order, portion by portion, working through the Torah over a fixed cycle, with the prophetic reading chosen to match it; in Hebrew, often with an Aramaic paraphrase for those who no longer spoke it.

And do Jews still do this? Yes — with a continuity that is striking. To this day, in synagogues across the world, the Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll on the Sabbath (and on Mondays, Thursdays, and festivals), following the annual cycle that finishes and begins again each year at the feast of Simchat Torah ('rejoicing in the Torah'); it is still paired with a reading from the Prophets and followed by a teaching. The very practice Luke describes here is observed by Jews now as it was two thousand years ago. For the church, this is also our own inheritance: the public reading of Scripture followed by its exposition is the pattern Paul charged Timothy to keep — 'devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching' (1 Tim. 4:13) — and the shape of Christian worship ever since. The deep irony of this verse is that the Law and the Prophets had just been read aloud, and Paul rises to show that every line of them was pointing to the Jesus he is about to preach (Luke 24:27, 44). The reading set the table; Paul served Christ from it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's address to both constituencies — born Jews and Gentile God-fearers — frames the gospel from the beginning as inclusive: both communities are addressed as potential recipients of the salvation that follows. His survey of Israel's history begins with divine election and the exodus: the 'uplifted arm' (Exodus 6:6) is the image of God's powerful intervention on Israel's behalf. Paul is establishing that the story he is about to tell is not a departure from Israel's story but its climax — the same God who parted the sea has now raised Jesus from the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: "And for about forty years he bore with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He bore with them' — the patient endurance of God through forty years of murmuring, idolatry, and rebellion in the wilderness. The exodus generation gave God every reason to abandon them; he bore with them, sustained them, and brought them to the border of the promised land. The conquest narrative — 'destroying seven nations' and giving Israel 'their land as an inheritance' — is told in one verse, compressing decades of history to make the theological point: God's faithfulness overcomes Israel's faithlessness, and divine promise achieves what human obedience alone cannot.

'Destroying seven nations' — Paul passes over it in a phrase, but it is one of the hardest things in Scripture, and an honest reader (believer or not) feels the weight of it: how could a good God order the destruction of the Canaanites? We must not be glib; the loss of life is real and grievous. But several truths, held together, show that this is not the arbitrary cruelty it is often imagined to be.

It was judgment, not ethnic hatred. This was never a licence to slaughter foreigners; Israel was given no general warrant to harm Gentiles, and was even commanded to offer peace to distant cities (Deut. 20:10). It was a specific, bounded act of divine justice on particular nations for particular, appalling sin. And God says so plainly. He had told Abraham, four centuries earlier, that his descendants would not yet receive the land 'for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete' (Gen. 15:16) — that is, God waited four hundred years, holding back judgment, giving those nations centuries of space. What had they done? Among other things, they burned their own children alive in sacrifice to their gods (Deut. 12:31; Lev. 18:21) — a culture of entrenched idolatry, cultic prostitution, and the murder of infants. Scripture frames the conquest as the land itself, defiled, 'vomiting out its inhabitants' (Lev. 18:24–25). This is the wrath of a holy God against great and violent evil, long endured.

And it was not Israelite favouritism. God twice tells Israel: this is 'not because of your righteousness... but because of the wickedness of these nations' (Deut. 9:4–6) — and he warns that if Israel does the same things, the land will vomit them out too (Lev. 18:28). Centuries later it did exactly that: God sent Israel into exile for the same sins. The standard is God's holiness, applied impartially, not ethnic preference — which dismantles the charge of 'tribal genocide.' Note too that mercy stood open throughout: Rahab the Canaanite and her household were spared through faith, and she stands in the very bloodline of the Messiah (Josh. 6:25; Matt. 1:5). Any Canaanite who turned to the God of Israel found refuge; the issue was never race but allegiance.

Underneath lies a question the objection usually skips. We instinctively assume the Canaanites had a right to life that God violated. But Scripture's view is that God is the Author and rightful Lord of all life (Deut. 32:39, 'I kill and I make alive'), and that every one of us has already forfeited life through sin (Rom. 6:23). On that reckoning the thing needing explanation is not that God judges sin, but that he is so patient, and that anyone at all is spared. The Canaanites were not innocents struck down by a capricious deity; they were guilty people under the just sentence of a Judge who had waited centuries. (On the hardest part, the children, Scripture gives us no glib answer; we rest in the One who 'shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?' (Gen. 18:25), trusting his mercy toward little ones — as David trusted it for his own child, 2 Sam. 12:23 — and we refuse to pretend we see more than we do.)

Finally, and most importantly for a Christian. This was a unique, one-time event in redemptive history — Israel as a covenant nation, executing God's judgment in a particular land. It is emphatically not a model for today. Jesus refused the sword: 'my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would fight' (John 18:36); the church's weapons 'are not of the flesh' (2 Cor. 10:4); we are sent to love our enemies and to leave vengeance to God (Matt. 5:44; Rom. 12:19). No one may ever invoke Joshua to justify violence in Christ's name. Rather, the conquest is a sober, localized preview of the final judgment, when sin will be judged perfectly and universally. And here the gospel speaks its deepest word: at the cross the judgment we all deserve fell on Jesus. The same holy God who judged Canaan 'did not spare his own Son' (Rom. 8:32) but laid our condemnation on him — so that wrath and mercy met, and the only refuge from judgment, as for Rahab, is faith in the God of Israel, now revealed in Christ. That is exactly where Paul's sermon is heading: all this history runs to a Saviour (v. 23).

verseByVerse.quote: "All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary: The 450-year span covers the patriarchal sojourn in Egypt, the wilderness wandering, and the period of conquest — the entire pre-monarchic history of Israel compressed into a number that conveys the patience and persistence of divine faithfulness across generations. 'He gave them judges' — each judge was God's provision for Israel's need in a specific crisis; the pattern of Israel's need and God's provision is the rhythm of the book of Judges. Samuel stands at the threshold of the monarchy, preparing Israel for the king who will prepare the way for the King.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's mention of 'Saul' (his own Hebrew name, the tribe of Benjamin) may carry conscious self-awareness — the rejected king, replaced by the one after God's heart. David's description ('a man after my heart, who will do all my will') comes from 1 Samuel 13:14 and Psalm 89:20 combined. It is the highest possible royal commendation: not a man after his own heart (as Saul was) but one whose heart was aligned with God's. The Davidic covenant is the bridge Paul is building toward Jesus, and David's character is the theological foundation of that covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised' — the thesis of the entire sermon in one sentence: the promise to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16) has been fulfilled in Jesus. 'As he promised' — the resurrection of Jesus is not an unexpected event but the fulfillment of covenantal promise. 'Savior' — the title that encompasses the entire gospel: Jesus saves his people from their sins, from the law's condemnation, from death, from the wrath of God. The saving that the exodus prefigured, the kingdom of David anticipated, the prophets foretold — has arrived in the person of Jesus of Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: John the Baptist is the hinge between the prophetic preparation and the messianic fulfillment: his baptism of repentance prepared Israel to receive the greater one. His explicit self-denying witness — 'I am not he... I am not worthy to untie his sandals' — is the model of authentic ministry. The Baptist understood his role as preparatory and himself as secondary: every element of his ministry pointed away from himself toward the one who was coming. The measure of a ministry's authenticity is the consistency with which it directs attention toward Christ rather than toward itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'To us has been sent the message of this salvation' — Paul's application is personal and inclusive. Both the Jewish 'sons of Abraham' and the Gentile God-fearers are addressed as recipients of the same salvation: 'to us.' The message has been sent — divine initiative, not human discovery. 'This salvation' — the specific, historical, embodied salvation accomplished in Jesus of Nazareth, the message that distinguishes Christianity from philosophy: not a theory about salvation but the news of what God has done to accomplish it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt deserving death, they asked Pilate to have him executed."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets' — the tragedy of fulfilled prophecy unrecognized. The Jerusalem authorities had the prophets read to them every Sabbath and fulfilled those very prophecies by rejecting the one they foretold. The blindness is not moral failure alone but spiritual incapacity: without the Spirit's illumination, even the closest proximity to Scripture does not produce recognition of the one Scripture proclaims. The sermon is simultaneously an explanation of why the Messiah was rejected and an implicit warning against repeating the error.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When they had carried out all that was written of him' — every detail of the passion narrative was the fulfillment of prophetic Scripture (Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, Zechariah 12, etc.). The crucifixion and burial are presented as complete: 'the tree' (Deuteronomy 21:23 — the curse of the law) and 'the tomb' together constitute the depth of the descent. Jesus bore the curse, died, and was buried — the completeness of his death is essential to the completeness of his resurrection. You cannot have a resurrection without a genuine, verifiable death and burial.

Why 'the tree' here, and not 'the cross'? The word is xylon, which means simply 'wood' or 'timber' — a beam, a stake, a tree. The apostles use it of the cross on purpose (also 5:30; 10:39; Gal. 3:13; 1 Pet. 2:24), to sound a deliberate echo of the Law: 'if a man... is hanged on a tree... a hanged man is cursed by God; you shall bury him the same day' (Deut. 21:22–23). To call the cross a 'tree' is therefore to load the word with meaning: Jesus hung where the accursed criminal hung, bearing the curse of God in our place — as Paul spells out, 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree' (Gal. 3:13). And notice the precise fit right here: they 'took him down from the tree' and buried him at once, fulfilling that very command not to leave the body on the tree overnight. The word is no loose synonym; it preaches the heart of the cross — he took our curse. (Some also hear a quiet echo that the curse which entered the world by a tree in Eden was undone on a tree at Calvary — a lovely thought, though the plain reference is Deuteronomy's curse.)

verseByVerse.quote: "But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'But God raised him from the dead' — the divine reversal that transforms every element of the passion narrative. God's 'but' is the hinge of all history. The resurrection appearances are grounded in eyewitness testimony: 'for many days,' 'to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem,' 'who are now his witnesses.' The continuity from Galilee to Jerusalem to the present ('who are now') grounds the resurrection proclamation in living, accessible witnesses — people the audience can in principle speak with.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'We bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled' — the resurrection is presented as promise-fulfillment, not innovation. The citation of Psalm 2:7 ('you are my Son, today I have begotten you') is applied to the resurrection as the moment of the public declaration of Jesus's divine sonship: the resurrection is God's formal pronouncement that this crucified man is his eternal Son. The 'today' of Psalm 2 is the day of resurrection, when what was always true was publicly declared by the Father's act of raising the dead Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' Therefore he also says in another psalm, 'You will not let your Holy One see corruption.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Two Old Testament texts converge on the resurrection. Isaiah 55:3 — 'the holy and sure blessings of David' — speaks of the eternal covenant with David that will be fulfilled in the resurrection of his ultimate Son. Psalm 16:10 — 'you will not let your Holy One see corruption' — speaks of one who will not decompose in the tomb. Both texts require a fulfillment that David himself could not provide: his own body saw corruption. Therefore both texts must be prophetically pointing to the one who actually rose without corruption: Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'David served the purpose of God in his own generation' — the highest possible summary of a godly life: purpose-driven service to the God of one's generation, within the specific scope of one's calling. But even such a life ends in death and decomposition: 'he fell asleep and saw corruption.' The contrast with Jesus is absolute: Jesus 'did not see corruption' because God raised him. The one who serves not just his generation but all generations forever is the one whose body the grave could not hold. David's purpose was fulfilled; Jesus's purpose is eternal.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary: The sermon's application: forgiveness through Jesus, justification by faith, freedom from what the law could not provide. 'Everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses' — the law could not justify because no one kept it perfectly; Jesus's death bears the law's condemnation, his resurrection vindicates his righteousness, and faith receives the benefit. This is the seed of the theological argument that will fill the letters to the Galatians and Romans — already fully formed in Paul's first recorded sermon, because it is the gospel itself. (cf. Rom. 3:21–24; Col. 2:13–14) (cf. Rom. 3:21–24; Col. 2:13–14)

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: 'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'" As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary: Habakkuk 1:5 provides the warning that frames the sermon's application: the resurrection of Jesus is God's 'incredible work' in these days, and those who refuse to believe it — who hear it and scoff — are fulfilling the same prophecy that forewarned Israel about God's incredible works they could not believe. The crowd's response is enthusiastic: 'they begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath.' The hunger for the gospel is genuine; the word has found its mark. What happens next Sabbath will reveal which hearts are merely curious and which have genuinely received it.

verseByVerse.quote: And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they talked with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas' — the word 'followed' implies attachment, discipleship, the beginning of a community. This is not a polite request for more information but the beginning of the congregation. Paul and Barnabas' response is pastoral: they urge these new believers 'to continue in the grace of God.' The first pastoral instruction to the first converts in Pisidian Antioch is not a command to do more but an exhortation to remain in what they have received. The Christian life begins in grace and continues in grace; the danger is always drifting out of it.

What does it mean, for Old Joe, 'to continue in the grace of God'? 'Grace' is God's free, undeserved kindness to sinners in Christ — salvation as a gift, never a wage, never earned. To continue in it (the word means to remain, to abide, to hold fast) is to go on living every day on that same footing of free grace on which you first came in. You were welcomed home freely, with empty hands; continuing in grace means staying there — not slipping back onto the treadmill of trying to make God love you by being good enough, and not despairing when you fail, as though grace had run out. It is the very thing Paul urges on the Colossians: 'as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him' (Col. 2:6). The way in is the way on.

Picture the prodigal son. He came home expecting to earn his keep as a hired servant, and instead the father ran to him, put the robe on him, and welcomed him as a beloved son — sheer grace. Now imagine that son, a week later, quietly slinking off to the servants' quarters to start earning his place after all. That is exactly what it looks like to drift out of grace. 'Continue in the grace of God' means: stay at the Father's table as a freely-loved child. Keep coming to Christ with empty hands; keep drawing on his daily mercy for strength, forgiveness, and growth (grace is not just the door you enter by but the room you live in — 'grow in the grace... of our Lord Jesus Christ,' 2 Pet. 3:18). And keep going — persevere, do not give up. Lest this make Old Joe anxious about whether he can hold on, remember what was said at Colossians 1:23: the call to continue is real, yet the God who began this grace is the one who keeps us in it; we persevere because he preserves us. Even our continuing is grace.

verseByVerse.quote: The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Almost the whole city' — the week between the first and second Sabbath has been busy: word has spread throughout Pisidian Antioch that something extraordinary is being proclaimed in the synagogue, and the city turns out. The Jewish leaders' response to this success is jealousy — the same motivation that drove Herod's persecution of the church (12:1) and the Sadducees' arrest of the apostles (5:17). When the gospel's popularity threatens the institution's authority, the institution often responds with opposition rather than participation. 'Reviling' — the argument has given way to abuse: they cannot refute Paul, so they attack him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The explicit turn to the Gentiles is here given its theological foundation: Isaiah 49:6, the Servant Song in which the Servant is given 'as a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth.' The mission to the Gentiles is not a contingency plan prompted by Jewish rejection; it is the fulfillment of Israel's prophetic calling, now carried by those who receive the Servant's mission. 'You judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life' — the rejection of the gospel is self-judgment; the missionaries do not condemn, they declare the consequence of the hearers' own choice. (cf. Isa. 49:6; Rom. 1:16)

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As many as were appointed to eternal life believed' — Luke's most explicit statement of election in Acts. The believing is real and free; the appointment is divine and prior. Both are true simultaneously, and Luke does not explain the philosophical relationship between them. The word of the Lord spreading 'throughout the whole region' shows that the mission's reach extended far beyond the city of Pisidian Antioch: the gospel multiplied through the new believers and the surrounding communities in ways the missionaries could not track.

Why this is one of the strongest single verses for election. Three things give it force. The word 'appointed' (tetagmenoi) is a perfect passive participle: a completed action done to them by another — and the unnamed agent, as so often in Scripture, is God ('the divine passive'). So it reads, 'as many as had been appointed [by God] to eternal life believed.' Next, the order is decisive: the appointment comes first and the believing follows from it. They did not believe and so get appointed; they were appointed and therefore believed — faith is the fruit, God's prior choice the root. And the context sharpens it: just two verses earlier the unbelieving Jews 'judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life' (v. 46) — their rejection laid at their own door — while the Gentiles who come to faith are those 'appointed to eternal life.' Luke sets the two side by side without embarrassment: responsibility in unbelief, grace in belief. The verse fits a steady biblical pattern — 'all that the Father gives me will come to me' (John 6:37); 'you do not believe because you are not among my sheep' (John 10:26); 'the Lord opened her heart' (Acts 16:14); Eph. 1:4–5; Rom. 8:29–30.

How our non-Reformed brothers read it — fairly stated. Godly, Bible-loving Christians who are not Calvinist (many of our Arminian and dispensational friends) honour this verse and read it mainly in two ways. First, some take the participle not as a passive ('appointed by God') but as a middle voice, 'as many as had disposed themselves toward eternal life' — that is, those who were ready, open, rightly inclined, believed; the verse then describes the people's own receptivity rather than a prior decree. (The form can grammatically be middle or passive; Reformed readers answer that, given Luke's usage and the contrast with v. 46, the passive with God as agent is far more natural — but the middle is a real option, honestly held.) Second, the classic Arminian reading affirms a genuine appointing, but grounds it in God's foreknowledge: foreseeing who would freely believe, God appointed those to eternal life (Rom. 8:29, 'whom he foreknew'). Election is real, but conditioned on foreseen faith, so that human free will is preserved. A few read 'appointed to eternal life' corporately — of the destiny of the believing people as a body, which individuals enter by faith.

Held in charity. It is worth saying plainly what unites us before what divides us: every side here believes salvation is by grace through faith in Christ alone, that God is sovereign and good, that sinners are truly responsible, and that the gospel must be freely offered to all — which is exactly what Paul is doing in this chapter. The difference is over how God's sovereignty and our believing fit together. In honesty, many even non-Calvinist scholars grant that the plain passive ('appointed by God') is the most natural sense of the Greek here; but this is a long-standing, in-house disagreement among brothers who love the same Lord and the same Bible, and it should be carried with humility, not point-scoring. And note what the verse does not do: it does not make God the author of anyone's unbelief (v. 46 puts that squarely on the rejecters), nor does it dampen evangelism — in Acts, the truth of election runs right alongside the most tireless gospel preaching the world has seen. Rightly held, election humbles the believer, banishes all boasting, and turns assurance into worship: if I believe, it is because grace appointed me, sought me, and opened my heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
verseByVerse.commentary: The persecution is organized through the most influential channels: devout women of high standing and the leading men — the religious and civic establishment working together to expel the missionaries. Paul and Barnabas shake the dust from their feet — the symbolic gesture of prophetic rejection (Matthew 10:14) — and move on. The gesture is not vindictive but declaratory: the responsibility has been transferred. They do not stop the mission; they relocate it. The expulsion from one city is the introduction of the gospel to the next.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit' — the community left behind in Pisidian Antioch is not abandoned; it is Spirit-filled. The missionaries' departure does not leave the congregation spiritually impoverished; the Spirit who was poured out at Pentecost remains with every community he has filled. The joy that marks them is the same joy that marked the Samaritans after Philip's preaching (8:8) and the eunuch after his baptism (8:39): the Spirit-given gladness that no persecution can extinguish, because it is rooted in the risen Lord who cannot be killed again.

13.theology: Election and Evangelism. Acts 13:48 is the Reformed doctrine of election stated with apostolic directness: the believing of the Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch is grounded in their prior appointment to eternal life. This is not fatalism — it does not prevent preaching; it undergirds it. Paul and Barnabas preach with everything they have, to everyone who will listen, in the synagogue and in the streets. They do not know who is appointed; they preach to all. And God, through the preaching, brings to faith those he has appointed. Election is the guarantee that the mission will not ultimately fail: there are sheep in every flock that God is calling, and the voice of the gospel will reach them. This is the ground of missionary confidence in every hostile city.
13.examples:
Then: Barnabas and Saul, sent out from a worshipping, fasting, praying church, arriving in city after city with nothing but the word and the Spirit — and the word going out, and the appointed ones believing, and the disciples filled with joy even when expelled. The first missionary journey is a portrait of how the kingdom advances: through weakness and proclamation and sovereign grace.

Now: The church sends when it worships. Mission flows from the presence of God, not from strategic planning. The Antioch church was not looking for a missionary project; they were seeking God — and God spoke. The question for every congregation is not “what is our mission strategy?” but “are we in the kind of sustained, attentive, fasting prayer in which the Spirit can speak?” When he speaks, we must be ready to send our best.

14.title: Suffering and Strengthening
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. <sup>2</sup>But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. <sup>3</sup>So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. <sup>4</sup>But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. <sup>5</sup>When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat and to stone them, <sup>6</sup>they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, <sup>7</sup>and there they continued to preach the gospel. <sup>8</sup>Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. <sup>9</sup>He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, <sup>10</sup>said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and began walking. <sup>11</sup>And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” <sup>12</sup>Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. <sup>13</sup>And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds. <sup>14</sup>But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, <sup>15</sup>“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. <sup>16</sup>In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. <sup>17</sup>Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.” <sup>18</sup>Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them. <sup>19</sup>But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. <sup>20</sup>But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. <sup>21</sup>When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, <sup>22</sup>strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. <sup>23</sup>And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. <sup>24</sup>Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. <sup>25</sup>And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia, <sup>26</sup>and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled. <sup>27</sup>And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. <sup>28</sup>And they remained no little time with the disciples.
14.overview:
The pattern of the first missionary journey is by now familiar: the Word is proclaimed, some believe, others oppose, the apostles are driven out, and they preach in the next city. At Lystra, the pattern intensifies. Paul heals a lame man and the crowd, speaking in Lycaonian, decides that the gods have come down. They want to sacrifice oxen to Barnabas and Paul. The apostles tear their garments — the Jewish gesture of horror at blasphemy — and push back into the crowd to preach the living God who made heaven and earth. They scarcely hold back the sacrifice.

And then the same crowd stones Paul. The speed of the reversal is breathtaking: one moment they are bringing garlands and oxen; the next, stones. The crowd that wanted to worship Paul drags his body out of the city, supposing him dead. And Paul gets up and walks back into the city. He does not leave the region; he does not change his message; he goes on to Derbe and comes back through Lystra and Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the disciples.

What he tells them on the return journey is the sentence that threads through the whole of Acts: “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” Not may — must. Suffering is not the exception for the follower of Jesus; it is the road. The kingdom does not come without the cross — not for the King, and not for those who follow him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The First Journey Continues and Returns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final leg of the first missionary journey takes Paul and Barnabas through Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe — a sequence of proclamation, opposition, suffering, and stubborn continued witness. At Lystra, the healing of a man lame from birth triggers a near-catastrophe: the crowd concludes that Paul and Barnabas are gods (Zeus and Hermes) and prepares to offer sacrifice to them. The missionaries' response — ripping their garments, running into the crowd, insisting they are 'men of like nature with you' — is the most explicit natural theology in Acts, but it cannot prevent the sacrifice attempt. When Jewish opponents arrive from Antioch and Iconium, the mood shifts instantly: the crowd that was about to worship Paul stones him and drags him out of the city for dead.

The summary of the return journey is the most important missiological passage in Acts for the church's ongoing life: Paul and Barnabas retrace their steps, strengthening every church they had planted, 'saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God,' appointing elders in every church, praying with fasting, and committing the new communities to the Lord. The pattern is established here — plant, strengthen, appoint leadership, entrust to God — and it will be the pattern of every missionary effort that follows.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as the Path into the Kingdom

Paul and Barnabas's declaration in v. 22 — 'through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God' — is not pessimism but theology: the path of the crucified Lord is the path of his followers. Reformed theology insists that suffering is not a sign of God's absence but often a sign of his presence and approval: the servant who shares his Lord's cross shares his Lord's resurrection. The 'must' (dei) is the divine necessity — the same 'must' applied to Christ's suffering in Luke 24:26. The pattern of dying and rising is the pattern of life in the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul was stoned and dragged out of Lystra for dead, then got up and went back into the city the next day. The courage required to re-enter the city where you were nearly killed is the courage of the man who has nothing to fear from death. Now: The willingness to re-enter dangerous territory — to continue faithful witness after suffering for it — is the distinctive quality of those whose security is not in this world's preservation of their lives but in Christ's resurrection that awaits them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Iconium pattern mirrors Pisidian Antioch: great success (both Jews and Greeks believing), followed by organized opposition (unbelieving Jews stirring up the Gentiles). The word 'poisoned' (ekakōsan) — made wicked or bitter — captures the deliberate character of the opposition: this is not honest disagreement but the intentional corruption of the community's perception of the missionaries. When the word cannot be refuted on its merits, the strategy shifts to character assassination and social pressure.

verseByVerse.quote: So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'They remained for a long time' — the opposition does not determine the mission's length; the Spirit does. Paul and Barnabas stay despite the stirred-up Gentiles because the Lord is bearing witness to the word through signs and wonders. 'The word of his grace' — the gospel is named for its essential character: grace, unmerited favor, the good news that God gives what human beings cannot earn. The Lord's authentication of this word through miracles is his endorsement of its content: this grace is real, and he will confirm it with power.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat and to stone them,
verseByVerse.commentary: The gospel always produces division before it produces unity, because it requires a decision. Iconium is divided: some with the Jews (maintaining the status quo), some with the apostles (following the new word). When the opposition hardens into a formal conspiracy — 'both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers' — the alliance of religious and civil authority against the missionaries mirrors the alliance that condemned Jesus. The attempt to stone them is the same impulse that stoned Stephen: silence through violence what cannot be silenced through argument.

verseByVerse.quote: they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul and Barnabas exercise prudence: they flee when the plot becomes known. Jesus had modeled this wisdom himself (Luke 4:30; John 10:39), and commanded it in Matthew 10:23: 'when they persecute you in one town, flee to the next.' The flight is not cowardice but mission-wisdom: preserve the missionaries to continue the mission in the next city. And they do continue — immediately, in Lystra and Derbe and 'the surrounding country.' The geographical expansion driven by persecution mirrors the pattern established in chapter 8: opposition becomes mission strategy.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well,
verseByVerse.commentary: The lame man at Lystra parallels the lame man at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3) and the healing of Aeneas (Acts 9): crippled from birth, never walked, healed by an apostle's word in the name of Jesus. But the context is entirely different — this is Gentile territory, outside the synagogue, in a community with no prior exposure to the God of Israel.
