verseByVerse.commentary: The charge is economic before it is religious: 'their hope of gain was gone.' The gospel's power to free people from spiritual and commercial exploitation triggers violent opposition from those whose interests depend on that exploitation. The charge before the magistrates is shrewdly reframed as civic disturbance and ethnic threat — 'these men are Jews' — appealing to Roman anti-Jewish prejudice and civic order rather than admitting the real motive.

verseByVerse.quote: "'They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The legal accusation: Rome permitted Jewish religious practice (religio licita) but scrutinized new religious movements that sought to convert Roman citizens. The owners claim the missionaries are propagating an unlawful religion among Roman colonists. This is the Roman Empire's encounter with the gospel reduced to its political and economic threat assessment. Pilate, Gallio, Festus — the Roman machinery will keep encountering the gospel and keep being unable to condemn it justly.

verseByVerse.quote: "The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely."
verseByVerse.commentary: The beating with rods is a Roman punishment — painful, humiliating, potentially dangerous. Paul will later cite this beating in 2 Corinthians 11:25 as part of his suffering catalog. The magistrates act without proper procedure — no hearing, no verdict, just mob pressure and summary punishment. The injustice is real and unambiguous. Into a Roman prison, with wounds unattended, goes the gospel of the Most High God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks."
verseByVerse.commentary: The inner prison — the most secure cell — and stocks: maximum security for maximum gospel. The jailer fulfills his orders exactly. He does not know what he is guarding or what is about to happen. Luke's irony is gentle but unmistakable: no prison can contain the word of God, and this particular jailer is about to become its most unexpected convert.

verseByVerse.quote: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God' — after beatings and stocks, in the inner prison, at midnight. This is the most extraordinary detail in the entire Philippian episode. The Spirit who fills the church for witness fills the suffering church for worship; the songs at midnight are not denial but defiance, not the absence of pain but the presence of a joy that pain cannot extinguish. 'The prisoners were listening' — even the other prisoners, who have no stake in Paul and Silas's faith, are arrested by the sound. Then the earthquake: divine confirmation of the worship that preceded it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried out with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here."
verseByVerse.commentary: The jailer's immediate impulse toward self-destruction reveals the stakes: a Roman official who loses his prisoners faces death by his superiors anyway; self-administered death in the moment of failure was the honorable Roman alternative. Paul's intervention — 'Do not harm yourself, for we are all here' — is the first act of the gospel for this man: literally saving his life, refusing to exploit his moment of vulnerability for escape, staying when he could have gone. The other prisoners also remain — another miracle, since the earthquake has opened everyone's doors and unfastened everyone's bonds. No one fled.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The earthquake has shaken loose every chain and every door — and the jailer's certainties. He rushes in with lights, falls before Paul and Silas in the posture of supplication, and asks the question that is the hinge of every human life: What must I do to be saved? The earthquake and the open prison have confronted him with his mortality — he expected to die for the escape of his prisoners — and in that moment, the question of eternal significance breaks through.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer is the simplest and most complete in the New Testament: believe in the Lord Jesus. Not 'do' but 'believe'; not 'earn' but 'receive.' The gospel is addressed not to the jailer's competence but to his need. 'You and your household' is not a promise of automatic salvation for his family but an invitation that extends to all who will believe — and in the story that follows, they do believe. The household is saved because the household hears and responds. (cf. John 3:16; Rom. 10:9)

('You and your household' — and the household's baptism in v. 33 — is one of several 'household' texts that feature in the friendly baptism discussion noted at 2:39: believer's-baptist readers stress that the household 'rejoiced... having believed' (v. 34), each coming to personal faith; covenant-baptist readers hear the familiar Scriptural pattern of God dealing with believers together with their households. The promise, all agree, reaches as wide as faith reaches.)

verseByVerse.quote: "And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the Lord is spoken to the whole household, then baptism follows immediately — the same hour of the night. But notice the order of the jailer's actions: he washes their wounds before his own baptism. The man who has just beaten them (or ordered them beaten) now tenderly cares for the wounds he caused. Conversion produces this kind of immediate, concrete reversal: the oppressor becomes the servant.

'The word of the Lord' is the gospel message — the good news about the Lord Jesus (who he is, his death and resurrection, the call to believe, v. 31) and from the Lord, carrying his own authority. When Paul and Silas spoke it, the jailer was not hearing two men's opinions but the Lord's word delivered through his messengers (as Paul says elsewhere, 'you received the word of God... not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God,' 1 Thess. 2:13).

But how can Old Joe — no scholar — know that it means what it means? Three things give him solid confidence. First, God made the saving word clear (what theologians call the perspicuity of Scripture): the central message is plain enough that a rough jailer and his household grasped it and believed at midnight (v. 34). 'The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple' (Ps. 119:130); God speaks to be understood, not to be decoded by experts. Second, he does not leave Old Joe to puzzle it out alone: the same Spirit who gave the word opens the heart and mind to receive it (the Lord 'opened' Lydia's heart, 16:14; 'the Spirit... will guide you into all the truth,' John 16:13; 1 Cor. 2:12). Third, the word proves itself — it does what no mere human word can, converting and transforming (a jailer is a new man by dawn) — and we test it against the rest of Scripture, as even the apostle Paul was tested by the Bereans (17:11). One honest limit: not every passage is equally easy (even Peter said some of Paul's writing is 'hard to understand,' 2 Pet. 3:16); the clarity is chiefly of the things needful for salvation and life. So Old Joe may hold the heart of it — how to be saved, how to live — with real confidence, while reading the harder edges humbly, in the church, under faithful teaching. His assurance rests not on his own cleverness but on God's clarity and the Spirit's witness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God."
verseByVerse.commentary: The meal in the jailer's house is a foretaste of the feast of the kingdom: the one who was imprisoned is now the guest of honor. The jailer's joy — and the household's joy — is the joy of justification, of sins forgiven, of death defeated. 'He had believed in God' is the simple summary of everything: faith has transferred him from one kingdom to another, from condemnation to life. The prison has become a house church.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, 'Let those men go.' And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, 'The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The morning-after reversal: the magistrates, perhaps alarmed by the earthquake and its implications, send to release the prisoners. They expect quiet compliance. They have beaten men without trial and imprisoned them without charge, and they expect these men to slip away gratefully. Paul's response will disabuse them of that expectation. The peace offered is genuine but the justice has not been done.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said to them, 'They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Roman citizenship is Paul's trump card: beating an uncondemned Roman citizen was a serious violation of Roman law (the Valerian and Porcian laws). Paul is not claiming rights for personal comfort — he is protecting future missionaries. If the magistrates can abuse Roman citizens without accountability, the mission in Philippi will be perpetually vulnerable. Public accountability for the public injustice is a matter of justice, not pride.

verseByVerse.quote: "The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. So they came and apologized to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city."
verseByVerse.commentary: The magistrates come personally and apologize — a remarkable reversal of the beatings and public humiliation. But their fear is civic and legal, not spiritual; they want Paul and Silas gone to minimize the damage. They ask them to leave, which is expulsion by request rather than order. Paul's standing on his rights has secured an apology, but he will comply with the request — his work in Philippi, for now, is done.

verseByVerse.quote: "So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed."
verseByVerse.commentary: The final act in Philippi: encouragement of the brothers. The church planted in this Roman colony — gathered at Lydia's house — receives a pastoral visit before the missionaries move on. This is the church of Philippi that Paul will later call his joy and crown (Phil. 4:1), the church whose partnership in the gospel he will celebrate. It begins with a riverside prayer meeting, a merchant, a slave girl, a jailer, and an earthquake.

16.theology: Effectual Calling and the Opened Heart. Acts 16:14 is one of the clearest statements in Scripture of what the Reformed tradition calls effectual calling: “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul.” The Word is preached by Paul; the heart is opened by the Lord. Both acts are real and necessary. Without Paul’s preaching, Lydia has no content to respond to. Without the Lord’s opening of her heart, Paul’s words remain external noise. The Spirit works through the Word, but the Spirit’s work is the decisive one — the inward illumination that turns external proclamation into saving faith. This is why prayer for the lost must accompany every act of evangelism: we can preach; only God can open hearts.
16.examples:
Then: A purple-goods merchant, a slave girl, a Roman jailer — three people who could not have been more different in status, ethnicity, or circumstance — all brought to faith in one day in one city by one gospel. The Philippian church is born from this unlikely trio, and Paul will write his most joyful letter to it from a prison cell twenty years later.

Now: The Lord who opened Lydia’s heart still opens hearts today. The Spirit who directed Paul away from Asia and toward Macedonia still directs his church. The closed doors are guidance; the midnight songs are witness; the simplest answer is still the truest: believe in the Lord Jesus. The gospel has not grown more complicated. We have.

17.title: Athens and the Unknown God
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. <sup>2</sup>And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, <sup>3</sup>explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.” <sup>4</sup>And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. <sup>6</sup>And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also.” <sup>10</sup>The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. <sup>11</sup>Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. <sup>12</sup>Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing and men. <sup>16</sup>Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. <sup>17</sup>So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. <sup>18</sup>Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, “What does this babbler wish to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities”—because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. <sup>19</sup>And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? <sup>20</sup>For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.” <sup>22</sup>So Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said: “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. <sup>23</sup>For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you. <sup>24</sup>The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, <sup>25</sup>nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. <sup>26</sup>And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, <sup>27</sup>that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us, <sup>28</sup>for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’ <sup>29</sup>Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. <sup>30</sup>The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, <sup>31</sup>because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.” <sup>32</sup>Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” <sup>33</sup>So Paul went away from among them. <sup>34</sup>But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.
17.overview:
Athens is the intellectual capital of the ancient world — full of philosophers, full of altars, full of the cleverest people alive and the most comprehensively wrong ideas about God. Paul’s spirit is provoked by the idolatry; he cannot stay quiet. He reasons in the synagogue, he argues in the marketplace, and then he is brought to the Areopagus — the great court of Athenian intellectual life — to explain himself.

The sermon Paul preaches is unlike any other in Acts. He does not begin with the Hebrew Scriptures — his audience does not know them. He begins where they are: the altar to the Unknown God. He finds in their own religious instinct the reaching-out for the God they do not know, and he announces that God: the Creator of all things, Lord of heaven and earth, Giver of life and breath, the one in whom they live and move and have their being — and the one who has set a day of judgment and given proof of it by raising a man from the dead.

The resurrection stops the sermon. Some mock. Some defer. Some believe. The response to the gospel in Athens is the same as in every other city — except that here, uniquely, the mockers get the last word in the chapter. Athens is not a triumph. It is a faithful proclamation in hard soil, with a handful of converts, and Paul moves on to Corinth. The gospel is not always received well. It is always to be proclaimed truly.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The mission in Thessalonica and Berea presents the two characteristic responses to the gospel that Acts has been documenting: jealous opposition that drives the missionaries out, and noble openness that examines the Scriptures daily to see whether the proclamation is true. The Thessalonian Jews who reject the gospel organize a mob and drag Jason (who has hosted Paul) before the city authorities with the most accurate charge ever leveled against the missionaries: 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also.' They have — and the turning upside down is the gospel's constant effect on every human order that opposes the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Berean Standard for Scripture Engagement

The Bereans 'received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.' Reformed theology has always prized this as the model of how the gospel should be received: not credulity (accepting whatever the preacher says without examination) and not skepticism (dismissing the gospel without engagement), but eager reception combined with rigorous scriptural testing. The Berean standard is the Protestant hermeneutical ideal: sola Scriptura applied in the actual practice of hearing and evaluating proclamation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'These men who have turned the world upside down' — the Thessalonian accusation is the most accurate description of the gospel's social effect in Acts. Now: The gospel still turns every human order that opposes the kingdom upside down. The question for the church is not whether the gospel is socially disruptive but whether it is disrupting the right things — the powers of sin, death, and injustice — rather than merely producing comfortable religious experience.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's missionary method is consistent: he goes to the synagogue first, where he has a ready audience of people who already have the Old Testament Scriptures, who are waiting for Israel's God to act, and who are open to theological reasoning. Three sabbaths of sustained argument from the Scriptures — this is not an altar call but a careful, sustained exposition of what the Bible has been saying all along about the Christ.

(On what a synagogue was, see 6:9; on how its service of Scripture-reading and teaching ran — the very platform Paul uses here, 'reasoning with them from the Scriptures' — see 13:15.) Note the deliberate pattern: Paul goes 'as was his custom' to the synagogue first in each new city, taking the gospel 'to the Jew first and also to the Greek' (Rom. 1:16) — beginning with those who already hold the Scriptures and await Israel's God, and showing them that the Christ they hoped for is Jesus.)

verseByVerse.quote: "explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The content of Paul's synagogue preaching: two claims the Jewish audience would find shocking — that the Christ must suffer (a stumbling block, as 1 Cor. 1:23 says) and that the Christ must rise from the dead. Paul proves both from the Scriptures, then identifies Jesus as the Christ who has done both. This is not abstract theology but the hermeneutical claim that Jesus is the key that unlocks all of Israel's Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob and set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary: The conversion of 'a great many devout Greeks and not a few leading women' — the God-fearing Gentiles and prominent women who are the most receptive audiences throughout the mission — provokes the characteristic jealousy. The opposition is organized through 'wicked men of the rabble' — paid agitators, the instruments of crowd manipulation. The attack on Jason's house is the attack on the community; the missionaries are the target, but the host family bears the cost. Wherever the gospel takes root, those who provide hospitality to its proclaimers share in both the blessing and the danger.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Turned the world upside down' — the accusers speak truer than they know. The gospel is the most disruptive force in history precisely because it announces a different king, a different kingdom, a different ordering of all things. The charge of acting against Caesar's decrees is politically calculated but theologically accurate: Jesus as Lord and Caesar as Lord are mutually exclusive claims, and the first-century world understood this more clearly than many modern Christians do.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things."
verseByVerse.commentary: The authorities are disturbed — agitation, unsettlement, the disruption of civic order. This is the Roman Empire's recurring response to the gospel: not outright condemnation (the charges are often legally thin) but unease, disturbance, anxiety. The gospel does not fit neatly into the categories of Roman religious tolerance because its claims are totalizing: Jesus is Lord, not merely a lord.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary: The night departure is protective urgency: the mob's anger requires the missionaries' removal for everyone's safety. But they do not flee the mission — they go directly to the next synagogue in Berea. The pattern is consistent: opposition drives forward movement, and the forward movement takes the same shape as before. Paul and Silas do not adapt their method to avoid controversy; they adapt their location.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Bereans are commended for nobility of mind — not credulity, but eagerness combined with rigorous examination. They receive the word eagerly and then test it against Scripture daily. This is the model of faithful reception: not passive acceptance, not skeptical rejection, but engaged, Scripture-anchored investigation. The fruit of this nobility is belief — and a notably diverse community including Greek women of high standing.

Note well what Old Joe should take from this: the Bereans tested even the apostle Paul against Scripture, and were called 'noble' for it. No teacher, however gifted, learned, or authoritative, stands above the Bible; the Word is the final court, and every sermon, every book — these very notes included — must be checked against it (the principle later named sola Scriptura, Scripture alone as the final rule). This is not suspicion but discernment: 'test everything; hold fast what is good' (1 Thess. 5:21; 1 John 4:1). The Berean way is to receive the Word eagerly and to search the Scriptures daily to see whether these things are so — never one without the other.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off to go as far as the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there."
verseByVerse.commentary: The opposition follows the mission — the Thessalonian Jews travel to Berea to agitate. The Berean mission is not defeated but relocated: Paul is sent ahead while Silas and Timothy remain to consolidate the work. This division of labor is missional wisdom: the lightning rod moves on, while the pastors remain to strengthen what has been planted. The word of God is not silenced by opposition; it changes location.

verseByVerse.quote: "Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they left."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul arrives in Athens alone — an unusual situation for the apostle who almost always worked in teams. The command for Silas and Timothy to follow 'as soon as possible' reveals Paul's awareness of his own need for co-workers. Even the greatest apostle was not designed for solitary mission. But Athens will not wait, and Paul's spirit is provoked by what he sees before his team arrives.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Athens is the intellectual capital of the ancient world — the city of Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, and the Epicureans. Paul's encounter with Athenian philosophy is the most sophisticated cross-cultural apologetic in Acts, and the Areopagus address is the most carefully crafted sermon in the New Testament. Paul begins where his audience is: their unknown god, their own poets, their genuine (if misdirected) religious instinct. He moves from common ground to the particular claim that cannot be accommodated within any philosophical system: God has raised a man from the dead, and by this raised man he will judge the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
Natural Theology and Its Limits

Paul's Areopagus address is the New Testament's most extended engagement with natural theology — the knowledge of God available through creation. He acknowledges that God has left himself without witness (14:17), that all nations are made from one blood and live in God-given boundaries (17:26), that the divine nature is reflected in creation sufficiently to leave humanity without excuse (Romans 1:20). But natural theology has limits: it can establish God's existence and general character; it cannot reveal the gospel of Jesus Christ. The movement from 'the God who made everything' to 'the man he has appointed' requires the Word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some mocked the resurrection; some said 'we will hear you again'; some believed. The three responses to the Areopagus address are the three responses to every gospel proclamation: dismissal, deferral, and faith. Now: The gospel continues to divide its hearers along these same three lines. The church's task is not to ensure the first response never comes but to preach in such a way that the third response is genuinely available to all who will receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'His spirit was provoked' — he is sharply stirred, cut to the soul by the sight of God's glory displaced by idols. Athens's idols were magnificent art; they were also profound spiritual tragedy. Paul's response to his provocation is not despair or denunciation but engagement: he reasons in the synagogue (with the religiously prepared) and in the marketplace (with whoever is present). The agora, the Athenian marketplace and civic center, is the space of public discourse — the most appropriate setting for proclaiming the gospel of a risen Lord who is Lord of all public life.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, 'What does this babbler wish to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities' — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, 'May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Epicureans and Stoics represent Athens's two dominant philosophical schools — one teaching that the gods are indifferent to human affairs and pleasure is the chief good, the other teaching that reason governs the universe and virtue is the chief good. Both are being addressed by a message about a God who is deeply involved in human affairs, suffered death, and rose from the dead. 'Babbler' (spermologos) is a contemptuous term for someone who picks up scraps of others' ideas — they underestimate what they are hearing.

And what was 'the Areopagus'? The name means 'the hill of Ares' (in Latin, Mars' Hill — Ares/Mars being the god of war). It was both a literal rocky outcrop northwest of the Acropolis and, more importantly here, the name of the venerable council that had long met there — Athens's most respected body of elders, its supreme court in matters of religion, morals, and education. By Paul's day the council likely convened down in the marketplace rather than on the hill itself, but it kept the old name. So to be 'brought to the Areopagus' was to be summoned before the cultural and intellectual gatekeepers of the most sophisticated city in the world, to give account of this 'new teaching' — not a formal trial so much as an examination by those who oversaw what ideas and gods Athens would entertain. It is the gospel getting its hearing before the philosophers, at the very summit of human wisdom — and Paul, far from being intimidated, will preach Christ and the resurrection straight into it (vv. 22–31).

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Athenian curiosity is genuine — Athens is a city addicted to novelty (v. 21), and Paul's message is genuinely new to them. They want to understand. The Areopagus is both a place and a court — the ancient council of Athens — and being brought before it is both an honor and an examination. Paul will use this platform to present the most intellectually ambitious speech in the book of Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new."
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's aside is gentle irony: Athens's cultural addiction to novelty is both its openness and its shallowness. The Athenians will hear anything; the question is whether they will be changed by anything. Paul's message is genuinely new in one sense — the resurrection of Jesus has never been proclaimed here — but it is the fulfillment of the oldest reality: the God who made heaven and earth.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown god." What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's opening is a masterpiece of contextualization: he finds the point of contact within Athenian religious culture — the altar to the unknown god — and declares that he is about to name that god. He does not begin with their sin (though he will get there); he begins with their seeking. He honors their religious impulse while redirecting it toward the God who actually made them and is not far from them. This is not compromise but missional intelligence.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's description of God as Creator, Lord, and self-sufficient provider is carefully crafted for a philosophical audience: it echoes both the Jewish understanding of the Creator God and the Stoic concept of the divine logos. 'Does not live in temples made by man' — Stephen's argument (7:48), now applied to the Athenian Parthenon and all its counterparts. The God who made everything cannot need anything from his creatures — he is not the recipient of human service but the source of human existence. Every breath taken by every Athenian philosopher is a gift from the God they do not yet know. (cf. Isa. 66:1–2; 1 Kings 8:27)

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's creation theology challenges both Epicurean indifferentism (the gods do not care) and Stoic pantheism (the divine is diffused through everything). The one God has made all humanity from one — shattering Athenian racial superiority — and has ordered history and geography with a purpose: that humanity might seek and find him. The seeking is possible because God is not far. The tragedy is that humanity, surrounded by evidence of the seeking-God, worships idols instead.

Linger on 'having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place.' Paul is saying that God has sovereignly fixed two things for every nation: the times they exist (the appointed seasons, the rise and the fall, the duration of every people and empire) and the places they live (the borders of their lands). 'Determined' (horisas) means marked out, appointed, decreed. So when and where every nation — and every person — lives is no accident of blind chance (the Epicurean's view) nor of impersonal Fate (the Stoic's), but the appointment of the living, personal God who writes the timeline of history and draws the map of the world (Deut. 32:8, 'he fixed the borders of the peoples'; Dan. 2:21, 'he changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings'). Empires rise and fall on his schedule, not their own — a humbling word to proud Athens, and a steadying one for us when the headlines look out of control: history is not adrift; God reigns over it.

And mark why he does it (the next words): 'that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him.' God arranges the times and places of the nations with a gracious, missionary aim — so that people might seek and find him, 'for he is actually not far from each one of us.' This lands very personally on Old Joe. Your own century, your country, your town, the family you were born into — none of it is random. The God who sets the seasons of empires set your time and place on purpose, that you would seek him and find him (cf. Esther 4:14, 'for such a time as this'; Ps. 139:16). Where and when you live is not an accident; it is an appointment — a kindness designed to bring you home to the God who is near.

verseByVerse.quote: "'for "In him we live and move and have our being"; as even some of your own poets have said, "For we are indeed his offspring."'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul quotes Epimenides and Aratus — Greek poets speaking of Zeus — and appropriates their language for the God of Israel. This is bold hermeneutical strategy: the best insights of pagan wisdom point, despite themselves, toward the God who made the world. 'In him we live and move and have our being' describes not pantheism but the total creatureliness of all life before the Creator. Every breath is borrowed from the one who breathed life into Adam.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,'"
verseByVerse.commentary: From the acknowledgment that humans are God's offspring comes the devastating conclusion about idolatry: if we are God's offspring, made in his image, then making God in our image — gold, silver, stone shaped by human art — is a profound category error. The idol-maker is reducing the Creator to the level of the creature. And now — after the incarnation and resurrection — 'the times of ignorance God overlooked' are over. The resurrection of Jesus marks the end of the age of permissible idolatry. Repentance is no longer optional. (cf. Luke 13:3; 2 Cor. 5:10)

verseByVerse.quote: "'because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The resurrection is Paul's climactic argument: it is God's public declaration that Jesus is the appointed judge of all the world. The resurrection is not merely a miracle of new life; it is a historical, public act of divine certification. The judgment day is fixed — not contingent on human agreement — and the judge is identified. The proof of his appointment is the resurrection. Athens can ignore this, but it cannot change it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this.' So Paul went out from their midst."
verseByVerse.commentary: The resurrection is the dividing line. Greek philosophy had no category for resurrection — the soul's release from the body was liberation, not the body's return to life. Some mock outright; others defer — 'we will hear you again' may be polite dismissal or genuine interest. Paul leaves. He does not adjust his message to avoid the stumbling block of resurrection; the resurrection is the message. The preacher's job is faithfulness, not consensus.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them."
verseByVerse.commentary: The fruit of the Areopagus sermon: not a mass revival but Dionysius, Damaris, and 'others with them.' Dionysius is an Areopagite — a member of the council before which Paul spoke — and Damaris is named specifically, suggesting she was a person of some social standing in the early Athenian church. The harvest is smaller than Corinth or Thessalonica, but it is real. God's word does not return empty even when the response seems thin.

17.theology: General Revelation and the Necessity of the Gospel. Acts 17 contains the New Testament’s most developed account of what theologians call general revelation: the knowledge of God available to all humanity through creation and conscience (Romans 1:18–20). Paul acknowledges the Athenians’ religious instinct as genuine — they are groping toward God. But groping is not finding. General revelation creates the question; the gospel alone provides the answer. The God who made all nations from one man, who determined their times and boundaries, who is not far from any of us — this God has now spoken definitively in a man he raised from the dead. The times of ignorance are over. The command is universal: all people everywhere must repent. General revelation without the gospel leaves no one saved; it only leaves everyone without excuse.
17.examples:
Then: Paul in Athens, spirit provoked, standing before the intellectual elite of the ancient world with nothing but the story of a crucified and risen Jew. Some mock. Some believe. He moves on. The church in Athens is small, but Dionysius and Damaris are there — and the gospel is in Europe to stay.

Now: The contemporary West is increasingly like Athens: intellectually sophisticated, spiritually restless, full of altars to unnamed gods, suspicious of exclusive truth claims. The Areopagus sermon is the model for engagement: begin where people are, affirm what is true in their searching, and then announce the resurrection without apology. The resurrection is still the scandal. It is also still the only answer to the altar inscribed “To the unknown god.”

18.title: Corinth
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. <sup>2</sup>And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them, <sup>3</sup>and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. <sup>4</sup>And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. <sup>5</sup>When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” <sup>7</sup>And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. <sup>8</sup>Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. <sup>9</sup>And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, <sup>10</sup>for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.” <sup>11</sup>And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. <sup>12</sup>But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, <sup>13</sup>saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.” <sup>14</sup>But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. <sup>15</sup>But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.” <sup>16</sup>And he drove them from the tribunal. <sup>18</sup>After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. <sup>24</sup>Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. <sup>25</sup>He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. <sup>26</sup>He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. <sup>27</sup>And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, <sup>28</sup>for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
18.overview:
Corinth is the last place a fastidious missionary would choose. It is the Las Vegas of the ancient world — a great port city famous for commerce, vice, and the worship of Aphrodite. Paul arrives from Athens, where the reception was mixed, and he comes, as he later writes, “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). He finds Aquila and Priscilla, works with them at their trade, preaches every Sabbath, and waits.

Then the Lord speaks in the night: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you… I have many in this city who are my people.” This is the doctrine of election turned into pastoral comfort. God already has people in Corinth — people who are his, who will be gathered by the proclamation of the gospel. Paul does not need to manufacture a harvest; he needs to be faithful, and God will bring in what is his. He stays a year and a half. The church at Corinth — with all its chaos, all its gifts, all its problems — is born.

The chapter closes with Apollos — eloquent, fervent, scripturally competent, but knowing only the baptism of John. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside privately and explain the way of God more accurately. They do not embarrass him publicly; they instruct him privately. And Apollos, genuinely humble, receives the teaching and goes on to powerfully confute the opponents of the gospel. The church grows not only by addition but by the deepening of those already in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Corinth and the Return to Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Corinth is the unlikely setting for one of the most fruitful and sustained periods of Paul's missionary work. A prosperous, cosmopolitan, morally notorious Roman colony — the Las Vegas of the ancient Mediterranean — Corinth would seem to be the least promising soil for a gospel community. But God tells Paul in a vision: 'I have many in this city who are my people.' The sovereignty of election precedes the labor of mission: there are people in Corinth whom God has appointed for salvation, and Paul's task is to preach to them until they come to faith. He stays eighteen months.

The divine encouragement to Paul in the night vision (vv. 9–10) is the theological heart of the Corinthian mission: 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.' The promise of divine protection, the command to speak, and the assurance of predetermined harvest together give Paul the perseverance the Corinthian mission will require. Every new congregation faces the challenge of whether to trust the promise or to succumb to discouragement; the vision at Corinth is the answer to that challenge.
verseByVerse.theology:
Tent-Making Ministry and the Support of Proclamation

Paul's tent-making partnership with Aquila and Priscilla is the first explicit mention of Paul's manual labor as a means of supporting his missionary work. Reformed theology has often discussed whether 'tentmaker ministry' (self-supported missionary work) is a normative apostolic pattern or a situational adaptation. Paul's own letters suggest the latter: he worked with his hands to avoid being a burden on new churches and to model the dignity of labor, but he accepted support from established communities (Philippians 4:15–16). The Corinthian mission itself was eventually supported by the arrival of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gallio decision — the Roman proconsul's dismissal of the Jewish charge against Paul — established a legal precedent protecting Christian preaching as an internal Jewish dispute. Now: God continues to use civil authorities and legal processes to protect the gospel's proclamation, even when those authorities have no understanding of or sympathy with the gospel. Providence works through the decisions of those who know nothing of its purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: "After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,"
verseByVerse.commentary: Corinth is the commercial capital of Greece — wealthy, cosmopolitan, morally notorious, strategic. The expulsion of Jews from Rome (under Claudius, c. AD 49 — likely related to disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus,' possibly about Christ) has brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth, where they will become Paul's most significant co-workers. Providence works through imperial edicts: the very persecution that uprooted this couple placed them exactly where the mission needed them.

verseByVerse.quote: "and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's tentmaking is both economic necessity and theological principle: he does not burden the new churches financially, and he maintains the dignity of manual labor against the cultural prejudice of the Greco-Roman world, which looked down on artisans. The shared trade creates the bond that becomes a missionary partnership. Aquila and Priscilla will travel with Paul, plant churches, and instruct Apollos — all from this tentmaker's workshop in Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, devoting himself completely to testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The arrival of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia — apparently bringing financial support from the Philippian and Thessalonian churches (Philippians 4:15) — frees Paul from tent-making and allows him to focus entirely on proclamation. 'Occupied with the word, devoting himself completely' — the whole-person investment in proclamation that Paul will later describe as his primary calling (1 Corinthians 9:16). The arrival of team members and material support is itself a providential provision: the mission intensifies when the missionary's practical needs are met by the community behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.' And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary: The shaking out of garments is a prophetic gesture of dissociation — Paul's version of the 'shaking the dust off feet' of Luke 9:5. 'Your blood be on your own heads' is Ezekiel's language (Ezek. 33:4) for individual moral responsibility: Paul has warned them, and the rejection is theirs. 'From now on I will go to the Gentiles' is not a permanent abandonment of Jewish mission but a local pivot — and the next gathering point is right next to the synagogue, maximally visible to the rejected community.

verseByVerse.quote: "Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized."
verseByVerse.commentary: Crispus — the ruler of the very synagogue that has just rejected Paul — believes with his whole household and is baptized (Paul baptized him himself, 1 Cor. 1:14). The gospel penetrates the institution that has just opposed it, through its own leader. Many Corinthians believe and are baptized. The turn to the Gentiles does not mean the end of Jewish response; it means the widening of the river of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vision comes at a moment of vulnerability — Corinth's opposition, Paul's aloneness before Silas and Timothy arrived, the weight of the mission. The Lord's word is threefold: do not be afraid, keep speaking, I am with you. Then a remarkable promise: 'I have many in this city who are my people.' These people are not yet Christians; they are the elect whom God has fore-known. The mission will find them because God has already claimed them. This is the Calvinist confidence that fuels missionary boldness: the preacher goes to find those God has already chosen to save. (cf. Isa. 41:10; Matt. 28:20)

'I have many in this city who are my people' — spoken of Corinthians who had not yet believed. Notice how God's election here does not cool evangelism but fires it: because God has a chosen people in Corinth who will come to faith through the preaching, Paul can keep speaking, unafraid, certain his labour will not be wasted. Election does not make sowing pointless; it makes the harvest sure, for the Lord gathers his own through the gospel preached (cf. 13:48; 2 Tim. 2:10, 'I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation'). It is the discouraged evangelist's deepest comfort: somewhere in your 'city' are people God means to save, and your faithful witness is the means he will use.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them."
verseByVerse.commentary: Eighteen months — the longest single stay in Paul's missionary career to this point. The vision gave him permission to put down roots, and he did. The church in Corinth is the most troubled of Paul's churches, as his letters reveal, but it is also the most deeply formed — eighteen months of sustained teaching. Depth of formation and subsequent struggle are not contradictory; the Corinthian letters are evidence that even deep teaching requires ongoing pastoral attention.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gallio's proconsulship is historically datable (c. AD 51–52 from the Delphi inscription), giving Acts one of its most secure chronological anchors. The Jewish charge is carefully legal: persuading people to worship contrary to the law — hoping Gallio will interpret this as a violation of Roman law governing religious practice. If they can get a Roman ruling against Paul's mission, it becomes legally binding throughout the province.

A quick word on 'proconsul' (Greek anthypatos). Rome's provinces came in two kinds: the settled, peaceful ones governed on behalf of the Senate by a proconsul, and the frontier ones governed by the emperor's own appointees. Achaia (southern Greece, capital Corinth) was a senatorial province, so its governor was a proconsul — usually a senior senator sent out for about a year, holding supreme civil and judicial authority, which is why Paul is hauled before his 'tribunal' (the bēma, the judgment seat) for a ruling. In modern terms he was something like a centrally-appointed regional governor who was also the province's chief judge — combining in one man the executive and judicial powers our democracies usually keep apart, answerable not to local voters but to Rome. (Luke's precise title here is also a quiet mark of his accuracy: Achaia's status shifted over the years, and he names it correctly for this moment — the same Gallio whose term the Delphi inscription dates to c. AD 51–52.)

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, 'If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Gallio's ruling is one of the most important legal decisions in Acts: the dispute about Jesus is an internal Jewish religious matter, not a Roman legal concern. Gallio refuses jurisdiction — inadvertently protecting the Pauline mission from provincial suppression. The charge of teaching people to worship contrary to the law is dismissed as an intramural Jewish debate about 'words and names and your own law.' Providence works through the disinterest of a proconsul who does not care about theological questions.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I refuse to be a judge of these things.' And he drove them from the tribunal."
verseByVerse.commentary: The driving away from the tribunal — Gallio physically dismisses the case and the crowd — functionally extends the legal protection of Judaism (religio licita) to Christianity, at least in this moment and province. This ruling will not last forever, but it creates a window for the mission. The gospel's legal vindication before Roman authority is a recurring theme in Acts: wherever fair procedure is applied, the gospel is declared innocent of criminal charges.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sosthenes's beating by the crowd (apparently Gentile crowd frustration at the failed prosecution) may explain why 'Sosthenes the brother' appears as Paul's co-sender in 1 Corinthians 1:1 — the synagogue ruler who bore the cost of the failed legal action against Paul became a believer. Gallio's indifference to the beating confirms his studied neutrality in Jewish-Christian disputes. Paul's Nazirite vow (Numbers 6) — the hair-cutting at Cenchreae marking its completion — shows the complexity of Paul's practice: free from the law as a condition of salvation, still willing to engage its disciplines as expressions of devotion.

Paul's vow raises a real question for Old Joe: is it all right, now that Christ has come, for a believer still to keep the law, or parts of it? The Reformed answer starts by distinguishing three strands the older theologians saw in the law of Moses. The moral law (the Ten Commandments, summed up as loving God and neighbour) reflects God's unchanging character and abides for everyone, always; we are not saved by keeping it, but the believer gladly obeys it as the Spirit-enabled pattern of a thankful life. The ceremonial law (sacrifices, priesthood, temple, feasts, clean-and-unclean foods, circumcision as a rite) was the shadow that pointed to Christ and is fulfilled in him (see on Col. 2:16–17) — so no Christian is bound to keep it as a religious duty. The civil law that governed Israel as a nation expired with that nation, though its underlying justice still instructs. So: the moral law stands; the ceremonial and civil are not binding as obligations.

But notice the careful line Paul himself walks — for he takes a Jewish vow here, later purifies himself in the temple (21:23–26), and circumcises Timothy (16:3), yet flatly refused to circumcise Titus (Gal. 2:3–5) and thundered against anyone who made law-keeping a condition of salvation (Gal. 5:2–4). The difference is always why. When a practice is made a means of being right with God, or imposed on others as necessary, it denies the gospel of grace and is forbidden. But when it is kept freely — as heritage, devotion, conscience, or love that wins a hearing ('to the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might win Jews,' 1 Cor. 9:20) — it belongs to Christian liberty. Paul kept his vow not to earn anything but as a free act of devotion; that is the model.

So, to Old Joe's two cases. A Jewish believer may, in liberty, go on keeping ancestral customs — feasts, food traditions, even a vow — as heritage and devotion and witness among his people, exactly as Paul did, provided he never treats them as the ground of his standing with God nor binds them on others. A Gentile believer is under no obligation whatever to the ceremonial law (that was the whole verdict of Acts 15); he may, as a matter of indifference, find devotional value in some Old Testament root — 'one esteems one day above another... let each be fully convinced in his own mind' (Rom. 14:5) — but he must heed Galatians' special warning never to put himself under the law as a system, for that is to fall from grace (Gal. 4:10–11; 5:1). The simple test in every case: am I doing this to be saved or accepted, or imposing it on others as necessary? — then stop. Is it a free, loving, Christ-honouring practice that binds no one else? — then you are free. Christ alone for salvation; liberty in the rest, governed by love. (Where exactly the Lord's Day and the Sabbath fit is one place Reformed and other believers weigh things differently — a discussion for another verse.)

verseByVerse.quote: "They came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The brief visit to Ephesus is a reconnaissance: Paul reasons in the synagogue, the Jews respond positively and want him to stay, but he cannot — he has a vow to fulfill in Jerusalem and a church network to report to in Antioch. He promises to return if God wills, and he will — for three years. Ephesus is the future, not the present. The gospel's advance requires both the willingness to plant briefly and the discernment to know when to stay.

verseByVerse.quote: "but he said farewell to them, saying, 'I will return to you if God wills,' and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If God wills' — Paul's consistent acknowledgment that the mission's itinerary belongs to God, not the planner. The return to Jerusalem ('went up' is the technical term for ascending to the holy city) and Antioch closes the second missionary journey. Antioch is home base: the church that sent him receives him back. The apostle is accountable to his sending community, not merely to his own vision.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Apollos's appearance in Acts is brief but significant. He is introduced as 'an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures,' who 'taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.' His knowledge is genuine and considerable; it is also incomplete. Priscilla and Aquila's response to Apollos's preaching is the model of wise, humble theological correction: they 'took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.' Not a public rebuke, not a formal confrontation, but a private, respectful completion of what was missing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Importance of Thorough Gospel Formation

Apollos's incomplete knowledge — accurate as far as it went but stopping before the resurrection — is the permanent challenge of theological formation. Every generation needs to receive not just the part of the gospel that resonates with its existing categories but the complete gospel that the Scriptures teach. Priscilla and Aquila model the ministry of theological completion: receiving those who are partially formed, honoring what is genuine, and filling in what is absent. This is the ministry of discipleship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Apollos went to Achaia and was of great help to those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. Now: The church continues to be built by ministers whose gifts complement each other — some plant (Paul in Corinth), some water (Apollos in Corinth, 1 Corinthians 3:6), and God gives the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: "After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary: The third missionary journey begins with the same pastoral work that marked the second: strengthening the disciples. The word means making firm what is already standing. Paul is not always planting; he is also watering, supporting, reinforcing. The churches planted on earlier journeys need ongoing formation, and Paul understands that apostolic ministry includes the long work of consolidation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apollos is introduced as a remarkable figure: eloquent, Scripturally competent, fervent in spirit, teaching accurately about Jesus — and yet his knowledge stops at John's baptism, before Pentecost. He knows the Messiah but not the fullness of what has been given in the Spirit. This is not a defect of character but of catechesis — he teaches what he has been taught. The church's response to his incompleteness is instructive.

What does 'he knew only the baptism of John' mean? John the Baptist's baptism was a preparatory one — 'a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins' (Luke 3:3), in which people confessed their sins, turned to God, and got ready for the Messiah who was coming. John pointed beyond himself: 'I baptize you with water... but he who is coming after me... will baptize you with the Holy Spirit' (Matt. 3:11). So it looked forward to Jesus; it was the 'getting ready' baptism, not yet the full Christian one. To say Apollos 'knew only John's baptism,' then, is to say his grasp of the gospel reached accurately up to that preparatory point — he knew and proclaimed Jesus as the Messiah truly, as far as it went — but had not yet been brought up to the fuller apostolic message that followed: Pentecost, the outpouring and gift of the Holy Spirit, and baptism in the name of Jesus. His faith was real but incomplete, the fault of his teaching, not his heart — he taught what he had been taught, probably away from the centre in Alexandria before the fuller news reached him.

(He is the cousin of the Ephesian 'disciples' of 19:1–7, who also knew only John's baptism — though note the difference: Apollos, already fervent in the Spirit and teaching accurately, is simply taught 'more accurately' by Priscilla and Aquila (v. 26) and is never re-baptized, whereas those men, who had not even heard the Spirit was given, are baptized into Jesus and receive the Spirit; see on 19:1–2.) And the lovely lessons for Old Joe: even a brilliant, eloquent, fervent Bible teacher still had more to learn — and humbly received it from a tentmaking couple (Priscilla named first). None of us has arrived; we keep growing. And the way to help someone whose understanding is incomplete is Priscilla and Aquila's way: not to attack him publicly, but to 'take him aside' and explain the way of God more accurately — gently, privately, helpfully.

verseByVerse.quote: "He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
verseByVerse.commentary: Priscilla and Aquila — Paul's tentmaking co-workers from Corinth — model the right response to incomplete but sincere teaching: they take him aside privately and explain more accurately. Not public correction, not dismissal, but patient, careful, private instruction. The woman is named first — unusual in antiquity — suggesting she was the primary teacher. The church grows in understanding through this kind of generous, accurate, humble correction of those who teach imperfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary: The fully catechized Apollos is a force: he greatly helps those who have believed and powerfully refutes the Jews in public — the same activity Paul did, now done by one trained more fully in the apostolic faith. The chain of teaching — Paul to Priscilla and Aquila, Priscilla and Aquila to Apollos, Apollos to Achaia — is how the gospel multiplies. Every teacher who teaches accurately creates new teachers who teach accurately. (cf. 1 Cor. 1:17–18; 2 Tim. 2:15)

18.theology: Election as the Ground of Courage in Mission. “I have many in this city who are my people” (v. 10) is the doctrine of election functioning as a promise to a frightened missionary. Paul is afraid — he says so later. And God’s answer to his fear is not “it will go well” or “people will respond positively” — it is “I have my people here.” The ground of missionary perseverance is not optimism about human receptivity; it is confidence in divine election. God has sheep in every city, in every culture, in every hostile context — sheep who will hear the shepherd’s voice when it is proclaimed through his servants. This is not a reason for laziness; it is a reason for courage. Preach. His people will come.
18.examples:
Then: Paul in Corinth, afraid, working as a tentmaker, preaching every Sabbath, sustained by a vision and a promise, staying eighteen months because God told him to stay. The church that emerged from that eighteen months will cause him more trouble than any other — and will receive his most profound letters about the cross, the resurrection, and love.

Now: Every city has people who are God’s — people the Spirit is already preparing, already drawing, already making ready to hear. The task of the church is to be in the city, to preach the word, to stay when the Lord says stay, and to trust that the harvest belongs to him. The missionary who preaches in the hardest city is not alone. God is already there, and his people are waiting.

19.title: Ephesus and the Power of the Word
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. <sup>2</sup>And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” <sup>3</sup>And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” <sup>4</sup>And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.” <sup>5</sup>On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. <sup>7</sup>There were about twelve men in all. <sup>8</sup>And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. <sup>9</sup>But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. <sup>10</sup>This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. <sup>11</sup>And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, <sup>12</sup>so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. <sup>13</sup>Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” <sup>14</sup>Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this. <sup>15</sup>But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” <sup>16</sup>And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. <sup>17</sup>And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. <sup>18</sup>Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. <sup>19</sup>And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. <sup>20</sup>So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. <sup>21</sup>Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” <sup>23</sup>About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. <sup>24</sup>For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. <sup>25</sup>These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. <sup>26</sup>And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. <sup>27</sup>And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.” <sup>28</sup>When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>34</sup>But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>41</sup>And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.
19.overview:
Ephesus is Paul’s most sustained ministry in any single city: three months in the synagogue, then two years in the hall of Tyrannus — reasoning daily, so that all the residents of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord. Not all of Ephesus came to hear Paul; the word went out through those who heard and carried it. Two years. Daily. All of Asia. This is what sustained, patient, Word-centred ministry produces.

The power of the word in Ephesus is confirmed by two vivid episodes. The sons of Sceva attempt to use the name of Jesus as a formula — and the evil spirit recognises the difference between the name wielded by authority and the name borrowed without relationship: “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognise, but who are you?” The name of Jesus is not magic; it is the delegated authority of the living Lord, available only to those who are his. And the new believers burn their magic books — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth — in a public bonfire of repentance that is one of the most vivid pictures of genuine conversion in the New Testament.

Then the riot. Demetrius the silversmith has done the economic analysis: if people stop worshipping Artemis, the shrine-making trade is finished. His complaint is one of the most honest in Acts: it is not primarily about theology but about money. The Word of God is economically disruptive. When people stop giving themselves to idols, the industries built on those idols suffer. The gospel always costs someone something.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Ephesian ministry is the climax of Paul's third missionary journey and the most sustained and fruitful period of his missionary career. Over two years of daily lectures in the hall of Tyrannus, 'all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.' Ephesus was the commercial and religious capital of the Roman province of Asia — home of the temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, and a center of magical arts and occult practice. The gospel's victory in Ephesus is therefore the gospel's victory over the most formidable concentration of spiritual opposition in Paul's experience.

The Ephesian episode contains three defining moments: the disciples of John who receive the Holy Spirit through Paul's ministry (completing what Apollos had begun teaching), the seven sons of Sceva whose attempt to exploit the name of Jesus results in their violent expulsion, and the riot of Demetrius the silversmith whose economic interests are threatened by the gospel's displacement of Artemis worship. Each moment illustrates a different dimension of the gospel's power: its completion of incomplete faith, its sovereignty over demonic opposition, and its economic disruption of idolatry.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word of the Lord Prevailing Over Magic and Idolatry

The burning of the magical books — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth — is one of the most dramatic acts of new-believer repentance in Acts. The magicians do not gradually reduce their practice; they make a clean, costly, public break. Reformed theology sees in this the pattern of genuine repentance: the thoroughgoing abandonment of what the gospel has displaced, at whatever cost. The summary in v. 20 ('So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily') is the theological verdict on the entire Ephesian episode: the word wins, over magic, over economics, over riot.
