verseByVerse.examples: Then: Demetrius the silversmith's complaint — 'there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing' — is the most honest statement of why people oppose the gospel: it costs them something they value. Now: The gospel continues to threaten economic arrangements built on idolatry, and the opposition it meets is often economic before it is theological.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' And they said, 'No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's diagnostic question is immediate: Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed? The question presupposes that receiving the Spirit is the normal, expected experience of Christian initiation. These twelve men are disciples — followers of some form of Jewish teaching about the coming one — but they have not heard of the Pentecostal Spirit. Their honest answer reveals the frontier of the mission: there are people sincerely seeking God who have not yet received the fullness of the gospel.

This passage is the cousin of Acts 8, and is read the same several ways (see there). These men knew 'only the baptism of John' and had not even heard the Spirit was given (v. 2) — so the Reformed reading sees them not as ordinary Christians awaiting a second blessing, but as disciples still standing at the old, pre-Pentecost stage of John the Baptist, who on hearing of Jesus believe fully, are baptized into him, and receive the Spirit — their deficiency being in the gospel they had yet to hear, not a missing 'stage two' for already-complete believers. (Pentecostal brothers read it, with Acts 8, as evidence of a Spirit-baptism subsequent to conversion.) Note that Paul's question, 'did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?', naturally ties the receiving of the Spirit to believing, not to a later experience — which is how the letters speak of it (Eph. 1:13; Rom. 8:9). Said, as ever, with respect for those who differ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he said, 'Into what then were you baptized?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.' And Paul said, 'John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: John's baptism was preparatory — pointing forward to one who was coming. These disciples have received the preparatory sign but not the fulfillment. Paul's catechesis is swift: John's baptism was a baptism of repentance toward one coming after him, and that one is Jesus. The bridge from John to Jesus is the bridge from anticipation to fulfillment, from the forerunner to the king. Every aspect of John's ministry finds its completion in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary: Christian baptism — 'in the name of the Lord Jesus' — follows immediately upon hearing. These disciples do not resist or delay; they receive what they have been taught and are baptized. The simplicity of their response is the model of all Christian initiation: hearing, believing, receiving the sign. The church grows by this simple, repeated pattern of proclamation and response.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all."
verseByVerse.commentary: The laying on of hands and the coming of the Spirit mirrors Pentecost and Samaria. The twelve — a number resonant with the twelve apostles and the twelve tribes — receive the Spirit with visible manifestations: tongues and prophecy. This is the Ephesian Pentecost, completing the geographic mandate of Acts 1:8. The Spirit is poured out at the frontier of the mission, authenticating the extension of the gospel to this outpost of Asia.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three months in the synagogue, then withdrawal — Paul's Ephesian pattern follows Corinth's. When the synagogue becomes hostile, he does not leave the city; he relocates the school. The hall of Tyrannus is a lecture hall where Paul rents space during off-hours (a Western text adds 'from the fifth to the tenth hour' — 11am to 4pm, during the afternoon siesta when the hall is otherwise unused). The mission moves from sacred space to secular space without missing a beat.

For Old Joe, what is Paul doing when he 'persuades them about the kingdom of God'? In plain terms, he is making the case for King Jesus. The 'kingdom of God' is God's kingly rule, and the great news is that the King has come: Jesus, crucified and risen, now reigns and will one day return to reign in full. So to 'persuade about the kingdom' is to show people from the Scriptures who Jesus is and to urge them to bow to him as Lord — and so enter his kingdom, which a person does the moment he repents and trusts the King. (For what 'the kingdom of God' means, and why the phrase fills the Gospels but is rarer in the letters, see on 8:12; for the 'already, but not yet' of it — we are brought into it now, yet await its full coming — see on 14:22.)

And notice how he does it: 'reasoning and persuading.' He did not merely announce; he argued (the word means to discuss, to dialogue) and sought to convince, patiently, from the Scriptures, for three whole months. The faith is reasonable and invites the mind; commending Christ can mean kindly, patiently making the case and answering objections over time, not just a single quick pitch. Old Joe need not be a clever debater — but he can take heart that to 'persuade about the kingdom' is, at bottom, simply to help people see and trust the King.

verseByVerse.quote: "This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two years of daily teaching in Tyrannus's hall — and the result is that all of Asia hears. Ephesus is the hub: travelers, merchants, pilgrims, students all pass through the commercial capital of Asia Minor, hear Paul in the lecture hall, and carry the word back to their home cities. The seven churches of Revelation — Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea — likely trace their origins to this period. The strategy of Ephesus is to teach in the center and let the word radiate outward.

A little more on this 'hall of Tyrannus.' The word is scholē — our 'school' — a lecture hall where a teacher or rhetorician would hold his discourses and discussions. 'Tyrannus' (the name means 'ruler' or 'tyrant') was either the owner of the building or the lecturer who normally taught there; we know nothing more of him, save that his hall outlived his name by housing the gospel. As an early manuscript tradition notes, Paul used it 'from the fifth hour to the tenth' — roughly 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the heat of the day, the afternoon siesta when the hall stood empty and most people rested. Picture it: Paul at his tent-making bench in the cool early hours (20:34), then teaching through the sweltering midday while the city slept, and his hearers giving up their own rest to come and learn — labour and sacrifice on both sides. And note the move: shut out of the synagogue (sacred space), Paul carried the gospel straight into a public lecture hall (secular space), the open marketplace of ideas, where any Jew or Greek could wander in. For Old Joe the encouragement is plain: the gospel needs no grand temple. A rented room, used in the leftover hours of the day, by a man who also worked a trade, became the hub from which 'all Asia' — Colossae, Laodicea, the cities of Revelation — heard the word of the Lord. Ordinary, borrowed, off-peak means, and a whole province reached.

verseByVerse.quote: And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Extraordinary miracles' — Luke signals that even by Acts's standards, the Ephesian miracles are exceptional: handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched Paul's skin conveying healing power. Luke does not explain the mechanism; he records the result. The point is not a theology of physical objects but the demonstration that God's healing power through Paul extended even beyond direct contact — appropriate in a city saturated with magical arts that claimed to channel power through physical objects. The miracles authenticate the word being proclaimed and demonstrate that the power behind the gospel exceeds any competing power the city has to offer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.' Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of Sceva represent the ancient pattern of magical appropriation of divine names: if Paul's Jesus-invocations produce results, perhaps the name can be used as a formula by those who do not know Jesus. This is magic thinking, not faith — using sacred language as a tool rather than as address to a person. The name of Jesus is not a spell; it is the name of a living Lord who knows those who are his.

A word for Old Joe on these 'Jewish exorcists.' Exorcists were people who tried to drive evil spirits out of the afflicted — and in the ancient world it was a common, and often paid, trade, a kind of spiritual technician or magician-for-hire. They worked by technique: incantations and spells, secret formulas, herbs and charms, and above all the reciting of powerful names believed to compel the spirits to obey. Jewish exorcists were especially sought after, precisely because they could invoke the name of the one true God and the sacred names of Scripture, which were thought to carry unusual power over the dark world (Josephus describes them, and legend traced their arts back to Solomon). The point to grasp is that it was all about harnessing power by the right words, not about knowing God — they treated a holy name as a magic word.

That is exactly their fatal mistake here. Seeing Paul cast out demons in Jesus' name, the sons of Sceva simply added 'the Jesus whom Paul proclaims' to their list of power-words, as one more spell to try — and it ended in disaster (vv. 15–16), the evil spirit answering, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' before the man fell on them and beat them. The lesson is sharp and freeing: the name of Jesus is not a magic formula anyone can wield. It carries authority only on the lips of those who truly belong to him by faith. Real power over the powers of darkness is not a technique to be mastered but a gift that flows from being united to Christ — you cannot borrow Jesus' authority while keeping Jesus himself at arm's length.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."
verseByVerse.commentary: The demonic response is withering: Jesus I know, Paul I recognize — but you? The spirit distinguishes between the Lord himself, his authorized apostle, and these unauthorized imitators. The violent repulse is both judgment on the magical appropriation and a demonstration that the name of Jesus is not a power that can be harnessed by anyone who speaks it. The authority belongs to Jesus and extends to those he sends; it cannot be borrowed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices."
verseByVerse.commentary: The failure of the magical exorcism does not discredit the gospel — it glorifies it. The name of Jesus is extolled precisely because it cannot be hijacked. The believers' response is striking: many come to confess and divulge their magical practices. The word for 'divulging' suggests a full disclosure of secrets — this is public, costly repentance from the occult practices that were woven into Ephesian religious life. The gospel does not coexist with magic; it displaces it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. And the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fifty thousand silver pieces — an enormous sum, representing the economic cost of full repentance from the lucrative trade in magical formulae. The public burning is an act of worship and a witness: these believers count the cost and burn the books anyway. This is the radical economic implication of the lordship of Jesus: whatever competes with him must go, whatever its value. The result: the word of the Lord prevails mightily. Obedience and mission are not separate tracks. (cf. Isa. 55:10–11; 2 Thess. 3:1)

Two small phrases worth a word. 'The word of the Lord' is Luke's regular name for the gospel message — the Christian message about and from the Lord Jesus, his own word carrying his own authority (much like 'the word of Christ,' explained at Col. 3:16). It is, in short, the gospel as God's living, authoritative word.

And Old Joe's instinct about 'increased' is exactly right: it does not mean the gospel grew larger in content, but that it spread, multiplied, and triumphed — more and more people heard and believed, and the message gained ground and overcame opposition ('prevailed mightily' — here, over the magic arts whose books had just gone up in smoke). But why does Luke put it so oddly, making the word itself the thing that grows, rather than simply saying 'more people believed'? On purpose — it is one of his favourite ways of speaking (6:7, 'the word of God continued to increase'; 12:24, 'the word of God increased and multiplied'; 13:49). Two reasons. First, he is deliberately picturing the gospel as a living seed: the very word for 'increase' (auxanō, 'grow') is the language of living, fruitful things, the word of Jesus' parables where the kingdom-seed sprouts and grows of its own God-given life (Mark 4:8, 26–29; the seed is the word, Luke 8:11). The gospel is planted in the world and grows like wheat, and believers are its fruit. Second, and more pointedly, by making the word the actor Luke takes the credit off the preachers and puts it on God: it is not Paul's cleverness or the church's strategy that conquers Ephesus, but the word itself, alive with God's own power (Rom. 1:16; Isa. 55:11, 'my word... shall not return empty'). So the 'strange' phrasing is really a confession of faith: watch the word, not the men — and take heart, for that same living word is still growing and prevailing in the world today.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome." And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'He resolved in the Spirit' — the planning is both Paul's decision and Spirit-guided. The itinerary Paul outlines — Macedonia, Achaia, Jerusalem, Rome — is precisely the route that Acts follows for the rest of the book. 'I must also see Rome' — the divine necessity (dei) that has governed Christ's mission and Paul's throughout Acts. Paul's determination to reach Rome is not personal ambition but the Spirit's confirmation that the mission's geographic horizon extends to the imperial capital. The sending of Timothy and Erastus ahead maintains the missionary network while Paul completes the Ephesian ministry.

(A word first on the phrase: 'resolved in the Spirit' is slightly ambiguous in the Greek — it may mean 'in his own spirit,' i.e. he inwardly made up his mind, or 'in the Holy Spirit,' under the Spirit's leading. Given how the Spirit steers Paul all through Acts, and that the Lord later confirms this very plan — 'you must testify also in Rome,' 23:11 — the Spirit-guided sense fits well.)

But Old Joe's question is the practical one: how can I know my decisions are Spirit-guided today? First, let the anxiety down. The apostles received extraordinary, direct steering because of their unique founding role (see on 8:26); God's ordinary way of leading us is quieter and more settled, and he has not promised Old Joe a voice in his head or a tingle in his chest for every choice. So how does the Spirit lead? Chiefly through the Word. The Spirit and the Scriptures always go together: he guides first by lighting up and applying the Bible he himself inspired ('a lamp to my feet,' Ps. 119:105; 'equipped for every good work,' 2 Tim. 3:16–17). Most of God's will is already plainly revealed there — be holy, love, forgive, flee sin, tell the truth, serve — so the Spirit-led life is, nine times in ten, simply the obedient life. Then through a renewed mind and sanctified wisdom. For the choices Scripture does not directly settle (which job, where to live), the Spirit leads not by bypassing your thinking but by maturing it: 'be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that... you may discern what is the will of God' (Rom. 12:2); and if you lack wisdom, 'ask God, who gives generously' (James 1:5). Add prayer (Prov. 3:5–6), the counsel of godly friends (Prov. 15:22), and the providence of opened and closed doors — and you have the ordinary toolkit by which the Spirit guides. Inner promptings and a sense of 'peace' may play a part (Phil. 2:13), but they are never trusted on their own; they must always be tested by Scripture and wisdom, for the heart can deceive (Jer. 17:9; 1 John 4:1).

And here is the most freeing thing of all: the clearest biblical mark of being 'led by the Spirit' is not a feeling about a single decision but the shape of a life. 'Those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God' (Rom. 8:14) — led, in context, to put sin to death and live as God's children; and 'the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience...' (Gal. 5:22–23). So a choice made in love, humility, holiness, and faith, by a person walking closely with God, is a Spirit-led choice — even if no special feeling attends it; while a choice driven by pride, lust, greed, or self-will is not, however 'peaceful' it feels. So Old Joe's checklist is simple: Does it square with Scripture? Have I prayed for wisdom and sought godly counsel? Is my heart surrendered, ready to do even the hard thing God might show? Does this flow from love and holiness, or from the flesh? Then decide, and trust him with the outcome. He is sovereign over your steps ('the heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps,' Prov. 16:9), big enough to guide a surrendered, Word-shaped heart, and kind enough to redeem even our wrong turns (Rom. 8:28). A Christian walking with God need not fear 'missing God's will'; the pressure is off, for the Guide is faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: "About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The riot in Ephesus has an economic trigger: the gospel's conversion of idol worshipers threatens the market for silver shrines of Artemis. Demetrius is not a theological opponent but a businessman whose livelihood is imperiled by the spread of the gospel. Luke's account of the Ephesian riot is one of the most vivid in Acts, and its inciting cause is commercial — the gospel disrupts economic systems built on idolatry.

'The Way' — here is one of the earliest names the Christian movement went by (Luke uses it repeatedly: 9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). Why 'the Way'? Three roots run together. First and deepest, Jesus said, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me' (John 14:6) — so to follow the Way is to follow him, the one road home to God. Second, it echoes the Old Testament, where the life of faith is pictured as a road one walks: 'the way of the LORD,' 'the Way of Holiness' (Isa. 35:8; 40:3). Third, it captures that Christianity is not merely a creed to hold but a way of life to walk — a whole road travelled after Jesus (recall 'as you received Christ... so walk in him,' Col. 2:6). It is a humble, vivid name: the faith is a path you travel with the Lord who is himself the Way, not just a box you tick.

And 'Artemis' (the Romans' Diana) was the great goddess of Ephesus — not quite the classical Greek huntress, but a distinctive local mother- and fertility-goddess, patroness and protectress of the city. Her temple at Ephesus, the Artemision, was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — vast, magnificent, and the heart of a huge pilgrimage and tourist economy. Demetrius and his guild made and sold silver models of the shrine, devotional souvenirs for the pilgrims, a very lucrative trade. So the gospel here collides with a formidable triple alliance — a famous false god, fierce civic pride (Ephesus called itself the goddess's 'temple-keeper,' 19:35), and big money. When people turned from idols to Christ, the idol-souvenir business suffered, and that — not theology — is what lit the riot (19:27). The gospel had already burned the magic books (19:19); now it threatens the idol trade. Wherever Christ truly advances, the kingdoms of money and idolatry feel the tremor.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Demetrius's speech is an unintentional tribute to the gospel's effectiveness: not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia, Paul has turned a great many people away from idolatry. The craftsmen's economic anxiety is the measure of the gospel's success. When the idol market collapses because people are turning to the living God, the mission is working exactly as it should. The gospel's disruption of the economy of idolatry is a sign of its power, not a problem to be managed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Gods made with hands are not gods' — Demetrius accurately summarizes Paul's preaching (and the Old Testament prophetic tradition, Isaiah 44:9–20). The admission is inadvertent but devastating: the silversmiths know that their silver shrines are hand-made objects, not divine beings. The danger Demetrius identifies — that Artemis 'may be counted as nothing' — is not a distortion of the gospel's effect but an accurate description of what the gospel always does to idols: it reveals them as nothing. The entire religious economy of Ephesus is built on the premise that Artemis is something; the gospel says she is nothing. (cf. Matt. 6:24; 1 Tim. 6:10)

verseByVerse.quote: "When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' And the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's companions in travel."
verseByVerse.commentary: The mob is theological in its outcry — 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians' — but economic in its motive. The confusion fills the city: this is not a controlled protest but a riot. Gaius and Aristarchus are seized as representatives of Paul — Paul himself is not present, but his companions bear the danger of his mission. The theater of Ephesus, seating twenty-five thousand, is the public space where civic passions are expressed at the largest scale.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul wanted to go in among the crowd, but the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's courage tends toward recklessness and his brothers restrain him — including the Asiarchs, the wealthy and politically prominent officials who superintended the imperial cult in Asia. That these figures are Paul's friends, and that they care for his safety, is a remarkable social detail: the gospel has reached into the highest levels of Ephesian society. Their concern is both friendly and prudent — nothing good can come from Paul in a riot of twenty-five thousand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews put forward. And Alexander, motioned with his hand, wishing to make a defense to the crowd."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chaos of the mob: most do not even know why they have gathered. Alexander — a Jewish representative seeking to distance Judaism from the Christian movement — attempts to address the crowd. The Jews are trying to make clear that they are not associated with this gospel that threatens the idol trade. The irony is that from the mob's perspective, Jews and Christians are equally suspect as monotheists who reject Artemis.

'Most of them did not know why they had come together' — it is indeed a touch of sad comedy, and Luke surely means us to feel the irony: a whole city roaring itself hoarse for two hours (v. 34) over a god, and most of the rioters cannot even say why they are there. But Scripture has a sober teaching that this little scene puts on display. The Bible takes a dim and realistic view of the mob: 'You shall not fall in with the many to do evil' (Exod. 23:2); crowds are fickle and passion-driven, the same Jerusalem voices crying 'Hosanna!' one week and 'Crucify him!' the next (Matt. 21:9; 27:22). And deeper still, this is what idolatry does to a mind. When men exchange the true God for idols, Paul says, 'they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools' (Rom. 1:21–22; Eph. 4:17–18). The psalmist is even more pointed: those who make idols 'become like them' — as deaf, blind, and senseless as the mute images they worship (Ps. 115:8). A senseless god makes for senseless worshippers; the confused babble of the Ephesian theatre is simply idolatry's darkened mind made audible.

Set against it is the gospel, for 'God is not a God of confusion but of peace' (1 Cor. 14:33). The riot is a little Babel — the proud city's voices dissolving into noise, as at the tower where God confused the tongues of the self-exalting (Gen. 11:7–9) — while the gospel is the Babel-reversing word that brings light, sanity, and order (think of Pentecost, Acts 2, undoing the confusion of tongues). It is the Word that gives a man back his right mind, as the delivered demoniac sat 'clothed and in his right mind' (Mark 5:15). For Old Joe it is a mirror held up to the world: so much of its frenzy — the crowds roaring for causes, fashions, and outrages — is people swept along without truly knowing why, defending empty things. The Scripture's counsel is plain: do not be carried by the herd, but let the truth of God steady and clear your mind (Rom. 12:2). The gospel does not merely save the soul; it brings the muddled head home to sanity and peace.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they cried out, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Alexander's Jewish identity triggers the crowd's anti-monotheist chanting — two hours of 'Great is Artemis.' The mob does not distinguish between Jewish and Christian monotheism; both reject the goddess. The chant is both religious affirmation and civic identity expression: Ephesus is Artemis's city, and Artemis's greatness is Ephesus's greatness. Two hours of chanting is the last gasp of a religious system losing its grip on the city.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, 'Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town clerk — the most important civic official in Ephesus, the liaison between the city and the Roman provincial government — steps in to end the riot. His appeal is to civic pride and legal prudence: Ephesus's status as temple keeper of Artemis is unassailable, so there is no need for this disorder. His concern is not theological but political: a riot could bring Roman intervention and cost Ephesus its civic privileges.

'The sacred stone that fell from the sky' — one Greek word, diopetes, 'fallen from Zeus/heaven.' It was almost certainly a meteorite. In the ancient world, before anyone understood such things, a stone that fell flaming out of the sky seemed an obvious gift from the gods — heaven-sent, holy, undeniable proof of the deity; several pagan cults treasured such 'fallen-from-heaven' stones. The Ephesians believed their goddess (or her very image) was bound up with one, and the town clerk waves it as his clinching argument: everyone knows Artemis is real and we are her guardians, so settle down. The quiet irony is sharp: they revered the falling rock and the goddess, while missing the true God who actually made the heavens and flung the stone — worshipping 'the creature rather than the Creator' (Rom. 1:25). A meteorite is a wonder, but it points to its Maker, not to a goddess; 'every good gift comes down from above, from the Father of lights' (James 1:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town clerk's legal analysis exonerates Paul's mission: not sacrilegious, not blasphemers, no chargeable offense. The proper channels — courts, proconsuls — are available if there are legitimate grievances. This is Roman due process operating correctly, and it vindicates the missionaries. Luke's point is consistent throughout Acts: where Roman legal procedure is fairly applied, the gospel is innocent of the charges leveled against it.

('Proconsul' is explained at 18:12: the Senate-appointed governor of a province like Asia, who held supreme civil and judicial authority — in modern terms, roughly a regional governor who is also the province's chief judge. The clerk's point is simply that lawful channels exist: 'the courts are open, and there are proconsuls' — so let Demetrius take any real grievance to the proper authorities rather than whipping up a riot. There is a quiet wisdom here for Old Joe too: the gospel does not fear due process, and the Christian's way is to seek justice through lawful order, not mob passion.)

verseByVerse.quote: "'But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The town clerk's final argument is prudential: the riot itself is the legal danger, not the missionaries' teaching. Ephesus risks losing its civic privileges with the Roman provincial government if it cannot explain why twenty-five thousand people assembled in the theater in disorder. The irony is complete: the city called to defend Artemis against Paul finds itself defending its own riot record. The gospel does not need the mob's suppression; it needs only for the law to work.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly."
verseByVerse.commentary: The dismissal is the gospel's vindication by Roman civic authority. The riot is over; Paul is free; the mission continues. Ephesus has had its encounter with the word of God — three years of daily teaching in Tyrannus's hall, signs and wonders, the burning of fifty thousand silver pieces worth of magic books, and now a riot that proves itself lawless. The word of the Lord has prevailed in Ephesus, and it departs with Paul toward Jerusalem and Rome.

19.theology: The Word of God as the Power of Mission. Ephesus is Luke’s great exhibit of what the Word of God, given time and sustained proclamation, can do. Two years in a lecture hall, and all of Asia hears. The mechanism is not apostolic travel or institutional strategy — it is daily teaching, received by hearers who carry it wherever they go. The Reformation insight that the Word creates the church (“verbum Dei creat ecclesiam”) is visible in Ephesus: the Word goes out, conversions happen, the old life is burned, fear of God falls on the city, new communities form. The Word is not one tool among many; it is the engine of the whole enterprise. This is why Paul will later write to Timothy: “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2). There is no substitute.
19.examples:
Then: All of Asia hears the word from a lecture hall in Ephesus. A bonfire worth a hundred and forty years’ wages lights the night. A silversmith’s trade is threatened by a theological truth. The word of the Lord prevails mightily — not with weapons, not with political power, not with cultural cachet, but with the truth about the living God and the risen Christ.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to replace sustained Word-ministry with more immediately impressive alternatives — spectacle, experience, technique, programme. Ephesus was not won by any of these. It was won by a man who reasoned daily from the Scriptures for two years. The Word still has this power. It has not diminished. The question is whether we are willing to give it the time and the centrality it requires.

20.title: Farewell to Ephesus
20.text: <sup>7</sup>On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. <sup>8</sup>There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. <sup>9</sup>And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. <sup>10</sup>But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” <sup>11</sup>And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed. <sup>12</sup>And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted. <sup>17</sup>Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. <sup>18</sup>And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, <sup>19</sup>serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews; <sup>20</sup>how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, <sup>21</sup>testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>22</sup>And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, <sup>23</sup>except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. <sup>24</sup>But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. <sup>25</sup>And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. <sup>26</sup>Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, <sup>27</sup>for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. <sup>28</sup>Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. <sup>29</sup>I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; <sup>30</sup>and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. <sup>31</sup>Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish everyone with tears. <sup>32</sup>And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. <sup>36</sup>And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. <sup>37</sup>And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him, <sup>38</sup>being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
20.overview:
The farewell at Miletus is one of the most moving passages in Acts, and the only speech Paul addresses to Christians. It is a pastor’s testament — the account of a ministry offered to its people before the man who gave it disappears from their sight. Paul did not shrink. He did not select the comfortable texts and leave the hard ones. He declared the whole counsel of God — repentance and faith, warning and promise, the cross and the coming judgment — to Jews and Greeks, in public and house to house, with tears, for three years. This is the standard.

And now he commends them to two things: God, and the word of his grace. Not to his successors. Not to an institution. Not to a programme. To God and his Word — the two sources of power that will outlast every pastor and sustain every flock. The Word that built them up will continue to build them up. The God who saved them will continue to keep them. Paul is going to Jerusalem with chains waiting; the Ephesian elders are going home to fierce wolves. Both are in the same hands.

They kneel on the beach and pray together, and then they weep — sorrowing most of all because they will not see his face again. The affection between shepherd and flock is total and mutual. This is what three years of tears and teaching and house-to-house ministry produces: a bond that no departure can finally break, because it is a bond forged in the gospel and sealed in the Spirit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third missionary journey enters its final phase as Paul turns his face toward Jerusalem. The route back — through Macedonia, Greece, and then by sea — is the reverse of the outward journey, and the pastoral quality of the narrative reflects Paul's awareness that he is saying goodbye. At Troas, the young man Eutychus falls from a window during an all-night sermon and is raised by Paul — a miracle that is also a portrait of the community gathered around the word and the table until dawn.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper as the Community's Center

The gathering at Troas 'on the first day of the week' to 'break bread' (v. 7) is the earliest explicit reference in Acts to the Christian practice of Sunday worship centered on the Lord's Supper. The resurrection day becomes the day of communal gathering; the bread broken in homes is the continuation of what Jesus instituted at the Last Supper. Reformed theology sees here the established pattern of Christian worship: Word and Table together, on the Lord's Day, as the community's defining weekly practice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked from Troas to Assos (about 20 miles) while the others sailed — apparently choosing the solitary walk for prayer and reflection as he moved toward Jerusalem and the suffering that awaited him. Now: The disciplines of solitude and prayer that prepare for costly obedience are as necessary for Christ's servants today as they were for Paul on the road to Assos.

verseByVerse.quote: "After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's departure from Ephesus is pastoral: he sends for the disciples and encourages them before leaving — he does not slip away in the night but says farewell, commending them to the grace of God. The journey through Macedonia is similarly characterized by 'much encouragement.' Paul is the pastor who encourages on the way out as surely as he teaches on the way in. The churches are formed not only by his arrival but by the grace of his departure.

verseByVerse.quote: "There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
verseByVerse.commentary: The plot against Paul redirects his return route — from a direct sea voyage to Syria, he goes back overland through Macedonia. Providence works through danger: the longer route will allow him to encourage more churches and will be described in verses 4–6 with the carefully listed traveling companions who represent the collection from the Gentile churches for Jerusalem. The plot intending harm becomes an occasion for extended pastoral ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The list of companions is a catalog of the mission's fruit: delegates from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe, and Asia — representatives of churches planted on the previous two journeys. They are likely carrying the collection for Jerusalem (2 Cor. 8–9) as delegates of their churches, making this journey both a pastoral tour and an act of inter-church solidarity. The diverse roster — Macedonians, Galatians, Asians — is a living demonstration of the one body of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days."
verseByVerse.commentary: The 'we' resumes — Luke rejoins the party at Philippi, where he has apparently remained since Acts 16:17. The notation of the days of Unleavened Bread (Passover season) suggests Paul observes Jewish feasts even in Gentile contexts — not for salvation but as the rhythm of his life as a Jew who follows the Messiah. Seven days in Troas: the mission pauses to worship, break bread, and teach.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered."
verseByVerse.commentary: The first day of the week — Sunday, the Lord's Day — is already the established day for Christian worship in this community. Breaking bread (the Lord's Supper) and the extended teaching of the word are the shape of the gathering. Paul, knowing he will depart the next morning, extends his teaching until midnight — pastoral urgency compressing all he wants to leave with them into one long night. The many lamps in the upper room create the warm, crowded scene that precedes the crisis.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead."
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's matter-of-fact candor: Eutychus falls asleep during Paul's sermon and falls from a third-story window. Luke, the physician, records him as 'taken up dead' — his clinical assessment, not a euphemism. The length of the sermon is not blamed; the young man's drowsiness is human and understandable. The miracle that follows will not make Paul's preaching briefer, but it will make the night unforgettable.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, 'Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.' And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he talked with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Elijah and Elisha parallel (1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34) — bending over and embracing — marks the miracle as prophetic in character. Paul's 'do not be alarmed, his life is in him' is reassurance to the community and acknowledgment of the miracle. Then, remarkably, Paul goes back upstairs and continues the Lord's Supper and the teaching — through the night until daybreak. The resurrection of Eutychus does not end the gathering; it transforms it into an all-night celebration of life.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted."
verseByVerse.commentary: The understatement of 'not a little comforted' is characteristically Lukan — an enormous relief expressed with restrained gentleness. The community that had seen a young man fall to his death now sees him walk out alive. The miracle is not merely a wonder but a sign: the apostle of the resurrection preaches in a city where a young man is raised, and the community is comforted — literally, encouraged — as Paul had been encouraging communities throughout this entire journey.

verseByVerse.quote: "But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and came to Mitylene."
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul walks the twenty miles to Assos alone — a deliberate choice, perhaps for prayer and reflection as he turns toward Jerusalem. The journey south along the coast of Asia is a farewell tour of the regions where he has ministered for years. Each port is named: Mitylene, Chios, Samos, Miletus — the geography of devotion, tracing the coastline that the mission has transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we came to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be in Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul bypasses Ephesus deliberately — if he stops there he will be detained by the beloved community, and Pentecost in Jerusalem is his goal. The urgency of Jerusalem is theological, not merely sentimental: something awaits him there, and Paul senses it. He will later say he goes to Jerusalem 'compelled by the Spirit' (v. 22). But he cannot leave Asia without a word to the Ephesian elders — so he summons them to Miletus.

Is this hurry to reach Jerusalem 'on the day of Pentecost' a proof text that Paul still kept the Jewish festivals? In part, yes — but read it carefully. It does show that Paul, himself a Jewish believer, still moved within the rhythms of the Jewish calendar and valued the feast. Yet his haste was very likely as much missional as ceremonial: Pentecost packed Jerusalem with diaspora pilgrims (a prime moment to bear witness, as at the first Pentecost, Acts 2), and Paul was carrying the relief collection from the Gentile churches, which he wanted to deliver to the saints (24:17; Rom. 15:25–26). So the verse shows him honouring the festival and the Jerusalem gathering — not that he kept it as a binding law required for righteousness. (Luke does not spell out his full motive, so we should not over-press it either way.)

And how does that square with Romans 7, where Paul says we 'have died to the law' (7:4–6)? It squares perfectly, once we see what 'died to the law' means. Paul is not saying the believer is now lawless, or that God's righteous will has been abolished — in the very same chapter he calls the law 'holy and righteous and good' (7:12). He means we have died to the law as a condemning covenant and master — the regime that could only accuse and curse us — so that we now belong to the risen Christ and bear fruit by the Spirit, not by the old written code. A believing Jew keeping Pentecost, then, is no contradiction at all: he is not under the law as a way of being justified (his justification is in Christ alone), so he is free to keep the feast — not to earn standing, but as heritage, devotion, and a bridge to his people. The fuller framework — the threefold division of the law, and the careful line between keeping a custom freely and keeping it as a requirement — is laid out at 18:18 (Paul's vow). The test there governs here too: a practice done to be saved or accepted, or imposed on others as necessary, denies grace and must go; the same practice done freely, in love, binding no one, is Christian liberty. Paul hurried to Pentecost as a free man in Christ, not as a slave under law — and that is the whole difference.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–38 — The Miletus Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's farewell address to the Ephesian elders at Miletus is the most personal and theologically rich speech in Acts — the only speech in Acts addressed entirely to a Christian audience and the only extended window into Paul's understanding of his own apostolic ministry. It is also, effectively, a last will and testament: Paul does not expect to see these elders again. Three years of sustained ministry in Ephesus have produced a community and a leadership team that Paul now entrusts entirely to God and to the word of his grace.

The speech moves through three movements: retrospect (how I served among you), prospect (what awaits me in Jerusalem), and instruction (how you must serve after I am gone). Each movement is saturated with Paul's characteristic theological categories — the grace of God, the kingdom, the gospel, the blood of Christ, the Spirit's oversight of the church, the danger of wolves, the example of the minister's life. The prayer and weeping that close the scene are the expression of a depth of pastoral love that the rest of Acts rarely makes visible.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Elder as Shepherd and Overseer

Paul's address to the Ephesian 'elders' (v. 17) whom he calls 'overseers' (episkopous, v. 28) and instructs to 'shepherd' (poimainein) the flock establishes the threefold nature of the pastoral office: elder (dignity of character), overseer (responsibility of governance), shepherd (work of care). The Reformed tradition has consistently seen in this passage the defining description of the ordained ministry: those who guard, feed, and care for the people whom the Holy Spirit has placed under their oversight.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul warned the Ephesian elders that 'fierce wolves' would come from outside and that 'men speaking twisted things' would arise from within the community itself. Both dangers materialized: the Ephesian letters of Revelation (chapters 2–3) show a community that had resisted external pressure but had lost its first love. Now: The threats Paul named are the threats every congregation faces in every generation: external persecution and internal doctrinal corruption. The antidote is the same: the word of God's grace, committed to Spirit-filled leadership whose lives embody what they preach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him."
verseByVerse.commentary: The summons to Miletus is a pastoral act of genuine love: Paul cannot go to Ephesus, so he asks the elders to come to him. They make the roughly thirty-mile journey, and what follows is the only speech in Acts addressed exclusively to Christians — Paul's farewell to the church he loves most deeply. This is the apostle as pastor, not as missionary pioneer; the tone is intimate, retrospective, and gravely forewarning.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they came to him, he said to them: 'You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's ministry is summarized in three phrases: humility, tears, and trials. These are not credentials of power but marks of servanthood. The one who has raised the dead and planted churches across a continent describes his ministry as humble, tearful, and tried. This is the apostolic self-portrait: not the triumphant hero but the servant who wept over his people and endured the plots of his opponents. The tears are the measure of the love.

verseByVerse.quote: "how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, declaring to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable' — the negative formulation is deliberate: Paul is naming the temptation to withhold difficult truth from audiences who might prefer comfortable falsehood. 'Not shrinking' is the courage of the minister who loves people enough to tell them what they need to hear. 'In public and from house to house' — the complementary settings of apostolic teaching: the formal gathering and the informal domestic context. 'Repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ' — the content of three years of Ephesian ministry compressed into two words: repentance and faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul goes to Jerusalem compelled — bound, constrained — by the Spirit. He does not know the specifics, but the Spirit has been warning him through prophets in city after city: imprisonment and afflictions await. He goes not in ignorance of the danger but in submission to the Spirit despite it. This is the obedience of faith: going toward what God has called you to even when the destination is suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The most defining statement of Paul's apostolic identity: my life is not precious to me if only I can finish the course. This is not death-wish but mission-clarity — the same clarity that enabled martyrs to face death without panic. The 'ministry received from the Lord Jesus' is not Paul's career but his calling, and callings are completed in obedience, not preserved in self-protection. 'The gospel of the grace of God' — this is what the ministry is: testifying to grace. (cf. Phil. 3:13–14; 2 Tim. 4:7)

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul's farewell is also his legal declaration: he is innocent of blood — Ezekiel's language for the watchman who has faithfully warned the people (Ezek. 33). He has proclaimed the kingdom for three years in Ephesus; if anyone in that community is lost, it is not for lack of warning. The apostle's final gift to the elders is this assurance: I have given you everything God gave me. Your blood is not on my hands.

Notice that Paul sums up his whole three-year ministry in Ephesus — to a Gentile city, in this church age — as 'proclaiming the kingdom.' That is no isolated word: Acts is framed front to back by the kingdom. The risen Jesus spent forty days 'speaking about the kingdom of God' (1:3); Philip preached 'the kingdom' to Samaritans (8:12); Paul 'reasoned and persuaded about the kingdom' in Ephesus (19:8); and the book closes with him in Rome 'proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus' (28:31). The apostolic, church-age mission is summarised, again and again, as kingdom-preaching — to Jews, Samaritans, Greeks, and Romans alike. (For what 'the kingdom of God' means and the 'already / not yet' of it, see on 8:12, 14:22, and Col. 1:13.)

This bears gently on a real difference among Bible-loving Christians. Many of our dispensational brothers are hesitant to speak of 'the kingdom' in connection with the church at all, preferring to reserve it — especially the Davidic, messianic kingdom of the Old Testament promises — for a future, literal reign of Christ over restored national Israel in the millennium. On the classic scheme, the kingdom was offered to Israel, rejected, and postponed, so that the present age is in some sense a parenthesis, and the kingdom proper still awaits. Their concern is a worthy one and should be honoured: they want to take God's promises to Israel seriously and literally, not have them quietly absorbed into the church (Rom. 11 does keep a future for ethnic Israel, and God keeps his word). It is also fair to add that the view has developed: progressive dispensationalists (Bock, Blaising) now affirm that the kingdom was genuinely inaugurated at Christ's exaltation (Acts 2:30–36), an 'already' as well as a 'not yet,' while still holding a future literal fulfilment for Israel.

From the Reformed side, the simplest point is that Scripture's own language — nowhere more than in Acts — treats the kingdom as a present reality now being preached and entered, not one held wholly in reserve. Believers have already been 'transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son' (Col. 1:13) and made 'a kingdom, priests to his God' (Rev. 1:6); 'the kingdom of God has come upon you,' said Jesus, wherever he casts out the powers of darkness (Matt. 12:28). The church is not simply identical with the kingdom (God's reign is wider than the church), but it is the kingdom's present people and outpost — those over whom King Jesus already reigns, the community through whom his reign advances, awaiting the day it is consummated over all the earth. So Old Joe need not be shy of the word: if he belongs to Christ, he already lives in the kingdom of God, under the reign of the King — even as he prays, 'your kingdom come,' for its full and glorious arrival. Reformed and dispensational believers will keep weighing the future of Israel and the millennium differently; but that the King reigns now, and that his kingdom was Paul's very message to the church, the text itself makes plain.

verseByVerse.quote: "'for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The whole counsel of God' — not selected doctrines, not comfortable topics, not the parts that would be well-received. The whole. Paul's ministry in Ephesus was three years of comprehensive theological formation: the kingdom, the cross, resurrection, judgment, grace, the Holy Spirit, the life of the church. A ministry that shrinks from any part of God's counsel fails the congregation it claims to serve. Full declaration is both apostolic duty and pastoral love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock' — the order is deliberate: self-care precedes flock-care, because the shepherd who neglects his own soul will eventually harm the sheep. 'Which he obtained with his own blood' — the church belongs to God because he purchased it with the blood of his Son. The preciousness of the blood that bought the church is the measure of the seriousness with which its overseers must care for it. 'Fierce wolves' — the language of Jesus's warning (Matthew 7:15): false teachers who consume the flock rather than feeding it are the first external threat Paul names. (cf. John 10:11–12; 1 Pet. 5:2–3)

Pause on those astonishing words: the church is 'the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood.' But God is spirit and has no blood — so how can God bleed? Only because the One who shed that blood, Jesus, is God. This is one of the Bible's most powerful affirmations of the deity of Christ: the blood of the cross can be called God's own blood, since the man who hung there is the eternal Son in our flesh (the same truth lets Paul say 'they crucified the Lord of glory,' 1 Cor. 2:8). For Old Joe two things shine here. The deity of his Saviour — the cross is the measure of how high the One who died for him truly is; and the worth of the church — a flock so precious that God purchased it with his own blood. (A note for the curious: a few manuscripts read 'church of the Lord,' and the phrase rendered 'his own blood' could just possibly mean 'the blood of his Own [Son]'; but the plain, well-attested reading proclaims that God bought his church with his own blood — and the elders are to shepherd it accordingly.)

'Made you overseers' — and Old Joe is right that the church struggles to find the line of what overseers should actually oversee. Start with the words, for they set the scope. The same men are called elders (v. 17, their maturity), overseers (episkopoi, their function of watching over), and they are told to shepherd the flock (v. 28). The shepherd-picture tells you what the oversight is: it is pastoral and spiritual — to feed the flock with sound teaching, guard it from wolves and error (vv. 29–30), lead it, and care for souls (Heb. 13:17, 'keeping watch over your souls'). It is the care of souls by the Word, not the management of people's private lives. (On the elders' mandate, qualifications, and authority generally, see on 14:23.)

Now the two ditches Old Joe names. Overreach first: Peter forbids it outright — elders are 'not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples' (1 Pet. 5:3); 'it shall not be so among you,' said Jesus of those who lord it over others (Matt. 20:25–26). The key principle is that an elder's authority is ministerial, not legislative: he administers and applies God's Word; he does not make new laws. He is not lord of your conscience — 'God alone is Lord of the conscience,' and elders may not bind believers with man-made rules where Scripture is silent (that was the Colossian error, 'do not handle, taste, touch,' Col. 2:20–23). To regulate matters God has left to Christian liberty (Rom. 14), or to intrude into private choices Scripture never addresses, is to go beyond the charge and meddle. Negligence is the opposite ditch, and just as serious: Ezekiel's terrible woe falls on shepherds who fed themselves and did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, or seek the straying (Ezek. 34). An elder who will not teach hard truth, will not stay alert to the wolves Paul warns are coming (vv. 29–31), or will not lovingly address serious, unrepentant, scandalous sin (1 Cor. 5) has abandoned his post — and abdication dressed up as 'tolerance' is no virtue.

Where, then, is the line? It is the Word of God. Elders are to be firm where God is firm — on the gospel, on sound doctrine, on clear moral commands, on the church's worship and order, and on grave unrepentant sin — and free where God leaves free, protecting liberty in disputable matters rather than policing it (Rom. 14:1–4). Real authority, exercised within Scripture's bounds, and real restraint beyond them. Two reminders keep the balance: the flock is not theirs but God's — 'the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood' — so they are under-shepherds of the Chief Shepherd, accountable to him (1 Pet. 5:2–4), not owners free to do as they please; and Paul's very first word is 'pay careful attention to yourselves' (v. 28) — the elder who watches his own soul, humble and accountable, is the one most likely to shepherd with the right blend of courage and gentleness. The aim throughout is the flock's good and growth, served willingly and gladly, never for power, money, or ego (1 Pet. 5:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: "and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears."
verseByVerse.commentary: The internal threat — 'from among your own selves' — is named alongside the external one: false teachers will arise within the community, not only from outside. 'Speaking twisted things' — distorted, perverted — taking genuine truth and bending it just enough to lead people away from Christ. The Ephesian letters in Revelation 2–3 confirm that Paul's warning was prescient. 'Three years... night and day... every one with tears' — the pastoral investment that gives Paul the moral authority to warn: he has earned the right to be heard by those he has served with such costly consistency.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one's silver or gold or apparel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's benediction: he commends them not to programs or strategies but to God and to the word of his grace. The word is able — able to build up, able to give the inheritance. When Paul is gone, the word remains. The church is not dependent on its founding apostle but on the apostolic word that he has fully declared. The disclaimer about silver and gold follows naturally: he has not ministered for personal gain, and his successor ministers — the elders — must embody the same financial disinterestedness.

verseByVerse.quote: "'You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's hands — the tentmaker's calloused hands — are the evidence of his integrity. He worked with them not only to support himself but to model the generosity that the gospel requires. 'It is more blessed to give than to receive' is a saying of Jesus not recorded in the four Gospels — one of the few such sayings preserved in Acts. The apostle who could have been supported by the churches chose to work so that he could give. This is the economic ethics of the kingdom made visible in a life. (cf. Luke 6:38; 2 Cor. 9:7)

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The farewell is physical and communal: kneeling, prayer, tears, embracing, kissing. The emotional intensity Luke records is not sentimentality but the depth of apostolic love and communal grief. These elders have been formed by three years of Paul's teaching and pastoral care; they are losing their father in the faith. The tears are evidence that genuine pastoral ministry creates genuine bonds of love — and genuine grief at parting.

verseByVerse.quote: "being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship."
verseByVerse.commentary: The specific cause of the deepest sorrow: his word that they would not see his face again. The community's grief is not generic but anchored to a specific loss — the presence of the man who has shaped their souls. They accompany him to the ship: even the farewell is extended, prolonged, reluctant to end. The journey to Jerusalem begins from this shore of tears, and Paul goes toward suffering carried by the love of those who cannot follow.

20.theology: The Whole Counsel of God and Pastoral Faithfulness. Acts 20:27 gives the church its standard for preaching: the whole counsel of God, without shrinking. This phrase has defined the Reformed tradition’s commitment to expository, systematic, comprehensive proclamation of Scripture — preaching through whole books, teaching the full range of doctrine, refusing to select only the comfortable and suppress the challenging. The shepherd who preaches the whole counsel will declare both the tenderness of the Father and the terror of the Judge, both the free grace of justification and the necessary fruit of sanctification, both the comfort of election and the urgency of repentance. Paul could stand before his people at Miletus and say “I am innocent of your blood” because he had given them everything. That is the standard every preacher must aspire to.
20.examples:
Then: A beach at Miletus, a group of weeping elders on their knees, a man who knew he was going to chains and possibly death — and who spent his last hours with these people not arranging his escape but commending them to God and declaring his conscience clear. The tears on the beach are the overflow of three years of tears in the houses of Ephesus. Ministry that produces this kind of grief at parting has been ministry that produced this kind of love in the doing.

Now: Paul’s farewell is the standard against which every pastoral ministry will be measured. Did we shrink? Did we select? Did we give them the comfortable Christ without the demanding Lord, the free grace without the costly discipleship, the promise without the warning? The whole counsel of God. Nothing less. The flock that has been given the whole counsel will be able to stand when the wolves come — because they will recognise the deviation when they hear it.

21.title: Bound for Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. <sup>2</sup>And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail. <sup>3</sup>When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo. <sup>4</sup>And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. <sup>7</sup>When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with one day. <sup>8</sup>On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. <sup>10</sup>While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. <sup>11</sup>And coming to us, he took Paul’s belt and bound his own hands and feet and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit, ‘This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’” <sup>12</sup>When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem. <sup>13</sup>Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” <sup>14</sup>And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” <sup>15</sup>After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. <sup>17</sup>When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. <sup>18</sup>On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. <sup>19</sup>After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. <sup>20</sup>And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed. They are all zealous for the law. <sup>26</sup>Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them. <sup>27</sup>When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple and stirred up all the crowd and laid hands on him, <sup>28</sup>crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.” <sup>30</sup>Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut. <sup>31</sup>And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. <sup>32</sup>He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. <sup>33</sup>Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done. <sup>36</sup>For the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!”
21.overview:
The journey to Jerusalem is a journey into known suffering. At every stop, the Spirit witnesses that chains and afflictions await. At Tyre, disciples urge Paul not to go. At Caesarea, Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and delivers the Spirit’s message with prophetic theatre: this is what Jerusalem will do to the man who owns this belt. Everyone weeps. Everyone pleads. And Paul, unmoved, asks why they are breaking his heart.

He is not reckless. He is not looking for martyrdom. He is constrained by the Spirit — the same Spirit whose warnings he hears and receives, and who nevertheless calls him forward. The will of the Lord leads into suffering. And Paul’s companions, when they cannot dissuade him, say the only thing that remains: “Let the will of the Lord be done.” This is not resignation; it is the profound submission of people who have learned that God’s purposes are not derailed by human suffering — they are often advanced through it.

Jerusalem receives Paul with joy — James and the elders glorify God over the Gentile mission. But within days the Asian Jews see Paul in the temple and the city erupts. He is dragged out, beaten, on the verge of death, and saved by Roman soldiers. As they carry him up the steps of the barracks, the crowd shouting “away with him” below, Paul asks the tribune for permission to speak. The prisoner wants to preach. He is not finished yet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Journey to Jerusalem and the Warnings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final journey to Jerusalem is framed by a series of increasingly urgent warnings: at Tyre, the disciples 'through the Spirit' tell Paul not to go to Jerusalem; at Caesarea, Agabus the prophet binds his own hands and feet with Paul's belt and declares that the Jews in Jerusalem will bind him just like this. The community's response is weeping, imploring Paul not to go. Paul's response is the response of Gethsemane: 'What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.' The community relents: 'The will of the Lord be done.'
verseByVerse.theology:
The Will of the Lord and the Cross-Shaped Life

The Caesarean community's submission to 'the will of the Lord be done' after every argument against Paul's Jerusalem journey is one of the most powerful statements of Christian relinquishment in Acts. They cannot change Paul's mind; they cannot change what the Spirit has revealed awaits him; all they can do is yield to the will of the Lord whose purposes exceed their understanding. Reformed theology sees here the Christian response to suffering that cannot be avoided: not stoic resignation but active trust, the 'Nevertheless, not my will but yours' of Gethsemane repeated in every generation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul went to Jerusalem knowing imprisonment awaited him, because the Spirit had told him to go. Obedience to the Spirit's direction sometimes leads toward suffering, not away from it. Now: The willingness to walk toward the suffering the Spirit assigns, rather than away from it, is the defining characteristic of the cross-shaped life that Paul modeled and calls his communities to follow.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail."
verseByVerse.commentary: The 'we' continues as the company sails south and east toward Jerusalem. The journey is described with the precision of a ship's log: Cos, Rhodes, Patara — the named ports mark the finality of the departure. Each port left behind is another step away from the churches of the Aegean mission and toward the Jerusalem that awaits. The directness of the route — 'by a straight course' — suggests favorable winds and providential guidance toward what Paul knows will be suffering.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo."
verseByVerse.commentary: Cyprus on the left — the island where the first missionary journey began, where Barnabas's home church was, now passed without stopping. The mission has moved beyond its first geographic horizons. Tyre, the ancient Phoenician port city, is the stopover point, and it will yield an unexpected and significant prophetic encounter while the ship unloads.

verseByVerse.quote: "And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed"
